lessons.title: V3·RC1 — Component API design and composition over configuration
lessons.summary: A component's props are a contract you will be living with for years. This sector is about designing that contract: why the tenth boolean prop is a design failure, how composition and slots replace configuration, what compound components buy you, and how discriminated unions make an invalid combination a compile error rather than a bug report.

# V3·RC1 — Component API design and composition over configuration Every component you export is a promise. Somebody will call it, ship it, and then a year later ask you to change how it behaves in one specific place. What happens next is decided almost entirely by the shape of the props you chose on the first afternoon. You have already built components that take props, pass `children`, and share state through context. Those are the mechanics. This sector is about the judgement: given a widget that has to serve eleven screens, which parts of it are props, which are slots, which are separate components, and which should not be configurable at all. Here is the failure mode you are learning to avoid, because you will recognise it immediately. A `Card` starts with `title` and `children`. Then somebody needs a subtitle, so `subtitle`. Then an icon: `icon`. Then a badge, and the badge needs a colour, so `badgeColor`. Then a variant with no padding: `noPadding`. Then one screen wants the title on the right: `titleAlign`. Six months later the props interface is forty lines long, nine of them booleans, three of them only valid in combination with each other, and the render body is a thicket of ternaries. Nobody can delete a prop because nobody knows who passes it. The interesting thing about that story is that every individual step was reasonable. Adding a prop is always the smallest possible change. The cost is never paid at the moment you add it; it is paid by the twentieth caller and by the person who has to change the layout. Composition is the alternative, and its whole argument is that a slot serves an unbounded set of futures while a boolean serves exactly one. ## Concept — the four levers You have four ways to let a caller influence a component, and they are not interchangeable. **Configuration** is a value the component interprets: `size="sm"`, `disabled`, `count={3}`. It is right when the set of choices is genuinely closed and the component owns the meaning. `size` on a button is a good prop — there are three sizes, the design system says so, and a caller inventing a fourth is a bug. **Composition** is JSX the caller supplies and the component merely places: `children`, or named slots. It is right when the content is open-ended. ```tsx // configuration: every new need is a new prop } badge="new" noPadding /> // composition: the caller brings whatever they need

Sales

Q3

new … ``` The second version has fewer props and more possibilities, which is the trade you are usually looking for. **Compound components** are the pattern that makes slots ergonomic: a parent that holds state and a set of children that read it through a private context. `Tabs`, `Tabs.List`, `Tabs.Tab`, `Tabs.Panel`. The caller controls layout and ordering; the parent controls behaviour. The context is an implementation detail — export the pieces, not the context — and the hook that reads it should throw a useful error when a piece is used outside its parent, because the alternative is an undefined-property crash three frames deeper. **Inversion** hands the caller a function or a hook instead of markup. A render prop (`children` as a function) or, better in modern React, a headless hook: `useCombobox()` returns state and prop-getters, and you write whatever DOM you like. Every serious component library eventually splits this way, because behaviour is reusable and appearance almost never is. **Ref and prop spreading** is the fifth thing, and in React 19 it got simpler: `ref` is an ordinary prop on function components. `forwardRef` is deprecated, not required, and not present in the reference answers here. A component meant to live inside somebody else's layout should accept the rest of the DOM props and spread them, and the order matters — spread first, then set what you insist on, so a caller cannot accidentally clobber your `type="button"`. **Types are part of the API.** If two props are only meaningful together, a discriminated union says so and the compiler enforces it. `{ kind: "link"; href: string } | { kind: "button"; onClick(): void }` makes "a link with an onClick and no href" unrepresentable. That is strictly better than a runtime warning nobody reads. **Controlled, uncontrolled, or both.** A `value`/`onChange` pair is controlled; `defaultValue` is uncontrolled. Most library components support both, decide which mode they are in on the first render, and never switch. Getting this wrong is the classic "a component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled" warning. ## Exercise 1 — a slot instead of a flag Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Replace a configuration prop with a slot. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex1 ``` ## Exercise 2 — defaults that make the common case free Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. An optional slot with a sensible default rendering. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex2 ``` ## Exercise 3 — a compound component Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. `Tabs` with a private context and a clear error when a piece is used outside its parent. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex3 ``` ## Exercise 4 — make invalid states unrepresentable Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. A discriminated union of props for an action that is either a link or a button. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex4 ``` ## Exercise 5 — controlled, uncontrolled, or both Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. A hybrid `Rating` that locks its mode on first render. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex5 ``` ## Exercise 6 — polymorphism and spreading order Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. A `Text` component with an `as` prop that keeps its prop types honest. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex6 ``` ## Exercise 7 — a small imperative surface Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. `ref` as a plain prop plus `useImperativeHandle` to expose exactly two methods and nothing else. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex7 ``` ## Exercise 8 — headless hook, thin component Edit `ex8/solution.tsx`. Split a disclosure into `useDisclosure` and a presentational shell that consumes prop-getters. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex8 ``` ## Challenge — the composed select Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. One component that is compound, hybrid-controlled and polymorphic at once. Honest difficulty note: no single idea here is new after ex1–ex8; the work is making three of them coexist without the parts knowing about each other. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design challenge ``` ## Review — deleting props Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. An over-configured `Alert` with nine props gets refactored into a composed API that renders byte-identical output. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design review1 ```

That asymmetry is the entire argument for keeping the surface small. The practical rule: add a prop when the component must *understand* the value, and add a slot when it only has to place it. **Booleans compose badly.** Two booleans are four states, and you have tested two of them. Three booleans are eight. When you find yourself writing `if (compact && !bordered && title)`, the props are describing a shape rather than a behaviour, and a slot or a variant union will say it better. Pay it when layout varies between call sites. # Long reading — designing the surface of a component

## The shape of the problem

React does not have an opinion about component APIs. A component is a function
from props to elements, and every constraint beyond that is one you invent. This
is a feature — it is why React outlived the frameworks that shipped a widget set
— and it is also why the same design mistakes recur in every codebase that
grows past a few dozen components.

The mistakes are not random. They follow from one structural fact: adding a prop
is a local change and removing one is a global change. A local change costs an
afternoon; a global change costs a coordination effort across teams. So the
gradient of least resistance always points toward more props, and the only thing
that stops it is a deliberate design decision made early, when nobody is
under deadline pressure yet.

## A short history of the escape hatches

Early React had `props.children` and not much else, which pushed people toward
configuration by default. Then came **higher-order components** — `withRouter`,
`connect` — which wrapped a component and injected props. HOCs solved reuse and
created three new problems: prop collisions you could not see, wrapper stacks
twelve deep in the DevTools tree, and static types that were genuinely difficult
to write.

**Render props** replaced them around 2017: instead of wrapping, pass a
function. `<Mouse render={({x, y}) => …} />` had no collisions and typed
cleanly, but nested render props produced a diagonal staircase of closures that
people called "callback hell with JSX".

**Hooks**, in 2019, made both largely unnecessary for state reuse. What survived
from the render-prop era is the *idea* — inversion of control, the caller
decides the markup — and it reappeared as the **headless component** movement:
Downshift, then Reach UI, Radix, Headless UI, React Aria. The bet those
libraries make is that behaviour (keyboard interaction, focus management, ARIA
wiring, controlled state) is worth sharing and appearance almost never is. A
decade of design-system rewrites suggests the bet is correct.

**Compound components** came from the same lineage. Ryan Florence's
`react-toggled` and Kent Dodds' teaching popularised the parent-plus-context
shape, and Radix made it the default idiom for primitives. The structure has a
real cost — more imports, less autocomplete, the possibility of a caller
arranging the pieces nonsensically — but it is the only structure that lets a
consumer put the label after the control on one screen and before it on another
without a `labelPosition` prop.

## What React 19 changed

Two changes matter here.

First, **`ref` is a prop**. Before React 19, a function component that wanted to
accept a ref had to be wrapped in `forwardRef`, which changed its type, changed
how you wrote it, and produced a second component in the tree. Now
`function Input({ ref, ...rest }: ComponentProps<"input">)` works, `forwardRef`
is deprecated, and a component that spreads props onto a DOM node forwards refs
for free. If you are reading an older codebase, the `forwardRef` wrappers are
mechanical to remove; a codemod exists.

Second, **`<Context>` is a provider**. `<ThemeContext value={theme}>` replaces
`<ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}>`. Cosmetic, but it removes one of the
small frictions that made people avoid context for genuinely local state.

React 19 also removed `defaultProps` for function components (default
parameters have been better for years), removed string refs, and removed
`propTypes` — all of which had been the "old way" of expressing parts of a
component contract. What remains is TypeScript, which is a stronger tool for
the job and now carries the whole load.

## Costs you should actually price

**Context re-renders.** A compound component's context value changes on every
state update, and every consumer re-renders. For a `Tabs` with four tabs this is
free. For a data grid with a context read by every cell it is the reason your
scroll drops frames. The mitigations are the ones from the performance sectors:
memoise the value, split the context into a rarely-changing half and a
frequently-changing half, or keep the volatile state out of context entirely and
subscribe to it.

**`cloneElement`.** The `asChild` pattern clones the child element to merge
props. `cloneElement` is not deprecated but it is discouraged, because it makes
the data flow invisible — a child receives props that appear nowhere at its call
site — and it breaks if the child is a fragment or an array. It is a reasonable
trade inside a primitive library and a poor one in application code.

**Generic polymorphic components.** `as` with a generic parameter type-checks
beautifully and compiles slowly. In a large project, deeply generic polymorphic
components are a measurable contributor to `tsc` time, and the error messages
when something does not fit are famously long. If you have three polymorphic
components, this is nothing; if every primitive in your system is polymorphic,
measure it.

**Prop-getters.** They cost a function call and an object allocation per render
and they defeat `memo` unless memoised, because they return a new object every
time. For a headless hook this is usually fine — the component consuming them is
one component, not a thousand rows — but it is worth knowing before you put a
prop-getter in a virtualised list row.

## When not to do any of this

Composition is a tool for variation. A component with exactly one call site
does not need slots, a context, or a polymorphic `as` prop; it needs to be
readable. The most common over-engineering failure in React codebases is a
private component built as if it were a public library primitive: three
sub-components, a context, a headless hook, and one consumer.

The honest test is whether the second call site exists. Before it does, the
right shape is the simple one, because you do not yet know which axis will need
to vary and any guess you make is likely wrong in a specific and annoying way.
Build the configuration version; when the third boolean shows up, that is the
signal — and refactoring configuration into composition is a mechanical change
you can do in an afternoon, whereas designing the perfect API for an unknown
future is a project that never ends.

The other genuine exception is the closed set. Do not compose what should be
constrained. A design system exists to make the wrong thing hard, and
`<Button variant="danger">` prevents a fourth variant in a way that
`<Button style={{background: "red"}}>` never will. Slots where content varies;
props where the system decides.

exercises.hints: ## Hint 1 Ask what the component actually does with `footerText`. It does not read it, it does not branch on it, it does not validate it — it puts it inside an element. Anything the component only positions can be a `ReactNode`, and then the caller can put a button, two buttons, or a paragraph with a link there without you changing anything. ## Hint 2 `footerAlign` disappears for the same reason: alignment is the caller's problem once the caller owns the content. If a caller wants a right-aligned footer they can write it: ```tsx …}> ``` ## Hint 3 The whole component is now three props and one conditional. The only decision left is how you test whether the slot was supplied — and the gate deliberately passes `0` and `""` to make sure you did not reach for `&&`. React renders `0`, so `{footer && …}` would print a bare zero; and `""` is falsy, so it would drop a footer the caller asked for.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Count the invalid combinations in the old API. `showFooter={false}` with a
`footerText` — what should happen? `showFooter` with no text? An align value
with nothing to align? Three props produce a state space where most of the
points are meaningless, and every one of them is a bug somebody can write.

## Hint 2

There is a general shape here worth naming: a `showX` boolean next to an `X`
value is almost always one optional slot. The presence of the value *is* the
boolean. This same reduction applies to `hasIcon`/`iconName`,
`showBadge`/`badgeText`, `hasAction`/`actionLabel`/`onAction`.

## Hint 3

Write the call site you want first:

```tsx
<Card title="Sales" footer={<Button>Export</Button>}>…</Card>
<Card title="Notes">…</Card>
```

Then make the component satisfy exactly that, and use `!= null` for the
presence test so both `0` and `""` count as content.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The sub-components have no props connecting them to the parent — no `selected`,
no `onSelect`. That is the point of the pattern: the caller arranges the pieces
and the wiring happens invisibly. The only mechanism React gives you for
invisible wiring down a subtree is context.

## Hint 2

Write the consumer hook once and use it in all three children, so the error
message is written once too:

```tsx
function useTabs(part: string) {
  const ctx = useContext(TabsContext);
  if (!ctx) throw new Error(`<${part}> must be rendered inside <Tabs>`);
  return ctx;
}
```

The `null` default on `createContext<TabsValue | null>(null)` is what makes the
check possible — a context with a plausible-looking default silently does the
wrong thing instead of failing.

## Hint 3

Two details left. First, the context value is an object created during render,
so memoise it (`useMemo`, dependency on the selected value) or every consumer
re-renders whenever `Tabs` re-renders for any reason. Second, in React 19 you
can render the context object directly as the provider —
`<TabsContext value={ctx}>` — though `<TabsContext.Provider>` still works.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the call site and let it dictate the design:

```tsx
<Tabs defaultValue="a">
  <TabList>
    <Tab value="a">First</Tab>
    <Tab value="b">Second</Tab>
  </TabList>
  <TabPanel value="a">…</TabPanel>
  <TabPanel value="b">…</TabPanel>
</Tabs>
```

Ask what each piece needs to know. `Tab` needs the current value and a way to
change it. `TabPanel` needs the current value only. Neither needs anything
else, so the context has exactly two members.

## Hint 2

The throwing hook is not defensive boilerplate, it is the error message. Without
it the failure is `Cannot destructure property 'value' of 'null'` pointing at a
line inside your library, which tells the caller nothing. Passing the part name
in as an argument is what lets one hook produce four different messages.

## Hint 3

On the "do not export the context" rule: if consumers can `useContext(TabsContext)`
themselves, then the shape of your internal state is public and you can never
rename `value` again. Keep it module-private, export only the components, and
if outside code genuinely needs to read the selection, expose a deliberate hook
like `useTabValue()` that you control.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt: ## Exercise 4 — make invalid states unrepresentable Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. The stub types an action element with everything optional and checks at runtime. Replace that with a discriminated union so the compiler rejects the invalid combinations. Export a type `ActionProps` and a component: ```tsx export function Action(props: ActionProps): ReactElement; ``` The three legal shapes, discriminated by a `kind` field: - `{ kind: "link"; href: string; children: ReactNode }` → renders `{children}`; - `{ kind: "button"; onClick: () => void; children: ReactNode }` → renders ``; - `{ kind: "submit"; children: ReactNode }` → renders ``. These must all be **type errors**, not runtime checks: ```tsx x // onClick not allowed here x // href not allowed here x // onClick not allowed here x // href required ``` Also include an exhaustiveness guard so that adding a fourth `kind` to the union without handling it fails to compile. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex4 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A union of object types is only *discriminated* if every member has the same
literal-typed field with a different value. That field is what TypeScript uses
to narrow inside a `switch` or an `if`, and without it you get the union's
intersection of guarantees — which is nothing useful.

## Hint 2

Narrowing looks like this, and note that inside each branch the compiler knows
different things:

```tsx
if (props.kind === "link") {
  props.href;     // string
  props.onClick;  // compile error: does not exist on this member
}
```

A `switch (props.kind)` gives you the same narrowing with less nesting.

## Hint 3

The exhaustiveness guard is the piece people forget. In the `default` branch,
assign `props` to a variable typed `never`:

```tsx
default: {
  const unhandled: never = props;
  throw new Error(`unhandled action: ${JSON.stringify(unhandled)}`);
}
```

If every member is handled, `props` has been narrowed to `never` and the
assignment is legal. Add a fourth member and it is not — the error appears at
compile time, at every switch that needs updating.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider what the runtime version in the stub actually achieves. It throws when
somebody passes `href` and `onClick` together — but only if that code path
runs, only in the environment where it runs, and only if somebody is watching.
A type error happens in the editor, before the commit, for every caller.

## Hint 2

There is a common near-miss worth avoiding: making the props one object with
all fields optional and then adding a JSDoc comment saying which combinations
are valid. Comments do not narrow. If two fields are only meaningful together,
put them in the same union member.

The general slogan is "make illegal states unrepresentable" — it predates
TypeScript by decades and shows up in every typed language's design advice.

## Hint 3

Write the type first and the component second. Once `ActionProps` is a proper
union, the component body almost writes itself: switch on the discriminant,
return the right element per branch, and let the `never` assignment in the
default branch keep future you honest.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two modes differ in exactly one place: where the displayed number comes
from. Everything else — the buttons, the labels, the `aria-pressed` logic, the
click handler calling `onChange` — is identical. Write the component once with
a single `rating` variable and make only its source conditional.

## Hint 2

Keep the internal state even in controlled mode. It costs one `useState` that
nobody reads, and it means you have no conditional hooks and no separate code
paths. The click handler becomes:

```tsx
function pick(n: number) {
  if (!isControlled) setInternal(n);
  onChange?.(n);
}
```

## Hint 3

The mode decision must be frozen. `useRef(value !== undefined).current` reads
the first render's answer and never updates, because a ref's initial value is
only used on mount. Compare that with `const isControlled = value !== undefined`,
which is re-evaluated every render and is the bug the last part of the gate
checks for.

Then `const rating = isControlled ? (value ?? lastValue) : internal;` — and
think about what `lastValue` needs to be for the "stays controlled" rule.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

You have seen the symptom of getting this wrong even if you have not built one:
"A component is changing an uncontrolled input to be controlled." React logs it
for DOM inputs; for your own components nobody logs anything, the state just
quietly resets and a user loses their selection.

## Hint 2

Ask what "controlled" means from the caller's side. It means *they* own the
value: your component is a pure function of their prop plus a callback. If your
component also changed its display on click, the caller would have two sources
of truth and they would drift — the same "derive, do not store" rule from the
lists sector, applied to a component boundary.

## Hint 3

The React state hook has a feature worth knowing here: the initial value passed
to `useState` and to `useRef` is used only on the first render and ignored on
every subsequent one. That is normally a gotcha; here it is exactly the
mechanism you want for freezing a decision at mount time.

For the last rule, hold the most recently seen defined `value` in a ref and
update it during render only when `value !== undefined`.

exercises.prompt: ## Exercise 6 — polymorphism and spreading order Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. `Text` renders whatever element the caller asks for while keeping the props typed for that element. Type-level requirements the gate checks by compiling: `` compiles, `` does not, and `` with no `as` accepts `` props. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc01_component_api_design ex6 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate problems live in this exercise and it helps to solve them
separately. The runtime problem is "render a tag whose name is in a variable" —
JSX resolves a capitalised identifier as a component, so assign to a
capitalised local and use it. The type problem is "describe props for an element
I do not know yet", which is what the generic parameter is for.

## Hint 2

```tsx
const Component = as ?? "span";
return <Component {...rest} data-tone={tone ?? "default"} />;
```

Lowercase `component` would be treated as the literal HTML tag `<component>`.
That is a real and confusing bug the first time you hit it.

## Hint 3

The `Omit` in the props type is doing load-bearing work: without it, if the
caller's element happens to have its own `tone` or `as` attribute the two
declarations collide and TypeScript produces an error that reads like a wall.

And the spread order is the last decision: `{...rest}` first means your
`data-tone` wins; `data-tone` first means the caller's does. The prompt tells
you which one it wants, and the general principle is that anything the component
guarantees goes after the spread.
exercises.importantHints: ## Hint 1 Destructuring is the mechanism that keeps `as` and `tone` off the DOM. Whatever you name in the destructuring pattern is removed from `rest`; whatever you do not name stays in it and gets spread. If `as` ends up in the DOM you will see React's "Received `true` for a non-boolean attribute" family of warnings, or a literal `as="a"` in the output. ## Hint 2 Consider the alternative design before you build this one. Radix-style `asChild` takes a single child element and clones it with merged props: ```tsx hi ``` No generics, no `ElementType`, and the caller writes the element they already understand. The cost is a `cloneElement` and a rule that children must be a single element. Knowing both designs is the point; this exercise builds the generic one because it is the one that stresses the type system. ## Hint 3 If the generic signature fights you, build it in two steps. First get it compiling with `as?: ElementType` and `rest: Record` and make the runtime correct. Then tighten the type to the generic version — the runtime does not change at all, which is a useful thing to notice about how much of this is a types-only concern.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two refs are in play and confusing them is the usual stumble. One points at the
real `<input>` and is yours, created with `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)`. The
other is the caller's, arriving as a prop, and it must end up holding your
handle object rather than a DOM node.

## Hint 2

`useImperativeHandle(ref, factory, deps)` is what connects them: React calls
your factory and assigns the result to the caller's ref, handling both the
object-ref and callback-ref forms for you.

```tsx
useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({
  focus: () => inputRef.current?.focus(),
}), []);
```

not be safe if a method closed over a prop or a piece of state — then the frozen
closure serves a stale value, and the fix is either to list the dependency or to
read the current value out of a ref inside the method.

Also: `type="search"` inputs fire the form's submit on Enter for free, so the
form's `onSubmit` handler with `event.preventDefault()` covers both the button
and the keyboard.

lessons.title: V3·RC2 — Error boundaries and failure UX
lessons.summary: An uncaught render error does not break one component — since React 16 it unmounts your entire application and leaves a white page. This sector is about what error boundaries actually catch, the four common throw sites they do not, how to place and reset them, and what a fallback should say to be worth showing.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC2 — Error boundaries and failure UX

Somewhere in your app there is a component that reads `user.profile.avatar.url`.
It has worked for eight months. Then one account has no profile, the read throws
`Cannot read properties of undefined`, and every user on that page sees a blank
white document. Not a broken avatar. The whole page.

That behaviour is deliberate, and it is worth understanding before you write any
code to work around it. Before React 16, a render error left the tree in
whatever half-updated state it happened to be in, and the app kept running with
corrupted UI — buttons that did nothing, forms that submitted the wrong thing,
money displayed incorrectly. The React team decided that a silently wrong
interface is worse than an obviously absent one, so an error that reaches the
root now unmounts everything. The white page is React telling you it does not
know what is true any more.

The escape hatch is the error boundary: a component that catches errors from its
subtree during render and renders a fallback instead. You have already handled
failure in the data-fetching sectors — a `catch` around a `fetch`, an `error`
piece of state, an error message in the JSX. That is still the right tool for
expected failures. A boundary is for the unexpected ones: the null dereference,
the bad response shape, the third-party widget that throws on a leap day.

## Concept — what is caught, what is not, and what to do about it

**A boundary is a class component**, still, in React 19. There is no hook
equivalent, because the mechanism needs a lifecycle React can call *while
unwinding a failed render*, and hooks are not available in that phase. You write
one class per project and never think about it again — or you use
`react-error-boundary`, which is that class plus the ergonomics.

```tsx
class ErrorBoundary extends Component<Props, State> {
  state: State = { error: null };

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error: Error): State {
    return { error };          // render phase: pick the fallback
  }

  componentDidCatch(error: Error, info: ErrorInfo) {
    this.props.onError?.(error, info);   // commit phase: report it
  }

  render() {
    return this.state.error ? this.props.fallback(this.state.error) : this.props.children;
  }
}
```

Two methods, two jobs. `getDerivedStateFromError` is static, runs during the
render phase, must be pure, and its only job is to return the state that makes
you render a fallback. `componentDidCatch` runs after the commit, may have side
effects, and is where logging belongs — it receives an `errorInfo` object whose
`componentStack` tells you which components were on the stack, which is
frequently more useful than the JavaScript stack.

**A boundary catches errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and
in constructors of the whole subtree below it.** That is the complete list. It
does not catch:

- **event handlers** — an `onClick` that throws runs outside React's render, so
  the exception goes to the window;
- **asynchronous code** — `setTimeout`, `requestAnimationFrame`, a `.then()`
  callback, an `await` after the first suspension point;
- **server-side rendering** — a boundary on the server does not resume the
  client's tree the way you might expect;
- **errors thrown in the boundary itself** — which propagate to the *next*
  boundary up, so a fallback that crashes takes out the page.

The gap is not an oversight; it is the definition. React can only catch what it
called. If you want an async failure to reach a boundary, you must put it back
into the render phase deliberately: catch it, store it in state, and throw it
during the next render.

**React 19 changed the reporting story.** The root options `onUncaughtError`,
`onCaughtError` and `onRecoverableError` let you install one handler per root,
which is where a real logging integration goes. React 19 also stopped
double-logging caught errors to the console, which had trained a generation of
developers to believe their boundary was not working.

**Placement is a UX decision, not a technical one.** One boundary at the root
turns a crash into a full-page error — better than white, still terrible. A
boundary per route means a broken settings page does not kill the header. A
boundary per widget on a dashboard means one failing chart shows "could not load
revenue" and the other five keep working. Every boundary you add makes failures
smaller and the code slightly noisier; the right granularity follows the
question "what would the user still like to be able to do?"

**A fallback should let the user act.** "Something went wrong" is a dead end.
The fallback that earns its place says what failed, offers a retry that actually
retries, and gives a way out — back to the dashboard, reload the page. Retrying
requires resetting the boundary's state *and* whatever caused the failure, which
is why real boundaries take reset keys.

# Reading — react/v3rc02_error_boundaries

## Notes

**Why the whole tree unmounts.** When a render throws, React unwinds the fiber
it was working on and looks up the tree for the nearest boundary. If it finds
none, it deletes the root's children. The reasoning, from the React 16 release
notes, is that leaving a corrupted UI in place is more dangerous than showing
nothing — a payments UI displaying a stale total is worse than a blank page.
Knowing this makes the boundary's job obvious: it is the place where you claim
"I know how to be correct even though my children failed."

**`getDerivedStateFromError` is static for a reason.** It runs during the render
phase, which React may abandon, restart, or run twice in development. A static
method has no `this`, cannot touch instance state, and cannot easily perform a
side effect — the API is shaped to prevent you doing logging there, because
logging during an abandoned render would fire more than once per real error.

**`componentDidCatch` runs after commit** and is the correct place for
reporting. Its second argument, `ErrorInfo`, carries `componentStack`: a
newline-separated list of the components between the throw and the boundary. In
production builds it is minified unless you ship source maps, which is worth
setting up before you need it.

**Boundaries do not catch what React did not call.** An `onClick` handler runs
in the browser's event dispatch. A `setTimeout` callback runs on the timer task.
A `.then()` runs on a microtask. In all three cases React's render stack is long
gone, so there is nothing to unwind. This is the single most common
misunderstanding about boundaries, and the fix is always the same: catch it
where it happens and re-throw it during render.

**Suspense and boundaries are siblings.** Suspense catches a thrown *promise*
and renders a fallback while it settles; an error boundary catches a thrown
*error* and renders a fallback permanently. A suspending component that then
rejects goes to the boundary. Ordering matters: put the boundary outside the
Suspense if a failure should replace the whole section, inside if only part of
it should be replaced.

**Resetting is two problems.** Clearing `state.error` is easy. Making the child
not fail again is the real work, and it usually means giving the child a new
`key` so it remounts and refetches, or changing the input that caused the
failure. A retry button that only clears the boundary's state re-renders the
same broken child and fails instantly, which looks to a user like the button is
broken.

## ex1 — the four lines that matter

The whole boundary is `getDerivedStateFromError` returning state and `render`
branching on it. Two details are easy to get wrong: the state must be able to
represent "no error" distinctly from "an error that is falsy" (use `null`, and
compare with `!== null`), and the fallback must not itself be able to throw,
because a throwing fallback escapes to the next boundary up.

## ex2 — reporting without swallowing

The point of the exercise is that `componentDidCatch` is not a `catch` block
that makes the error go away — the fallback is what does that. Reporting is a
separate, additive concern. Note that if the reporter itself throws, you have
turned a handled error into an unhandled one; wrapping the reporter call in its
own `try` is not paranoia in this one place.

## ex3 — the gap, deliberately

Running this before changing anything is the exercise. The click throws, the
boundary does nothing, and the error surfaces as an uncaught exception in the
console. Then you fix it by catching in the handler and storing the error in
state, and re-throwing it during the next render — at which point the boundary
does its job. The rethrow-in-render pattern is the general answer for every
non-render throw site.

## ex4 — reset keys

`resetKeys` is the idea `react-error-boundary` popularised: an array of values
that, when any changes, clears the error. The implementation is
`getDerivedStateFromProps` or a `componentDidUpdate` comparing the previous
array element-wise. The subtlety is the comparison: reference equality on the
array itself would reset on every render, since callers write
`resetKeys={[userId]}` inline.

## ex5 — a fallback that can act

Making the fallback a function of `{ error, reset }` rather than a fixed element
is what lets a caller write a retry button without the boundary knowing anything
about their UI. This is the render-prop shape from the component API sector,
used where it genuinely fits.

## ex6 — granularity

Three widgets, three boundaries. The measurable outcome is that a throw in one
leaves the other two mounted and interactive — which you can only assert if the
other two hold state that would be lost. That is the honest test of isolation.

## ex7 — pending versus failed

Wrapping the same child in both a `Suspense` and a boundary produces three
states rather than two, and the exercise is making all three distinguishable.
The retry has to remount the suspending child, which means changing its `key`;
clearing the boundary alone puts you straight back into the failed state,
because the cached rejected promise is still there.

## ex8 — throwing a rejection into render

```tsx
const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);
if (error) throw error;
```

Two lines, and they convert any async failure into something a boundary catches.
This is what `useErrorBoundary` in `react-error-boundary` does under the hood,
and it is worth writing once yourself so the mechanism is not magic.

## challenge — the host

The interesting decision is what a retry means for a widget that failed while
suspended: you must clear the boundary, reset any cached promise, and remount
the child, in that order, or you race yourself.

## review1 — classification

Six throw sites: render body, a lifecycle, a constructor, an event handler, a
timer, and a rejected promise. Three are caught natively, three are not, and the
repairs are all the same shape. If you can classify these six cold, you
understand boundaries.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — `Component` (`componentDidCatch`)](https://react.dev/reference/react/Component#componentdidcatch) — the reference for both boundary methods.
- [react.dev — `createRoot` options](https://react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/createRoot#createroot) — `onUncaughtError`, `onCaughtError`, `onRecoverableError`.
- [react.dev — React 19 release notes](https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19) — the error-reporting changes and the end of double-logging.
- [React 16 release post — error handling](https://legacy.reactjs.org/blog/2017/07/26/error-handling-in-react-16.html) — the original rationale for unmounting the tree.
- [`react-error-boundary`](https://github.com/bvaughn/react-error-boundary) — reset keys, `useErrorBoundary`, and the ergonomics worth copying.
- [MDN — `unhandledrejection`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/unhandledrejection_event) — the global net under everything a boundary cannot see.

# Long reading — failure as a design surface

## What actually happens when a render throws

React's work loop walks a tree of fibers, calling components and building the
next tree. When a component throws, the exception propagates out of `beginWork`
and React enters an unwind path: it walks up the fiber's return pointers looking
for a fiber that is a class component with `getDerivedStateFromError` or
`componentDidCatch` defined. If it finds one, it schedules that fiber to
re-render with the error state and discards the work below it. If it reaches the
host root without finding one, it marks the root as failed and, in the commit
that follows, deletes the root's children.

That deletion is the white page, and it is the part people find surprising.
Before React 16 the behaviour was to leave whatever had already committed in
place. In practice this produced applications that looked fine and were wrong:
half a table updated, a total from the previous state, a form bound to a stale
record. The React team's argument — stated plainly in the React 16 error
handling post — is that for the classes of application people build with React,
an inconsistent UI can cause real harm, and disappearing is the safer default.

An important consequence: a boundary does not "resume" the failed subtree. That
subtree is gone. When you reset the boundary, React mounts the children fresh,
running every effect again. Any state they held is lost. This is why resetting
often needs a deliberate refetch — the component's data was never in the
boundary, and the boundary has nothing to restore.

## Why there is still no hook

Every year someone asks for `useErrorBoundary` in core. The mechanism needs two
things hooks cannot currently provide. First, the catch has to happen during the
unwind of a *failed* render, at a point where the failing component's hooks are
in an unknown state — React cannot safely call into a hook-based component to
ask it what to do. Second, the boundary must be identifiable by React while
walking up the tree, which means a marker on the fiber type rather than
something discovered by rendering.

There have been RFCs, and the React team has said a hook-based API is possible
in principle. In the meantime the practical answer is that you write the class
once. `react-error-boundary` is that class, well-tested, plus `useErrorBoundary`
for the throw-into-render pattern and `withErrorBoundary` for wrapping. Using it
is not a failure of nerve; writing your own once, as this sector has you do, is
how you understand what it is doing.

## The evolution of the reporting story

React 16 through 18 logged caught errors to the console in addition to calling
`componentDidCatch`. The intent was that a developer should never lose an error
silently. The effect was confusion: an error your boundary handled correctly
still produced a red console message, so people concluded their boundary was
broken and added more logging. React 19 stopped the double log and introduced
the root-level `onCaughtError` and `onUncaughtError` hooks so that a project
can route everything to one place — a logging service, a breadcrumb trail, a
user-facing incident id.

`onRecoverableError` is the odd one out and the most interesting. It fires when
React hit a problem it repaired itself, and by far the most common source is
hydration mismatch: the server rendered one thing, the client another, React
threw away the server HTML for that subtree and re-rendered on the client. That
is not an exception anywhere in your code, but it is a bug, it costs real
rendering time, and before this API existed the only sign was a console warning
nobody was watching in production.

## Placement, granularity, and the cost of a boundary

A boundary costs one component in the tree and no measurable render time. So
why not wrap everything? Because a boundary is a *promise about behaviour*, and
a boundary that wraps something too small produces a fallback in a context where
a fallback makes no sense — a single table cell reading "something went wrong"
inside an otherwise perfect table is worse than a broken table.

The useful unit is the thing a user would describe as one part of the page. A
route. A dashboard widget. A modal. An embedded third-party component,
especially — an ad slot, a chat widget, a map — where the code is not yours and
the failure mode is not your fault.

There is one placement pattern worth naming: the boundary around a lazily loaded
route, whose fallback offers a reload. A chunk failing to load after a deploy is
one of the most common production errors in any single-page app, because the
user's tab is holding a build that no longer exists on the CDN. The correct
fallback for that specific case is a hard reload, and detecting it is a matter
of matching the error message against the loader's error text.

## Performance and reporting notes

`componentDidCatch` runs in the commit phase, and anything slow in it delays
paint of the fallback. Send your report asynchronously — `fetch` with
`keepalive`, or `navigator.sendBeacon` — rather than awaiting it.

Component stacks in production are minified. Uploading source maps to your error
service is the difference between a stack that names `Wr` and one that names
`RevenueChart`. This is a build-pipeline task, not a React one, and it is the
single highest-value thing you can do to make production errors actionable.

Deduplicate before you report. A boundary around a list item will happily fire
once per item, and an error loop — a fallback whose reset immediately re-throws
— can produce thousands of events in a second. Rate-limit at the reporter.

## When not to use a boundary

A boundary is not a `try/catch`, and using it as one produces bad UX. Expected
failures — a 404 for a resource, a validation error, an offline network — are
part of your domain. They have specific, useful messages and specific, useful
recoveries, and they belong in ordinary state: an `error` value, a rendered
message, a retry button that knows what it is retrying. Routing them through a
boundary flattens all of them into the same generic fallback and throws away
everything you knew about what went wrong.

A boundary is also not a retry policy. If a request fails intermittently, the
fix is retry-with-backoff at the request layer, not a boundary the user has to
click through. And it is not a validation layer: throwing during render to
signal bad props is a way of turning a type error into a runtime one.

The rule that holds up: if you can name the failure, handle it as data. Use a
boundary for the failures you cannot name — and make its fallback honest about
the fact that you did not expect this one.

## Exercise 1 — the minimal boundary Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. Write the smallest error boundary that works. Export: ```tsx export class ErrorBoundary extends Component< { children: ReactNode; fallback: ReactNode }, { error: Error | null } > {} ``` Behaviour: - while no error has been caught, render `children` unchanged; - when a descendant throws during render, render `fallback` instead; - once it has caught, it stays in the fallback state — re-rendering the same children must not put it back into the throwing state on its own. The gate mounts `Broken

}>` where `Boom` throws `new Error("boom")` from its render body, and asserts the document contains `Broken` and that the surrounding markup is still mounted. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc02_error_boundaries ex1 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is no hook for this. The class API is the mechanism, and React looks for
one specific static method on the class while unwinding a failed render — if the
method is not there, React does not know the component is a boundary and walks
straight past it.

## Hint 2

`static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` returns the next state. It runs during
the render phase, so it must be pure — no logging, no `fetch`, no `this`. The
instance's `render` then branches on that state:

```tsx
render() {
  return this.state.error !== null ? this.props.fallback : this.props.children;
}
```

## Hint 3

Two small decisions left. Initialise the state to `{ error: null }` — a class
property is the least ceremonious way, and it means you do not need a
constructor. And compare with `!== null` rather than truthiness, so a thrown
value that happens to be falsy still shows the fallback.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what React is doing when your component throws. It is midway through
building a tree, the exception unwinds out of the component call, and React
walks *up* the fiber chain asking each ancestor "are you a boundary?". Your job
is to answer yes and to supply the replacement UI.

## Hint 2

The reason the method is static is worth internalising because it explains the
whole API. React may abandon and restart a render — in development it renders
twice under StrictMode. A static, pure method can safely run more than once. A
method that logged to your error service could not. That is why reporting lives
in a *different* method, which is the next exercise.

## Hint 3

A boundary that has caught stays caught until something changes its state. That
is a feature, not a limitation: without it, React would re-render the children,
they would throw again, and you would loop. Notice that this also means "retry"
cannot be automatic — it has to be a deliberate state change, which is ex4 and
ex5.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The second boundary method exists for exactly this. `componentDidCatch(error,
info)` runs after the commit that rendered the fallback, so it is allowed to
have side effects — network calls, console output, anything.

## Hint 2

`info` is an `ErrorInfo`, and the field you want is `componentStack`: a
newline-separated list of the components between the throw and this boundary. It
is typed as `string | null | undefined` because React does not always have one,
so normalise it before handing it to the reporter.

## Hint 3

The "must not break the fallback" clause is the interesting one. If `onError`
throws inside `componentDidCatch`, that exception propagates out of the commit
and lands at the *next* boundary up — meaning your carefully handled error just
became an unhandled one. Wrapping the single call in its own `try {} catch {}`
is one of the few places where catching and ignoring is correct.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice the word "swallow" in the exercise title. There are two failure modes for
error handling and they pull in opposite directions: swallowing (the error is
handled and nobody ever learns it happened) and escalating (the handler itself
fails). A boundary that renders a fallback and reports nothing is the first.
A boundary whose reporter throws is the second.

## Hint 2

Why not report from `getDerivedStateFromError`? Because it is the render phase.
React may run it more than once for a single logical error — StrictMode's double
render in development is the everyday case — and you would get duplicate
incidents in your dashboard for one bug. The split between the two methods is
React telling you where each kind of work belongs.

## Hint 3

For the once-per-error requirement, you do not need any bookkeeping: React calls
`componentDidCatch` once per caught error per boundary. What you must avoid is
adding your own call from `render` or from an effect, both of which would fire
again on every subsequent render while the fallback is displayed.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — the event-handler gap

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. This one starts broken on purpose. Run it before you
change anything.

The stub exports a `DangerButton` whose `onClick` calls a supplied `action()`
that throws. It is rendered inside a boundary, and the boundary does nothing —
the exception reaches the window instead.

Export:

```tsx
export function DangerButton(props: {
  label: string;
  action: () => void;
}): ReactElement;
```

Make it so that when `action()` throws, the surrounding error boundary catches
it and renders its fallback — without changing the boundary, and without
wrapping `action` in something that hides the error.

Rules:

- a click whose `action()` returns normally must change nothing;
- a click whose `action()` throws must end with the boundary's fallback on
  screen;
- the error the boundary receives must be the original error object, with its
  original `message`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc02_error_boundaries ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Ask where the click handler runs. Not inside React's render — React attached a
listener, the browser dispatched an event, and your function is on the browser's
call stack. React's render loop finished long ago, so there is no in-progress
render to unwind and no ancestor chain to search. The boundary is not broken;
it was never involved.

## Hint 2

A boundary catches errors thrown *during render*. So the fix is to get the error
into a render. Catch it where it actually happens, keep it, and throw it the
next time the component renders:

```tsx
const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);
if (error) throw error;
```

## Hint 3

Two details. Setting state from the `catch` block is what schedules the render
in which the `throw` executes — the throw itself does nothing if it is not
reached. And the `throw` must sit at the top of the component body, before any
early return, so it always runs.

Also normalise: `throw "nope"` is legal JavaScript, so a `catch (e)` may hand
you something that is not an `Error`. Coerce it before storing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before writing the fix, be precise about the boundary's contract, because this
is the thing interviews probe. React can only catch what React called. Render
bodies, lifecycle methods and constructors are called by React. Event handlers,
timers, promise callbacks and `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks are called by
the browser. That single sentence predicts every case.

## Hint 2

Consider the alternatives and why they are worse. Wrapping the handler body in
a `try/catch` that shows a local error message loses the boundary's isolation
and duplicates the fallback UI at every call site. Adding a global
`window.onerror` catches it but cannot render anything in the right place in the
tree. Re-throwing into render is the only option that keeps the failure in the
component hierarchy where it happened.

## Hint 3

This pattern has a name in the ecosystem: `useErrorBoundary().showBoundary(e)`
in `react-error-boundary` is exactly these two lines. Writing it yourself once
is the point of the exercise — afterwards, reach for the library.

Extract it as a small hook if you like; the shape is `const throwToBoundary =
useThrowToBoundary()` returning a stable function you call from any `catch`.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The reset has to happen in response to a prop change while already in the error
state, which is a job for a lifecycle that sees both the previous and the next
props. `componentDidUpdate(prevProps)` is the straightforward one.

## Hint 2

The comparison is the trap. Callers write `resetKeys={[userId]}` inline, so the
array is a brand-new object on every render and `prev.resetKeys !==
this.props.resetKeys` is true every time — your boundary would clear on the
render immediately after catching and loop.

```tsx
const changed =
  a.length !== b.length || a.some((value, i) => !Object.is(value, b[i]));
```

## Hint 3

Guard the whole thing on `this.state.error !== null`, or you will call
`setState` on every update, which is harmless but wasteful and can loop if
anything upstream re-renders in response.

`Object.is` rather than `===` is a small correctness point: it treats `NaN` as
equal to itself, so a `NaN` key does not cause an infinite reset.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about why resetting on a key is the right shape at all, rather than a
`reset()` method the caller calls. The failure was caused by *something* — a
user id, a document, a filter. If that something has changed, the previous
failure is no longer relevant and there is no reason to keep showing an error.
`resetKeys` encodes "these are the inputs the failure was about".

## Hint 2

There is a second mechanism that does something similar and is worth
distinguishing: giving the boundary itself a `key`. Changing a component's key
unmounts and remounts it, which discards its state including the error. That is
blunter — it also remounts the entire subtree unconditionally — but it needs no
code at all, and for a route-level boundary keyed on the route it is often
exactly right.

## Hint 3

Consider what happens after the reset. `children` renders again from scratch,
with no memory of having failed. If the child's data-fetching is keyed on the
same value that changed, it refetches and everything works. If it is not — if
the child is going to throw again for the same reason — you get a flash of
content and then the fallback again, which is worse than not resetting. That is
the argument for tying reset keys to the actual input rather than to a counter.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Making `fallback` a function rather than an element is the render-prop shape
from the component API sector, and the reason is the same: the boundary has
information the caller needs (`error`, and a way to reset) and no business
deciding what the caller's error UI looks like.

## Hint 2

For the stable identity, define `reset` as a class property with an arrow
function rather than a method:

```tsx
reset = () => this.setState((s) => ({ error: null, attempt: s.attempt + 1 }));
```

A class property is created once per instance. A method bound in `render` with
`.bind(this)` or an inline arrow would be new every time.

## Hint 3

The remount is done with `key`, which you already know from the lists sector: a
changed key means React treats it as a different element, unmounts the old one
and mounts a new one. Wrap the children in a `Fragment` with
`key={this.state.attempt}` — a fragment is enough, you do not need a DOM node.

Use the updater form of `setState` for the increment, so two rapid clicks cannot
read the same stale `attempt`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the user's experience. They see an error, they click "Try again", and
either it works or it does not. What makes it *not* work in the naive
implementation is that clearing `state.error` re-renders the same child
component instances — same state, same refs, same everything that caused the
throw. The retry button appears broken, which is worse than not offering one.

## Hint 2

`key` is the tool React gives you for "I want this to be a genuinely new
instance". You met it as an identity rule for lists; here it is used
deliberately as a reset mechanism. React's own documentation calls this
"resetting state with a key", and it is the same idea applied to a whole
subtree.

## Hint 3

Be precise about what a remount does and does not fix. It resets component
state, re-runs mount effects, and refetches anything tied to a mount effect. It
does **not** clear a module-level cache, a promise stored outside React, or a
service-worker response. If the failure is stored somewhere outside the tree,
the retry has to invalidate that too — which is exactly the complication ex7
and the challenge build on.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — granularity on a dashboard Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. Place boundaries so one broken widget does not take out the page. The stub gives you `RevenueWidget`, `TrafficWidget` and `NotesWidget`. `NotesWidget` holds a piece of local state (a text box). One of the three throws depending on the data it is given. Export: ```tsx export function Dashboard(props: { widgets: { id: string; kind: "revenue" | "traffic" | "notes"; data: unknown }[]; }): ReactElement; ``` Behaviour: - render each widget inside a `
`; - a widget that throws during render is replaced by `

Could not load {id}

` **inside its own section**; - the other sections stay mounted, interactive, and keep their state. The gate types into the notes widget, then re-renders with data that makes the revenue widget throw, and asserts three things: revenue shows the failure message, traffic still renders, and the notes text box still contains what was typed. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc02_error_boundaries ex6 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1 The last assertion is the one that decides your design. Keeping the notes text means the notes widget must not unmount when the revenue widget fails — which means the boundary cannot be around the whole list. ## Hint 2 One boundary per widget, inside the `map`. Each one gets the fallback for its own id: ```tsx {widgets.map((w) => (
Could not load {w.id}

}>
))} ``` ## Hint 3 Watch the `key`. The boundary sits inside the section, so the section keeps the key — and because the keys are the widget ids and not indices, a widget failing does not shift its siblings' identities. That is the lists-sector rule doing real work here: with index keys, removing or reordering widgets would move the notes text into a different widget's box.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The question that decides boundary placement is always "what would the user
still like to be able to do?". On a dashboard, the answer is "read the other
five numbers". On a checkout page, the answer might be "nothing — if the total
is wrong I want the whole thing to stop", and one boundary at the top is the
right call. Granularity is a product decision expressed in component structure.

## Hint 2

Be suspicious of the reflex to wrap everything. A boundary around a table cell
produces "something went wrong" inside a table row, which is visually
incoherent. The unit should be something a user would name as a part of the
page. If you cannot write a sensible fallback for it, the boundary is too small.

## Hint 3

For the test to mean anything, the surviving widgets must hold state that would
be lost on unmount — which is why the notes box is in the fixture. When you
write isolation tests yourself, include that: asserting "the other widget is
still in the document" passes even if it was destroyed and rebuilt, and
rebuilding is exactly the failure you are trying to rule out.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three visible states and only two fallback mechanisms. `Suspense` owns pending;
the error boundary owns failed; the child owns success. Nest them so both
fallbacks can apply to the same child:

```tsx
<ErrorBoundary fallback={…}>
  <Suspense fallback={…}>
    <Child />
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>
```

## Hint 2

Think about what the retry must invalidate. Clearing the boundary's error puts
you back to rendering the child; the child calls `use()` on the *same cached
promise*, which is still rejected, and it throws again before you ever see the
loading state. The user sees the error flicker and return.

## Hint 3

So the retry has to bump the attempt number, which is both the cache key for
`load` and the `key` on the suspending child. Hold the attempt in state in
`AsyncSection`, pass it down, and use it as the boundary's `resetKeys` (or as
the key on a wrapper) so the boundary clears for the same reason the resource
changes.

Order matters in the handler: increment once, and let both the boundary reset
and the new promise fall out of that single state change.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Suspense and error boundaries are the same mechanism pointed at two different
thrown values. A component that throws a promise suspends; a component that
throws an error crashes. Both unwind the render and look up the tree for
something that knows what to do. Holding that symmetry in mind makes the nesting
question answerable instead of guesswork.

## Hint 2

Try swapping the nesting mentally. With `Suspense` on the outside and the
boundary inside, the boundary's fallback is itself inside the suspense
subtree — which means if your error UI ever suspends (an icon component that
lazily loads, say) you get the loading state again instead of the error. That is
occasionally what you want and usually a surprise, which is the argument for
boundary-outside as the default.

## Hint 3

The general lesson beyond this exercise: a retry has to invalidate every layer
that remembers the failure. Here that is the promise cache and the boundary. In
a real app it may also be a query client's cache entry, a service worker
response, or a module-level singleton. A "Try again" that only resets the
component is the most common broken retry button on the web.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You already built the escalation half in ex3: keep the error in state and
`throw` it at the top of the render. The new part is that the decision is now
conditional, so you need two pieces of state — one for the error you are going
to throw, one for the error you are going to display.

## Hint 2

Do not try to reuse one state field for both. `if (error) throw error` at the
top of the body would throw the local one too. Two fields make the intent
readable:

```tsx
const [escalated, setEscalated] = useState<Error | null>(null);
if (escalated) throw escalated;

const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);
```

## Hint 3

The unmount guard is the classic effect-cleanup problem in a new place. There is
no effect here — `start` is called from an event handler — so use a ref set in
an effect's cleanup:

```tsx
const alive = useRef(true);
useEffect(() => () => { alive.current = false; }, []);
```

and check it before every `setState` in the promise callbacks. Under StrictMode
in development the effect runs twice, so set `alive.current = true` at the top
of the effect body as well, or the second mount starts already dead.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The design question in this exercise is more interesting than the code: which
failures deserve a boundary? The rule from the briefing is that a boundary is
for failures you cannot name. A validation error has a name, a message the user
can act on, and a specific place it belongs — next to the field. Flattening it
into "Something went wrong" throws away everything you knew.

## Hint 2

That is why `escalate` is a predicate the caller supplies rather than a boolean
prop. The caller knows their error taxonomy. A common real implementation is
`(e) => !(e instanceof HttpError && e.status < 500)`: client errors are the
user's problem and get shown in place, server errors are your problem and get a
boundary plus an incident report.

## Hint 3

Note the ordering requirement hidden in "calling `start()` again clears
`error`". If you clear it after the promise settles rather than when `start`
runs, a slow retry leaves the old error on screen while showing `pending`, which
reads as two contradictory states at once. Clear it synchronously in `start`.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Decompose before you write. There is a host that maps over descriptors, and a
per-widget component that owns everything about one widget: its attempt
counter, its boundary, its Suspense, its fallback. The host should contain no
error logic at all.

## Hint 2

Inside the per-widget component, the attempt number is the single source of
truth for the retry. It is:

- the argument to `load`,
- the `useMemo` dependency that produces the promise,
- the boundary's `resetKeys`,
- the `key` on the suspending child.

One `setAttempt(n => n + 1)` therefore resets all four at once, which is what
removes the ordering problem rather than solving it.

## Hint 3

For "one report per failed attempt": `componentDidCatch` fires once per caught
error per boundary, and a reset followed by a new failure is a new caught error,
so you get this for free — provided you do not also report from an effect or
from the fallback's render.

The `optional` flag is a pure fallback-content decision. Resist making it a
different code path; it is `optional ? null : <the error UI>` inside the same
fallback function.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the user sees during a retry, frame by frame. Click. The error
must disappear immediately and be replaced by the loading state — not after the
request settles. If your implementation clears the boundary only when the new
promise resolves, there is a window where the old error is on screen while a
request is in flight, and a second click during that window does nothing
visible. Users double-click, and then triple-click.

## Hint 2

The reporting contract has a subtlety worth naming. Reporting from
`componentDidCatch` gives you one call per caught error, which is what you want.
Reporting from the fallback's render gives you one call per render of the
fallback — and the fallback re-renders whenever the host re-renders for any
unrelated reason, so a busy dashboard would produce a steady stream of duplicate
incidents. This is a real production failure mode, not a hypothetical.

## Hint 3

On `optional`: it is a small feature with a large design idea behind it. Not
every failure deserves visible acknowledgement. A recommendations strip that
fails is better absent than apologising — the user did not ask for it and does
not need to know. A revenue chart that fails must say so, because its absence
would be read as "revenue is zero". Deciding which of your widgets are which is
the actual failure-UX work; the code is four characters of ternary.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the six throw sites

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. The stub exports six components, each of which
throws `new Error(name)` from a different place:

| component        | throws from                          |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `RenderThrow`    | its render body                      |
| `EffectThrow`    | inside `useEffect`                   |
| `InitThrow`      | a `useState` lazy initialiser        |
| `ClickThrow`     | an `onClick` handler                 |
| `TimerThrow`     | a `setTimeout` callback              |
| `PromiseThrow`   | a rejected promise in an async click |

Two deliverables:

1. Export `const CAUGHT_BY_BOUNDARY: Record<string, boolean>` giving, for each
   of the six names, whether a plain error boundary wrapping it catches the
   throw with no changes to the component.
2. Repair `ClickThrow`, `TimerThrow` and `PromiseThrow` so that all three do
   reach the boundary, keeping their original error messages, and export the
   repaired versions under the same names.

Leave the three that already work alone — including `EffectThrow`, which is the
one people get wrong.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc02_error_boundaries review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Use the one-sentence rule rather than memorising a table: **React catches what
React called.** So walk each case and ask whose call stack the throw is on. A
render body: React's. A lazy `useState` initialiser: React's, during render. An
effect: React's, during the commit — which surprises people, and it is caught.

## Hint 2

The three that leak all leak for the same reason, and take the same repair —
the pattern from ex3. Catch at the throw site, store, re-throw during render.
For the timer, the `try` has to be *inside* the callback, not around
`setTimeout`, which returns immediately.

## Hint 3

The async one has two shapes and only one is right. `promise.catch(e =>
throwToBoundary(e))` works. `try { doAsync() } catch {}` around a call that
returns a promise catches nothing, because the rejection happens after the
function returned. If the handler is `async`, `try { await doAsync() } catch`
does work — and is the cleanest version.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The interesting entry to this exercise is `EffectThrow`, because most people
guess wrong. Effects run in the commit phase, synchronously called by React,
inside React's own error handling. So a throw in a `useEffect` body *is* caught
by a boundary. What is not caught is a throw inside a callback the effect
scheduled — a timer, a listener, a `.then` — because by then React's stack is
gone. The distinction is between the effect and what the effect starts.

## Hint 2

For the repairs, notice you are writing the same three lines three times. That
is the signal to extract the hook, and it is precisely why
`react-error-boundary` exposes `useErrorBoundary().showBoundary`. Writing the
extraction yourself makes the library's API obvious rather than magical.

## Hint 3

One thing to check when you think you are done: does a *successful* click still
work? A common regression is wrapping the handler so broadly that the normal
path also passes through the error state, or leaving a stale error in state so
the second render throws even though nothing failed. Clear or never-set is the
rule — the state should only ever hold an error you intend to throw.

lessons.title: V3·RC3 — Accessibility: focus management, roles and keyboard interaction
lessons.summary: Screen readers do not read your DOM, they read the accessibility tree, and a div with an onClick is invisible in it. This sector covers what that tree contains, how to give a control a name and a role, and the part React makes uniquely your problem: deciding where focus goes when the UI changes underneath the user.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC3 — Accessibility: focus management, roles and keyboard interaction

A `<div onClick={…}>` looks like a button, behaves like a button for a mouse
user, and does not exist for anybody else. It is not in the tab order. It has no
role, so a screen reader announces nothing useful. Space and Enter do nothing.
It cannot be reached by a switch device or by voice control saying "click
Submit", because it has no name.

Replacing it with `<button>` fixes every one of those in one edit, and that is
the shape of most accessibility work: the platform already implemented this, and
you opted out by accident.

The part that is genuinely yours is focus. In a server-rendered application, the
browser manages focus: you click a link, a new document loads, focus resets to
the top, and the user starts again. In a single-page app nothing loads.
Something opens, something closes, a list re-filters under the user's cursor,
and if you do not say where focus should go, it stays wherever it was — often on
an element you just removed from the DOM, at which point the browser moves focus
to `<body>` and a keyboard user is silently teleported to the top of the page.

You have the tools for this already. Refs give you the DOM node. Effects give
you a moment after commit to act. `useId` gives you the stable identifiers that
`aria-labelledby` and `aria-describedby` need. What this sector adds is the
contract: what a name is, what a role promises, and which keys a widget is
required to handle.

## Concept — the tree, the name, and the focus

**The accessibility tree is a parallel structure** the browser builds from the
DOM and exposes to assistive technology. Each node in it has a **role** (what
kind of thing this is), a **name** (what it is called), a **description**
(supplementary detail), and a set of **states and properties** (`expanded`,
`checked`, `disabled`, `current`). Every accessibility decision you make is a
decision about one of those four.

**Semantics come free with the right element.** `<button>` is
`role="button"`, focusable, and Enter/Space-activated. `<a href>` is a link and
Enter-activated. `<input type="checkbox">` carries a checked state the browser
maintains. The first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA. `<div role="button"
tabIndex={0} onKeyDown={…}>` is four things you had to remember, versus zero.

**A name comes from one of four places**, in priority order:
`aria-labelledby`, then `aria-label`, then the element's own content, then —
for form controls — a `<label>` associated by `htmlFor`. `title` is a fallback
so weak it should be treated as no name at all. An icon-only button has no
content, so it needs an explicit name:

```tsx
<button type="button" aria-label="Close dialog" onClick={close}>
  <XIcon aria-hidden="true" />
</button>
```

The `aria-hidden` on the icon matters — without it, a decorative SVG can
contribute stray text to the name.

**States are attributes, and they must be kept true.** `aria-expanded` on a
disclosure trigger, `aria-selected` on a tab, `aria-current="page"` on the
active nav link, `aria-checked` on a custom checkbox. A state attribute that
does not track the actual state is worse than none: it actively lies.

`disabled` and `aria-disabled` are not the same thing. `disabled` removes the
element from the tab order entirely, so a keyboard user cannot reach it and will
never learn why it is off. `aria-disabled="true"` keeps it focusable and
announces it as unavailable, which is usually the better experience for a submit
button that is waiting on a required field.

**Focus is a single, global, document-level thing** and your job is to say
where it goes at every transition:

- opening a dialog → move focus into it, usually to the first control or to the
  dialog itself;
- closing it → return focus to the element that opened it, which means you had
  to remember that element;
- deleting the focused item from a list → move focus to its neighbour before
  removing it, not after;
- navigating in an SPA → move focus to the new page's heading, or the browser
  gives it to `<body>` and Tab starts from the top.

**Composite widgets have a keyboard contract** you do not get to invent. A
tablist moves between tabs with Left/Right and is a single tab stop. A menu
opens with Enter or Down, moves with Up/Down, closes with Escape and returns
focus. These are written down in the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, and
"written down" is the important part: users have learned them from every other
application on their machine.

Two implementations of "one tab stop, arrows move within": **roving tabindex**,
where exactly one child has `tabIndex={0}` and the rest have `-1`, and DOM focus
actually moves; and **`aria-activedescendant`**, where DOM focus stays on a
container and an attribute points at the active child. Roving is right for
toolbars and tablists; activedescendant is right for a combobox, where focus
must stay in the text field so typing keeps working.

platform, and give an icon-only control a name.
