# Reading — react/v3rc03_accessibility_focus

## Notes

**The accessibility tree is computed, not authored.** The browser derives it
from the DOM: element type, attributes, CSS visibility, and the ARIA overrides
you supplied. This is why `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` remove a node
from it while `opacity: 0` and `clip-path` do not — the first two remove the box
from the layout, the last two only make it invisible to eyes. A visually hidden
label that must still be read uses the clip technique precisely because
`display: none` would remove it from the tree.

**Name computation has a defined algorithm** (accname). The short version that
covers 95% of cases: `aria-labelledby` wins, then `aria-label`, then contents,
then `<label for>`, then `title`. Two consequences people trip on:
`aria-labelledby` overrides visible text, so a mismatch means voice-control
users say a word that does not work; and content-derived names include the text
of nested elements, so a decorative icon with a `<title>` can corrupt a name.

**`aria-hidden` and focusability must never overlap.** An element that is
`aria-hidden="true"` but still tabbable creates a focus stop that does not exist
in the accessibility tree — a screen reader user tabs into a void. Browsers now
warn about this in DevTools. The fix is either `inert` (which removes focusability
too) or removing it from the tab order explicitly.

**Effects are where focus moves.** The DOM node has to exist before you can
focus it, which means after commit — so `useEffect` or `useLayoutEffect`, never
during render. Prefer `useLayoutEffect` when the move must happen before the
browser paints, which is the case for opening a dialog; a `useEffect` can show
one painted frame with focus still behind the overlay.

**Remembering the opener is your job.** `document.activeElement` at the moment
the dialog opens is the element to restore to. Capture it in a ref in the same
effect that moves focus in, and restore in that effect's cleanup so it runs
however the dialog closed — Escape, backdrop click, a router navigation, an
error boundary unmounting the whole thing.

**Roving tabindex versus activedescendant.** Roving moves real DOM focus, so
`:focus-visible` works, the browser scrolls the item into view, and everything
behaves normally — at the cost of managing `tabIndex` on every child.
Activedescendant leaves focus on the container and points an attribute at the
active item, which is the only option when focus must remain in a text input.
Its cost is that you must scroll the active item into view yourself and style
the "active" item without `:focus`.

**Live regions announce mutations, not existence.** A region added to the DOM
already containing text is often not announced at all, because the screen reader
saw no change. Render the empty region first and put text into it later. Use
`aria-live="polite"` for anything that is not urgent — `assertive` interrupts
whatever the user is currently hearing, and interrupting is nearly always the
wrong call.

## ex1 — the element does the work

Swapping a `div` for a `button` restores role, tab order, Enter/Space
activation, and the platform's own focus ring. The second half of the exercise
is the name: an icon-only button has no text content, so it needs `aria-label`,
and the icon needs `aria-hidden="true"` so it cannot contribute to the name.
Also `type="button"` — inside a form, a button without a type submits it.

## ex2 — three attributes and one hook

`useId` produces an identifier that is stable across renders and unique per
instance, and — importantly for SSR — matches between server and client.
`htmlFor` connects the label; `aria-describedby` connects the error message so
it is read after the name; `aria-invalid` marks the field as failing. Only set
`aria-describedby` when the description exists — pointing at a missing id is
silently ignored, which hides the bug.

## ex3 — a state attribute that stays true

`aria-expanded` goes on the *trigger*, not the panel, because it describes the
control's state. `aria-controls` points at the panel's id. The design question
is whether the collapsed panel is in the DOM: `hidden` keeps it there, removed
from the tree, with its content still costing render work; conditional
rendering removes it entirely, which is cheaper and loses any state inside it.

## ex4 — the two halves of dialog focus

Moving focus in is the half everybody does. Restoring it is the half that gets
skipped, and its absence is why a keyboard user who closes a dialog finds
themselves at the top of the page. Restoring in the effect's *cleanup* is what
makes it robust: it runs no matter how the dialog went away.

## ex5 — the page behind

`inert` is the modern answer and it does exactly what you want: everything
inside is unfocusable, unclickable, and hidden from assistive technology.
`<dialog>` with `showModal()` gets it for free. When you cannot use either, a
trap is a keydown handler on Tab that wraps from the last focusable element to
the first — and the interesting part is computing "focusable", which is a
longer list than people expect and has to exclude the currently hidden.

## ex6 — roving

Exactly one child has `tabIndex={0}` at any time. Arrow keys move the index and
then call `.focus()` on the new node — both, because changing the attribute does
not move focus. The bookkeeping trap is a list that shrinks: if the focused
index is now past the end, clamp it, or you have a toolbar with no tab stop at
all.

## ex7 — the polite announcement

The region must be in the DOM, empty, before the message arrives. Focus must
not move — moving focus to announce something interrupts the user and loses
their place, which is exactly the behaviour live regions were invented to avoid.

## ex8 — activedescendant

DOM focus never leaves the input, so typing keeps working while the "focused"
option changes. The attribute on the input points at the option's id; the option
gets a visual treatment that is not `:focus`. You must also handle scrolling the
active option into view, because the browser has no reason to.

## challenge — the state machine

The menu button's contract is a small state machine: closed, open with an item
focused, open with nothing focused. Enter and Down open with the first item;
Up opens with the last; Escape closes and restores focus to the button; Tab
closes and moves on. Writing it as an explicit reducer is easier to keep correct
than a pile of booleans.

## review1 — the five faults

They are all real ones you will meet: a positive `tabIndex`, an `aria-hidden`
around a focusable control, a `disabled` that should be `aria-disabled`, a
placeholder used as a label, and a `role` that contradicts its element.

## Further reading

- [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/) — the keyboard contracts, pattern by pattern.
- [MDN — ARIA states and properties](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/Attributes) — the reference for every attribute in this sector.
- [MDN — `inert`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/inert) — the modern way to make everything behind a modal untouchable.
- [react.dev — `useId`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useId) — stable ids for label and description wiring, SSR included.
- [MDN — ARIA live regions](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Live_Regions) — polite, assertive, and why timing matters.
- [Testing Library — about queries](https://testing-library.com/docs/queries/about/#priority) — the query priority ladder, which is an accessibility checklist in disguise.

# Long reading — the tree you cannot see

## How the accessibility tree is actually built

The browser maintains a second tree alongside the DOM. Each node in it maps to
a platform accessibility object — IAccessible2 on Windows, NSAccessibility on
macOS, AT-SPI on Linux — which is what a screen reader actually talks to. The
mapping is defined by specifications: HTML-AAM says what role each HTML element
gets, Core-AAM says how a role maps to each platform's API, and accname
specifies exactly how a name is computed.

Several things follow from that layering. Nodes with no semantic value are
pruned, which is why a wrapper `div` does not appear. CSS participates: a node
that generates no box is not in the tree, which is why `display: none` and
`visibility: hidden` remove it and why `content` from `::before` can *add* text
to a name. And the tree is recomputed as the DOM mutates, which is what live
regions listen to.

The practical consequence for React developers is that the tree is downstream of
everything, and you cannot inspect it by reading JSX. Chrome DevTools has an
Accessibility pane showing the computed role, name and properties for the
selected node, and it is the fastest way to settle an argument about whether a
label is working.

## Where ARIA came from, and why so much code is wrong

ARIA was standardised in 2014 for a web that had already outgrown HTML 4. There
was no `<dialog>`, no `<details>`, no `<input type="date">`, no way to say "this
div is a tab". Everyone building an application-like interface built it out of
divs and spans, and ARIA was the retrofit that let those divs claim semantics.

The retrofit worked, and it left a decade of tutorials teaching people to write
`role="button"` on a div — advice that was correct in 2012 and is now a mistake,
because `<button>` gives you the role plus focusability plus key handling plus
the platform's focus indicator. The first rule of ARIA — "do not use ARIA" —
exists because ARIA is a promise: `role="checkbox"` tells assistive technology
this element behaves like a checkbox, and if you have not implemented Space,
`aria-checked`, and a focus stop, you have lied. A wrong role is worse than no
role, because no role at least leaves the user's expectations intact.

The categories where ARIA is still genuinely necessary are shrinking but real:
composite widgets with no HTML equivalent (comboboxes, tree grids, menus), live
regions, relationships across the tree (`aria-describedby`,
`aria-controls`), and states that HTML does not model (`aria-expanded`,
`aria-current`).

## Focus order, visual order, and CSS

Tab order follows DOM order for elements with `tabIndex` of `0` or a default
focusable element type. It does not follow visual order. Flexbox `order`, grid
placement, `row-reverse`, and absolute positioning can all put a visually-first
element last in the DOM, and a keyboard user then tabs through the interface in
an order that does not match what they see. Sighted keyboard users — a much
larger group than screen reader users — find this genuinely disorienting.

The rule is that DOM order should match reading order, and CSS should be used
for presentation within that constraint. Where a design forces a mismatch, the
answer is to change the DOM, not to reach for positive `tabIndex` values, which
create a separate "tabindex-ordered" pass through the document that runs before
everything else and is essentially always a mistake.

`inert` is the newer piece of this puzzle and is now available everywhere. It
makes a subtree unfocusable, unclickable and invisible to assistive technology
in one attribute, which is precisely what "there is a modal in front of this"
means. Before it, everyone hand-rolled focus traps, and the hand-rolled versions
mostly did not handle the browser's own UI, iframes, or shadow DOM correctly.
The native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()` gives you inertness, an Escape
handler, and the top layer for free, and is the right starting point for any new
modal.

## Cost and performance

Accessibility work is cheap at build time and free at runtime, with two
exceptions worth knowing.

First, live regions on high-frequency updates. A region that changes many times
a second queues an announcement per change, and screen readers handle the
backlog differently — some interrupt, some queue, some drop. Throttle updates to
a live region to something a human can follow, on the order of one message per
second or slower.

Second, very large trees. The accessibility tree is recomputed as the DOM
mutates, and a 50,000-node DOM is expensive for assistive technology to
navigate as well as for the browser to maintain. Virtualisation helps both, but
virtualised lists need `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` so the user is told
"item 12 of 4,000" rather than "item 12 of 20".

## When not to reach for ARIA

If a native element exists, use it. `<details>`/`<summary>` for a disclosure,
`<dialog>` for a modal, `<select>` for a single-select, `<input type="date">`
where the native picker is acceptable. The native versions come with keyboard
handling, focus behaviour, mobile affordances and platform conventions you would
otherwise reimplement badly.

The honest counterweight is that native elements are hard to style — `<select>`
in particular has been the standard example for twenty years, though
`appearance: base-select` is beginning to change that. That is a real design
constraint and sometimes it wins. What should not happen is reaching for the
custom version by reflex, without having established that the native one cannot
be made to look right.

And do not add ARIA to compensate for a structure that is wrong. If you find
yourself writing `aria-label` on a `div` to explain what it is, the question to
ask is what element that div should have been. ARIA describes; it does not fix.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count what the div lost by not being a button: the role, the tab stop, Enter
activation, Space activation, the platform focus ring, and the ability of voice
control to say "click Delete invoice 42". You could add all six by hand with
`role`, `tabIndex` and an `onKeyDown` that special-cases two keys — or you can
change one tag name.

## Hint 2

An icon-only control has no text content, so the name has to come from
somewhere else. `aria-label` supplies it directly. The icon itself needs
`aria-hidden="true"` so that if it ever contains a `<title>` element, that text
cannot leak into the computed name.

## Hint 3

The form clause is the detail people miss. A `<button>` with no `type` inside a
form defaults to `type="submit"` — so an unrelated delete button submits the
form when pressed. Always write the type explicitly on a button that is not
meant to submit.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Rather than starting from the fix, start by predicting the failures. Render the
stub, press Tab, and note that the control is skipped entirely. Then imagine a
screen reader reading the page: it encounters a group with no role and no name,
and there is nothing to say. Then imagine voice control: "click delete" matches
nothing, because matching is done on the accessible name.

## Hint 2

The general principle is that HTML elements are not markup, they are behaviour.
`<button>` is a bundle of interaction contracts the browser implements and every
assistive technology already understands. Opting out of it means reimplementing
that bundle, and the reimplementation is always incomplete — most hand-rolled
div-buttons handle Enter and forget Space, because a mouse-using developer never
notices.

## Hint 3

Two smaller points worth carrying forward. First, do not add `role="button"` to
an actual `<button>`; a redundant role is noise and occasionally overrides
something useful. Second, resist the urge to add a `tabIndex={0}` — a button is
already in the tab order, and adding it suggests to a reader that something
unusual is happening.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You need identifiers that are unique per component instance and stable across
renders. Generating them with a counter or `Math.random()` breaks server
rendering, because the server and the client produce different values and
hydration complains. React has a hook for exactly this.

## Hint 2

`useId()` returns one identifier; derive the rest from it rather than calling
the hook three times:

```tsx
const id = useId();
const hintId = `${id}-hint`;
const errorId = `${id}-error`;
```

## Hint 3

`aria-describedby` takes a space-separated list of ids, and the order is the
order they are announced. Build the list from the descriptions that actually
exist, join it, and — this is the part the gate checks — pass `undefined`
rather than an empty string when the list is empty, so React omits the
attribute entirely.

## Hint 1 Think about what a screen reader user hears when they tab into this field. They get the name ("Email"), then the role ("edit text"), then the state ("invalid entry" if `aria-invalid` is set), then the description. If the error message is just a red `

` sitting nearby with no association, they hear nothing about it and have no idea why the form will not submit. ## Hint 2 Two associations are easy to confuse. `

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Decide first which element carries which attribute. `aria-expanded` describes
the *control*, so it goes on the button — a very common error is putting it on
the panel, where it means something else entirely. `aria-controls` also goes on
the button and points at the thing it controls.

## Hint 2

Labelling the region from the trigger is what makes `getByRole("region", { name
})` work: give the button an id and put `aria-labelledby={buttonId}` on the
region. That is one id used in two directions, which is normal for this pattern.

## Hint 3

The `aria-expanded={false}` versus absent distinction matters. In React,
`aria-*` attributes with a boolean value are rendered as the strings `"true"`
and `"false"` — unlike, say, `hidden`, where `false` removes the attribute. So
passing the boolean directly does the right thing here; passing `undefined`
would not.

For the render-nothing-while-closed rule, this is the conditional-rendering
point from the render-performance drills: `hidden` still builds and commits the
subtree and runs its effects.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before writing anything, consider whether you need this component at all.
`<details>` and `<summary>` are a native disclosure with keyboard handling,
state, and correct semantics, and they need no JavaScript. The reasons to build
your own are animation control and styling the marker; both are real, and both
are worth being deliberate about rather than reflexive.

## Hint 2

There is a genuine design trade in "render nothing while closed" that the
prompt settles for you but which you should be able to argue either way. Not
rendering is cheaper and means no effects run — no requests fired for a panel
nobody opened. Rendering with `hidden` keeps any state inside the panel alive
across open/close cycles, which matters if the panel contains a half-filled
form.

## Hint 3

A state attribute that drifts from reality is worse than no attribute, because
it actively misinforms. The way to keep them honest is to derive every attribute
from the same single piece of state in the same render — never to set them in an
effect, and never to keep a second copy. If you find yourself writing
`setExpanded(true)` and separately setting an attribute, the design has already
gone wrong.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate jobs. Moving focus in needs the DOM node, which exists only after
commit — so an effect, not the render body. Restoring focus needs to remember
which element had it *before* you moved it, which means capturing
`document.activeElement` at the top of that same effect, before you call
`focus()`.

## Hint 2

Put the restore in the effect's cleanup:

```tsx
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const opener = document.activeElement as HTMLElement | null;
  ref.current?.focus();
  return () => opener?.focus();
}, []);
```

Cleanup runs on unmount no matter why the unmount happened, which is exactly the
robustness the last requirement is testing.

## Hint 3

Two details. A `<div>` is not focusable, so it needs `tabIndex={-1}` — the one
legitimate non-zero tabIndex value, meaning "focusable by script, not by Tab".
And `useLayoutEffect` rather than `useEffect`: the move happens before the
browser paints, so there is never a frame showing the dialog with focus still
behind it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The half everybody implements is moving focus in. The half that gets skipped is
putting it back, and its absence produces a specific, miserable experience: a
keyboard user opens a dialog from a button halfway down a long page, closes it,
and finds themselves at the very top of the document with no idea where they
were. Every Tab from there walks the whole page again.

## Hint 2

Notice that `onClose` is the wrong place to restore focus, even though it looks
like the obvious one. A dialog can disappear for reasons that never touch
`onClose`: a route change, a parent's state update, an error boundary catching
something. Attaching the restore to the *unmount* rather than to the close
handler covers all of them with less code.

## Hint 3

There is a judgement call in where focus lands on open. Focusing the dialog
container announces the dialog's name and role, then lets the user Tab forward
into it — good for a confirmation dialog. Focusing the first input skips
straight to the task — good for a form. Focusing a destructive default button
is almost always wrong, because Enter is the key people press to dismiss things.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — nothing behind the dialog

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. Stop Tab escaping a modal into the page behind it.

Export:

```tsx
export function ModalLayer(props: {
  backgroundRef: RefObject<HTMLElement | null>;
  children: ReactNode;
}): ReactElement;
```

Requirements:

- while mounted, the element in `backgroundRef` is `inert` — set the property,
  restore its previous value on unmount;
- additionally implement a Tab trap inside the layer, because `inert` may be
  unsupported and because content inside the layer still needs wrapping: Tab on
  the last focusable element moves to the first, Shift+Tab on the first moves to
  the last;
- "focusable" means, inside the layer: `a[href]`, `button`, `input`, `select`,
  `textarea`, `[tabindex]` — excluding anything `disabled`, anything with
  `tabindex="-1"`, and anything not currently rendered;
- the trap must recompute the focusable list on each Tab, because the layer's
  contents can change.

The gate renders three buttons in the background and two in the layer, tabs
forward past the last, asserts focus wrapped to the first layer button, tabs
backward from the first, asserts it wrapped to the last, and asserts the
background element has `inert` set while open and not after close.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc03_accessibility_focus ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Understand what problem the trap solves before building it. Focus escaping a
modal is not a cosmetic issue: a keyboard user Tabs past the last button and
lands on a link behind the overlay that they cannot see. They press Enter and
navigate somewhere unexpected. The modal is still on screen, so nothing about
what they see explains what happened.

## Hint 2

There is a strong argument for not writing this at all. The native `<dialog>`
element with `showModal()` gives you inertness of everything behind it, the top
layer so nothing can overlap it, an Escape handler, and a backdrop
pseudo-element — all from the platform, all correct. Building the trap here is
to understand the mechanism; in production, start with `<dialog>` and only
hand-roll when you have a specific reason.

## Hint 3

Two traps within the trap, so to speak. First, a trap with no way out is a cage:
Escape must always work, and it is not part of this exercise only because ex4
already handled it. Second, restore the background's *previous* `inert` value
rather than assuming it was `false` — nested modals exist, and blindly clearing
it when the inner one closes re-enables a page that the outer one still wants
inert.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"One tab stop" is the requirement that shapes everything. A toolbar of eight
buttons that are each a tab stop means eight Tab presses to get past it, and
users with a dozen toolbars on a page give up. The convention across every
desktop application is Tab to enter, arrows to move within, Tab to leave.

## Hint 2

You need an array of refs to call `focus()` on:

```tsx
const refs = useRef<(HTMLButtonElement | null)[]>([]);
// in the map:
ref={(node) => { refs.current[index] = node; }}
```

Setting `tabIndex` does not move focus — it only decides where Tab would land.
Both have to happen.

## Hint 3

The clamp is the requirement that catches people. If the active index is 5 and
the list becomes 3 items long, `tabIndex={0}` is assigned to nothing and Tab
skips the whole toolbar. Deriving the effective index during render —
`Math.min(active, items.length - 1)` — is simpler and less error-prone than an
effect that corrects the state after the fact.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The pattern's name is "roving tabindex", and its defining property is that real
DOM focus moves. That is what gives you the browser's focus ring, automatic
scroll-into-view, and correct behaviour with browser find. The alternative —
`aria-activedescendant`, which ex8 covers — leaves focus in one place and points
an attribute at the active item, and you give up all three of those.

## Hint 2

Think about what the arrow handler owes the page. If you do not call
`preventDefault`, ArrowRight and ArrowLeft still do their default job in some
contexts and Home/End scroll the document to top and bottom — so pressing End in
your toolbar jumps the page to the footer while also moving the toolbar's
selection. Prevent the default only for the keys you actually handled; swallowing
every keydown breaks things you did not think about.

## Hint 3

A design question worth deciding consciously: should the arrows wrap around from
last to first? The APG allows either and says to be consistent. This exercise
specifies clamping, which is the more common choice for toolbars because it
gives a tactile sense of the ends. Menus and listboxes more often wrap. What is
not acceptable is doing one in one widget and the other in a widget beside it.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The requirement that the region exists while empty is not arbitrary. A live
region announces *changes* to its contents. If you render the region and its
text in the same commit, many screen readers see a new subtree rather than a
mutation and say nothing at all. The region has to be there first, watching.

## Hint 2

`role="status"` is `aria-live="polite"` plus `aria-atomic="true"` in one
attribute; `role="alert"` is the assertive equivalent. Using the roles rather
than the raw attributes is shorter and communicates intent. For the error case
you want assertive, so render a different element with `role="alert"` rather
than trying to flip `aria-live` on the same node — changing the politeness of a
live region while it is live is not reliably implemented.

## Hint 3

Visually hidden must mean *visually only*. `display: none` and `visibility:
hidden` remove the node from the accessibility tree, so nothing is announced.
The clip technique keeps a 1×1 box in the layout:

```tsx
const srOnly: CSSProperties = {
  position: "absolute",
  width: 1, height: 1,
  margin: -1, padding: 0,
  overflow: "hidden",
  clipPath: "inset(50%)",
  whiteSpace: "nowrap",
};
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from what the user is doing. They typed a query and are waiting. If you
move focus to the results to "announce" them, you have yanked them out of the
input mid-thought, and if they wanted to refine the query they must Shift+Tab
back. Live regions exist precisely so you can say something without taking
control.

## Hint 2

Politeness is a real decision with a real cost. `assertive` interrupts whatever
the screen reader is currently saying — including the user's own navigation
feedback. Reserve it for things that genuinely cannot wait: a session about to
expire, a submission that failed, a destructive action confirmed. "Your results
loaded" is not one of those, and using assertive for it trains users to dread
your page.

## Hint 3

A trap that bites in practice: rapid updates. A live region wired to a
keystroke-by-keystroke search fires an announcement per keystroke, and screen
readers handle the backlog inconsistently — some queue every one, so the user
hears a minute of stale counts. Announce on settled results, not on every
intermediate state. This exercise's `status` prop already does that for you;
notice that it is a design decision, not an accident.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Ask why roving tabindex cannot be used here. Moving DOM focus to an option
means the input no longer has focus, which means the next character the user
types goes nowhere. A combobox has to keep focus in the text field, so it needs
a way to say "this option is active" that is not focus.

## Hint 2

`aria-activedescendant` is that way. It lives on the focused element and holds
the **id** of the active descendant:

```tsx
<input
  role="combobox"
  aria-activedescendant={open ? filtered[activeIndex]?.id : undefined}
/>
<li id={option.id} role="option" aria-selected={index === activeIndex}>
```

The ids have to be real ids on the option elements — this is a DOM reference,
not an index.

## Hint 3

Two things the browser will not do for you because focus never moved. It will
not scroll the active option into view, so call
`element.scrollIntoView({ block: "nearest" })` from an effect keyed on the
active index. And `:focus` will never match an option, so the "active" styling
has to hang off the `aria-selected` attribute or a class you set yourself.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The clean way in is to notice that this widget has two independent notions of
"where I am". There is DOM focus, which the browser owns and which must stay on
the input. And there is the widget's own cursor through the option list, which
is your state. Keeping those two separate in your head is most of the work; the
attributes are just how you publish the second one.

## Hint 2

Before building a combobox, always ask whether `<select>` or an `<input
list=…>` with a `<datalist>` would do. Both are native, keyboard-complete on
every platform, and free. The reasons to hand-roll are async options, rich
option content, multi-select, and full styling control — all real, and all worth
naming explicitly rather than assuming.

## Hint 3

Watch the reset rule. If the user has ArrowDown'ed to the fourth option and then
types another character, the filtered list is different and index 3 may not
exist or may be a completely unrelated entry. Resetting the active index to 0
whenever the filtered list changes is the least surprising behaviour, and doing
it by deriving from the query rather than in an effect avoids a render where
the index points at nothing.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Model the state explicitly before writing JSX. There is `open` and there is
"which item is active", but the opening transitions carry *intent*: ArrowUp
means "open, and the active item is the last one". Trying to express that with
`setOpen(true)` followed by `setActive(items.length - 1)` works, but only if
both land in the same render — which they do in React 19, and which is worth
knowing rather than assuming.

## Hint 2

Two derived helpers make the rest short. First, the list of enabled indices:

```tsx
const enabled = items.flatMap((item, i) => (item.disabled ? [] : [i]));
```

Then every movement is an operation on a position within `enabled`, not within
`items`, and the "skip disabled" rule stops appearing in five separate places.

## Hint 3

Focus is moved with an effect, not in the handler, because the item must be
mounted before you can focus it — on the render that opens the menu, the items
did not exist when the handler ran. An effect keyed on `[open, activeIndex]`
that calls `refs.current[activeIndex]?.focus()` covers both the initial open and
every subsequent move with one piece of code.

Escape and Tab both close; the difference is that Escape returns focus to the
trigger and Tab must not, or you would trap the user.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the contract as a specification of user expectations, not a checklist.
Every one of those key bindings exists because the user learned it somewhere
else — from their operating system's menus, from every other application. A menu
that closes on Escape but does not return focus is not "mostly right"; it is a
menu that loses the user's place, which is the specific thing menus must not do.

## Hint 2

The disabled-item requirement is a good example of `aria-disabled` earning its
keep. With `disabled`, the item is out of the tab order and out of arrow-key
reach, so a keyboard user never learns it exists — they see a menu with three
items where a mouse user sees five. With `aria-disabled`, it is announced as
unavailable. This exercise then adds the twist that arrow movement should still
skip it, which is what the APG recommends for menus specifically.

## Hint 3

If the state machine is fighting you, write it as a reducer with named actions:
`OPEN_FIRST`, `OPEN_LAST`, `MOVE_NEXT`, `MOVE_PREV`, `HOME`, `END`, `CLOSE`.
Each action becomes three lines, the invalid transitions become impossible
rather than merely unlikely, and reading the reducer tells you the contract
without reading the JSX. A pile of `useState` calls for the same thing is where
"open but nothing focused" bugs come from.

The stub exports a `FilterPanel` that renders and looks correct and contains five specific accessibility faults: 1. a wrapper carries `aria-hidden="true"` while containing a focusable button; 2. the "Apply" button uses `disabled` while a required field is empty, so a keyboard user cannot reach it or learn why it is off; 3. the search input has a `placeholder` and no label; 4. a `` acts as the clear control; 5. the results count is rendered as a plain `

Constraints: - the visible design must not change: the same text in the same order, and the search field must still show its placeholder text; - "Apply" must remain visibly unavailable while the required field is empty, must still be reachable by Tab, must be announced as unavailable, and must do nothing when activated; - the clear control must be a real button in the natural tab order; - the count must be announced politely when it changes, without moving focus. Also export `const DEFECTS: string[]` — five short strings, one per fault, naming what was wrong. exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Take them one at a time and in each case name the *symptom* before the fix.
Fault 1: a tab stop that does not exist in the accessibility tree, so a keyboard
user focuses something a screen reader will not announce. Fault 2: a control
that vanishes from the keyboard. Fault 3: a field with no name. Fault 4: an
element that jumps ahead of the whole document in tab order. Fault 5: a change
nobody is told about.

## Hint 2

Two of them have a subtlety. For the label: keeping the placeholder *and*
adding a label is allowed and correct — the placeholder becomes a hint rather
than the name. If the design has no room for a visible label, a visually hidden
one is the fallback, not `aria-label` on top of a placeholder that says
something different.

For `aria-disabled`: it does not stop anything happening. The click handler has
to return early itself, or the button still fires.

## Hint 3

`tabIndex={3}` is not fixed by changing it to `tabIndex={0}` — it is fixed by
using a `<button>`, at which point no tabIndex is needed at all. Any positive
tabIndex anywhere in a document creates a separate ordering pass that runs
before every natural tab stop, so one stray `tabIndex={3}` reorders the whole
page.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A useful way to audit rather than guess: walk the component with the keyboard
only, then read it in DevTools' Accessibility pane. Fault 1 shows up as a focus
ring on something the pane says is not in the tree. Fault 3 shows up as an
"edit text" with no name. Fault 4 shows up the moment you Tab into the page and
land in the middle of it.

## Hint 2

The `disabled` versus `aria-disabled` decision deserves the most thought,
because both are defensible in general and only one fits here. `disabled` is
right when a control is irrelevant — a "next page" button on the last page.
`aria-disabled` is right when the control is relevant but blocked, because the
user needs to be able to find it, hear that it is unavailable, and ideally be
told why. A submit button waiting on a required field is squarely the second
case.

## Hint 3

Fault 5 is the one people fix wrongly by moving focus to the count. Do not.
Moving focus to announce something interrupts the user and loses their position
in the form. The whole reason live regions exist is to say something without
taking control — and remember from ex7 that the region has to be mounted and
empty before the message arrives, so it cannot be conditionally rendered.

lessons.title: V3·RC4 — Animation and layout without jank
lessons.summary: Animating `left` and `height` asks the browser to redo layout sixty times a second; animating `transform` and `opacity` asks the compositor to move a texture it already has. This sector is about that difference, the read-write interleaves that cause layout thrash, FLIP, and why reduced motion is a correctness requirement rather than a preference.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC4 — Animation and layout without jank

You have 16.7 milliseconds. That is the whole budget for one frame at 60Hz, and
the browser needs some of it for itself, so in practice you have around ten.
Inside that window the browser must run any expired timers, dispatch events, run
your JavaScript, recalculate styles, lay out the page, paint the changed
regions, and hand the result to the compositor. Miss the deadline and the frame
does not appear — the previous one is shown again, and the user sees a stutter.

Jank is not a mysterious property of slow devices. It is the specific,
diagnosable event of exceeding that budget, and there are about five ways to do
it. This sector is about recognising which one you have.

The React connection is direct. React's commit phase writes to the DOM
synchronously, and your layout effects run inside it — so a measurement in a
layout effect happens right after a batch of writes, which is the exact
condition that forces the browser to redo layout on the spot. Meanwhile every
animation library you might use is doing something you could do yourself with a
`requestAnimationFrame` loop and a ref, and knowing which of those you actually
need is worth more than knowing any particular library's API.

## Concept — the pixel pipeline and where you can get off it

**Every visual change runs some prefix of this pipeline:**

```
JavaScript → Style → Layout → Paint → Composite
```

Change `width`, `top`, `margin` or `font-size` and you invalidate **layout**:
the browser must recompute geometry for the affected subtree, then repaint it,
then composite. Change `color`, `background` or `box-shadow` and you skip layout
but still **paint**. Change `transform`, `opacity` or `filter` on an element the
compositor has promoted to its own layer and you skip both — the compositor
takes the texture it already has and moves or fades it, on the GPU, often on a
separate thread from your JavaScript.

That last point is why `transform: translateX(200px)` and `left: 200px` look
identical and cost completely different amounts. The first can run at 60fps
while the main thread is busy; the second cannot run at all while the main
thread is busy.

**Layout thrashing** is the other big cost, and it is entirely self-inflicted.
The browser batches style and layout work, invalidating on write and only
recomputing when someone reads. So this is fine:

```ts
for (const el of items) el.style.transform = `translateY(${offset}px)`; // writes
```

and this is a disaster:

```ts
for (const el of items) {
  const h = el.offsetHeight;              // read: forces layout NOW
  el.style.height = `${h * 2}px`;         // write: invalidates it again
}
```

Every iteration forces a synchronous layout of the whole document. A hundred
items is a hundred layouts. The fix is always the same shape: read everything,
then write everything.

The properties that force layout when read are worth memorising in outline:
`offsetTop/Left/Width/Height`, `clientTop/Left/Width/Height`,
`scrollTop/Left/Width/Height`, `getComputedStyle()`,
`getBoundingClientRect()`, and `focus()`.

**`useLayoutEffect` versus `useEffect`.** Both run after the DOM is updated.
`useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously *before* the browser paints, so a DOM
mutation you make there is never visible as an intermediate state — which is
exactly what you need for measure-then-position. `useEffect` runs after paint,
so the same code produces one frame of the wrong position, seen as a flicker.
The cost is that `useLayoutEffect` blocks painting, so anything slow in it
delays the frame, and it warns during server rendering because there is no
layout on the server.

**FLIP** is the general technique for animating a layout change cheaply. First,
record the element's box. Last, let the layout change happen. Invert, apply a
transform that puts it visually back where it started. Play, remove the
transform with a transition so it animates to its real position. The layout
happens once, and the animation is pure compositing.

**Exit animations are hard because unmounting is instant.** React removes the
node and there is nothing left to animate. The standard answer is to keep the
element mounted in an "exiting" state until the transition ends, then remove it
— with a guard, because `transitionend` may never fire if the transition is
interrupted or the property never changes.

**Observers instead of listeners.** `ResizeObserver` tells you when an element's
box changed, batched and delivered before paint; a `resize` listener fires only
for the window and tells you nothing about your element. `IntersectionObserver`
tells you when something entered the viewport without a scroll handler running
on every scroll event.

**`prefers-reduced-motion` is a correctness requirement.** Vestibular disorders
are real, and large parallax or zoom animations cause genuine nausea. Respecting
the preference does not mean removing the state change — it means arriving at
the end state immediately, or substituting a cross-fade.


# Reading — react/v3rc04_animation_layout

## Notes

**The compositor is a different thread.** Transform and opacity animations that
have been handed to the compositor keep running while the main thread is blocked
by JavaScript. That is the single largest practical difference between the cheap
and expensive properties: not that layout is slow, but that layout happens on
the thread you are also using for everything else.

**Promotion is not free.** An element gets its own compositor layer through
`will-change: transform`, a 3D transform, or being animated. Each layer costs
GPU memory proportional to its area, and too many layers is its own performance
problem. `will-change` should be added shortly before an animation and removed
after, not left on permanently — leaving it on a hundred list items is a
well-known way to exhaust memory on a phone.

**Forced synchronous layout has a name in the Performance panel:** "Layout
Shift" is a different thing, but "Recalculate Style" and "Layout" entries with a
warning triangle labelled *Forced reflow* are exactly this. The panel will even
tell you which line of JavaScript triggered it.

**React's commit phase is a write phase.** React mutates the DOM, then runs
layout effects, then the browser paints. A measurement in a layout effect
therefore reads after a batch of writes — a forced layout, unavoidably, because
you genuinely need the post-mutation geometry. What you can control is doing it
once rather than once per child.

**`transitionend` is not guaranteed.** It does not fire if the property never
actually changed, if the transition is interrupted, if the element is removed,
or if the tab was backgrounded. Any code path that waits for it needs a timeout
fallback, and it bubbles — so a transition on a child can trigger a parent's
handler unless you check `event.target`.

**View Transitions** are the platform's answer to FLIP: `document.startViewTransition(cb)`
snapshots the old state, applies your DOM change, snapshots the new state, and
cross-fades or morphs between them. React 19 has been building
`<ViewTransition>` support on top of it. It does not remove the need to
understand FLIP — it is FLIP, implemented by the browser.

## ex1 — proving it, not asserting it

The exercise is measurable because the gate spies on the properties that force
layout. Animating `left` means something in your code path read a layout
property; animating `transform` means nothing did. It is a small piece of code
whose value is entirely in the reasoning: two visually identical results, one of
which can run on a busy main thread and one of which cannot.

## ex2 — the flash you would otherwise ship

The tooltip needs its own width before it can decide which side to sit on, and
its width depends on being rendered. So: render at a default position, measure,
and correct — all before paint. With `useEffect` the correction lands after
paint and the user sees the tooltip jump. This is the canonical
`useLayoutEffect` case, and it is worth having one in your head so you can
recognise the shape.

## ex3 — the loop that costs a hundred layouts

The naive version reads `offsetHeight` and writes a style inside the same
iteration, which invalidates the layout it just computed, so the next read
recomputes everything. Splitting into a read pass and a write pass turns *n*
layouts into one. The gate counts forced layouts, so a solution that merely
looks tidier does not pass.

## ex4 — the loop that stops

Three failure modes to survive. The loop must not be restarted on every render
(store the id in a ref, start it in an effect with a stable dependency list); it
must be cancelled on unmount; and it must survive StrictMode's mount-unmount-mount
in development, which means the cleanup and the start must be symmetric. The
frequent bug is capturing a stale value in the loop's closure — read mutable
state from a ref, or restart the loop when it genuinely changes.

## ex5 — FLIP concretely

First: `getBoundingClientRect()` for each item, before the change. Last: let
React re-render into the new order. Invert: in a layout effect, set
`transform: translate(dx, dy)` with no transition, putting each item visually
back at its old position. Play: on the next frame, remove the transform with a
transition. One layout, then pure compositing.

The subtle part is the two-step at the end: setting the transform and removing
it in the same frame produces no animation, because the browser never observed
the intermediate state. You need a `requestAnimationFrame` — or a forced
read — between them.

## ex6 — exiting

The component keeps a small state machine: `entering`, `visible`, `exiting`,
`gone`. Removal happens on `transitionend` or on a timeout slightly longer than
the transition, whichever comes first. The timeout is not belt-and-braces; it is
the primary path in every case where the transition did not run.

## ex7 — observing an element

`ResizeObserver` delivers entries before paint, coalesced. Two rules keep it
safe: disconnect in the effect cleanup, and never write a style in the callback
that changes the observed element's size, or you get an infinite loop that the
browser reports as "ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered
notifications".

## ex8 — the media query as a subscription

Reading `matchMedia(...).matches` once in a `useState` initialiser is wrong for
the same reason reading a prop once is wrong: the user can change the setting
while your page is open, and on some platforms it changes with the time of day.
`useSyncExternalStore` is the right primitive — it handles the subscription, the
snapshot, and the server-side default in one API.

## challenge — `height: auto`

The three approaches, and their failure modes: `max-height` with a guessed value
(animation timing becomes wrong when the guess is far off), measured pixel
height with a transition to `auto` at the end (correct but needs a resize
observer to stay correct), and `grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`, which is the
modern trick and animates cleanly with no measurement at all.

## review1 — three independent causes

An animation on a layout property, a read-write interleave, and an uncancelled
frame loop that keeps running after unmount. They are independent, they compound,
and only one of them is visible in a naive profile.

## Further reading

- [web.dev — Rendering performance](https://web.dev/articles/rendering-performance) — the pipeline, and which properties trigger what.
- [MDN — `requestAnimationFrame`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestAnimationFrame) — timing, the callback's argument, and cancellation.
- [react.dev — `useLayoutEffect`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useLayoutEffect) — including the "this hurts performance, prefer useEffect" caveat and when to ignore it.
- [MDN — `ResizeObserver`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/ResizeObserver) — delivery timing and the loop error.
- [MDN — `prefers-reduced-motion`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion) — what the setting actually means.
- [MDN — View Transition API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) — FLIP implemented by the platform.
