# Long reading — frames, threads, and the cost of a pixel

## What the browser is doing while you animate

A browser renders in a loop driven by the display's refresh rate. Each turn of
the loop, in order: run expired timers and dispatch pending input events; run
`requestAnimationFrame` callbacks; recalculate styles for anything invalidated;
run layout if geometry was invalidated; update the layer tree; paint the
invalidated regions into layers; and hand the layers to the compositor, which
assembles them into the final image on the GPU.

Two of those steps happen on a different thread. The compositor thread owns
scrolling and any animation it has been given full control of, and it can
produce frames while the main thread is completely blocked. This is why a page
running a two-second synchronous script still scrolls smoothly, and why a
`transform` animation started before that script continues while a `left`
animation stops dead.

Getting an animation onto the compositor requires that it changes only
properties the compositor can handle by itself — `transform`, `opacity`,
and `filter` — and that the element has its own layer. The browser promotes
elements automatically when it sees such an animation, and you can hint with
`will-change`. Everything else is main-thread work by definition, because it
changes what the layer's contents should be, and only the main thread knows how
to compute that.

## Layout invalidation and the read-write dance

The browser's layout engine is lazy on purpose. Writing to `style.width`
marks the layout dirty and returns immediately; the recalculation is deferred
until either the frame needs it or someone asks a question that cannot be
answered without it. That deferral is what makes a hundred style writes cheap.

The questions that cannot be deferred are the geometry reads: `offsetWidth`,
`getBoundingClientRect()`, `getComputedStyle()`, `scrollTop`, and a longer tail
including `focus()` and some `Range` methods. Any of them, on a dirty layout,
forces the engine to lay out the document right now.

This is not a bug, and there is no way to make it fast: you asked for a number
that depends on layout. The only lever is *how many times* you ask after
dirtying. Read everything you need first, then write. Where you cannot
restructure — because a third-party library is interleaving — the escape hatch
is to batch through `requestAnimationFrame`, doing all reads in one callback and
scheduling writes for the next.

Chrome's Performance panel surfaces these directly. A purple "Layout" block with
a red triangle and the words "Forced reflow is a likely performance bottleneck"
is the signal, and expanding it names the exact call site.

## A short history of web animation

**jQuery's `animate()`** (2006) ran on `setInterval`, mutated inline styles per
frame, and touched layout properties by default. It defined a generation's mental
model of animation as "JavaScript changes a number sixty times a second", and
that model is precisely what makes modern code slow.

**CSS transitions and animations** (2009 onward) moved the interpolation into
the engine. Declaring `transition: transform 200ms` means the browser owns the
timing, can run it off the main thread, and continues correctly while your
JavaScript is busy. This is still the right default for state-to-state changes.

**`requestAnimationFrame`** (2011) fixed the timing problem for the animations
that genuinely need JavaScript: it runs once per frame, before paint, and pauses
in background tabs. It did not fix the property problem — a rAF loop writing
`style.left` is as expensive as a `setInterval` doing it.

**The Web Animations API** (2016 onward) exposed the engine's own animation
model to JavaScript: `element.animate(keyframes, options)` returns an `Animation`
you can pause, reverse, seek and compose. It gives you CSS-quality performance
with imperative control, and it is under-used in React codebases that reach for
a library first.

**Spring libraries** — react-spring, Framer Motion — model motion physically
rather than as a duration and easing curve, which produces interruption
behaviour that feels right: grab a moving element and it responds from its
current velocity rather than snapping. That is a genuine capability CSS
transitions do not have, and it is the honest reason to take on the dependency.

**View Transitions** (2023 onward) are the newest layer: `document.startViewTransition()`
lets the browser snapshot before and after states of a DOM change and animate
between them, including elements that moved across a re-render or a navigation.
It is FLIP, done by the engine, with correct handling of the cases hand-rolled
FLIP gets wrong. React 19 has been building a `<ViewTransition>` component on
top of it.

## Performance notes worth having as numbers

At 60Hz a frame is 16.7ms; the browser's own work is typically 4-6ms of that, so
budget under 10ms for your JavaScript plus style plus layout. At 120Hz, which is
now common on phones, the budget is 8.3ms.

A forced layout on a moderately complex page costs 1-10ms. Doing that once is
invisible. Doing it once per row of a 200-row table is 200ms-2s, which is not a
dropped frame but a visible freeze.

Compositor layers cost roughly `width × height × 4` bytes of GPU memory each. A
full-screen layer on a 1080p display is about 8MB. Promoting fifty list items
"to be safe" is how a phone runs out of GPU memory and the browser starts
falling back to software compositing, which is dramatically slower than not
promoting anything.

`content-visibility: auto` lets the browser skip layout and paint for offscreen
subtrees entirely, which is often a bigger win than any animation optimisation
on a long page. Pair it with `contain-intrinsic-size` so the scrollbar does not
jump as content is realised.

## When not to animate

Animation costs attention. Every transition asks the user to wait, and on a
screen they will visit forty times a day, the delightful 400ms flourish becomes
a 400ms tax. Interfaces that people use as tools should animate to communicate
— where did this come from, what just changed, is this loading — and not
otherwise.

There are specific cases where animation is actively harmful. Anything that
delays feedback on a direct manipulation should be under 100ms or absent.
Anything large-scale and involuntary — parallax, zooms, spinning transitions —
can cause nausea in people with vestibular disorders, which is why
`prefers-reduced-motion` exists and why respecting it is not optional. And an
animation on a list that updates from live data means the list is never still,
which makes it unreadable.

The reduced-motion response is worth getting right rather than blunt. The
setting does not mean "no animation"; it means "no large or unexpected motion".
A 150ms opacity cross-fade is generally considered acceptable under reduced
motion, while a slide-in across half the viewport is not. Removing all
transitions is a defensible simple answer; replacing large motion with a fade is
the better one.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — the cheap properties

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. The stub animates a panel by writing `style.left` and
`style.height` from a frame loop.

Export:

```tsx
export function SlidePanel(props: {
  offset: number;   // 0..1
  faded: boolean;
}): ReactElement;
```

Requirements:

- the panel moves horizontally by `offset * 200` pixels and fades to `0.3`
  opacity when `faded` is true;
- the movement must be expressed as a `transform`, and the fade as `opacity` —
  no `left`, `top`, `width`, `height`, `margin` or `padding` may vary;
- the styles must be applied declaratively through React's `style` prop, not by
  writing to the node from an effect;
- the element must carry `data-testid="panel"`.

The gate reads the computed style, asserts `transform` contains
`translateX(120px)` for `offset: 0.6` and `opacity` is `0.3` when faded, and
patches `Element.prototype.getBoundingClientRect` and the `offset*` getters to
fail the test if the component reads any of them.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc04_animation_layout ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two visually identical results, two completely different costs. `left: 120px`
invalidates layout, so the browser recomputes geometry for the subtree, repaints
it, and composites — all on the main thread, every frame.
`transform: translateX(120px)` changes nothing about where anything *is* in the
layout, so the compositor moves an existing texture.

## Hint 2

Because the values are pure functions of props, none of this needs an effect or
a frame loop at all:

```tsx
<div
  data-testid="panel"
  style={{ transform: `translateX(${offset * 200}px)`, opacity: faded ? 0.3 : 1 }}
/>
```

React writes the style during the commit, the browser transitions it if CSS says
so, and no JavaScript runs per frame.

## Hint 3

If you want the movement to be animated rather than instant, add
`transition: "transform 200ms, opacity 200ms"` to the same style object and let
the engine own the interpolation. That is the point of the exercise: the
cheapest animation is one where your JavaScript runs once and CSS runs the rest.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by asking what "faster" actually means here, because both versions look
the same on an idle laptop. The difference shows up when the main thread is
busy: a `transform` animation the compositor owns keeps running through a
200ms script, and a `left` animation freezes for exactly as long as that script
runs. On a phone parsing JSON while you animate, that is every frame.

## Hint 2

Notice that the stub's frame loop is doing work the browser was already going to
do. A `requestAnimationFrame` loop that writes a style each frame is a
hand-rolled reimplementation of a CSS transition, with worse timing, no
interruption handling, and main-thread cost. Reach for a loop only when the
value cannot be expressed as a start and an end state — physics, scroll linkage,
canvas.

## Hint 3

A note on `will-change`. You may be tempted to add `willChange: "transform"` to
guarantee promotion. Do not add it here: it costs GPU memory per element and is
meant to be applied shortly before an animation and removed after. The browser
promotes automatically when it sees a transform transition, and permanent
`will-change` on a list of items is a known way to exhaust memory on mobile.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach this by asking what "before paint" means mechanically. React's commit
writes to the DOM. Then layout effects run, synchronously, still inside the same
task. Then React returns control to the browser, which finally does style,
layout, paint. Anything you do in a layout effect happens in that gap, so the
browser never sees the intermediate DOM.

## Hint 2

There is a cost that the React documentation is explicit about: layout effects
block painting. Slow work in one delays the frame for everybody. So the rule is
to use `useLayoutEffect` only for the specific pattern of "read geometry, adjust
DOM" and keep it small. The default should remain `useEffect`, and reaching for
the layout version should be a decision you can justify in a sentence.

## Hint 3

One more caveat worth carrying: `useLayoutEffect` warns during server rendering,
because there is no layout on a server. The usual accommodations are to render a
sensible default that does not need measurement, or — if the component is
genuinely client-only — to gate it. This exercise's default placement is already
that sensible default, which is not an accident: designing measurement-dependent
components so the unmeasured state is *plausible* rather than broken is how you
keep them server-renderable.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The browser defers layout until somebody asks a question that needs it. Writing
a style marks layout dirty and costs almost nothing. Reading `offsetHeight` on a
dirty layout forces the engine to lay out the whole document immediately. So a
loop that alternates them pays that cost once per iteration.

## Hint 2

Two passes, explicitly:

```tsx
const heights = nodes.map((node) => node.offsetHeight);   // reads
const tallest = Math.max(...heights);
for (const node of nodes) node.style.height = `${tallest}px`;   // writes
```

One forced layout for the whole batch instead of one per row.

## Hint 3

The reset requirement is the one that bites. If you measure without first
clearing the inline height, you measure the height you set last time, and the
rows can only ever grow — a row whose text shrank stays tall forever. Clear all
heights (another write pass), then read, then write. Three passes, still one
layout each.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before optimising, notice that the whole component might be unnecessary. CSS
grid and flexbox equalise heights natively — `display: grid` with
`grid-auto-rows: 1fr`, or a flex row where items stretch — with no measurement,
no effect, and no layout thrash. Reaching for JavaScript to do a layout job is
the first mistake, and recognising it is more valuable than optimising the
JavaScript.

## Hint 2

That said, the read-then-write pattern is worth internalising, because you will
meet it in places CSS cannot help: virtualisation, canvas sizing, sticky
headers, scroll synchronisation. The general form is that any function which
both queries geometry and mutates it should be split into a query phase
returning plain data and a mutate phase consuming it.

## Hint 3

Where you cannot restructure — a third-party library interleaving inside its own
callback — the escape hatch is `requestAnimationFrame`: do all your reads in one
callback and schedule the writes in the next. That gets you one layout per frame
rather than one per operation, at the cost of a frame of latency.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three things must live in refs rather than state, and it is worth being explicit
about why. The frame id, because the cleanup needs the latest one. The
accumulated value, because updating it must not re-render. And the last
timestamp, because the delta is computed from it and it changes every frame.

## Hint 2

The stale-closure trap is `speed`. If the loop function is created once and
closes over the first `speed`, changing the prop does nothing. Two fixes:
restart the loop when `speed` changes (simple, but drops a frame and resets the
timestamp), or keep `speed` in a ref updated each render and read
`speedRef.current` inside the loop (no restart, which is what the prompt asks
for).

## Hint 3

The timestamp handling is what makes "resume without a jump" work. `rAF` hands
your callback a timestamp; compute `delta = (now - last) / 1000` and store `now`.
On the *first* frame after a resume, `last` is from before the pause, so the
delta is enormous — reset `last` to `null` on cleanup and treat a `null` last
as delta zero.

For StrictMode: cleanup must fully cancel and reset, and the second mount must
start cleanly from that state. If your effect assumes it only ever runs once,
the double invocation will show you.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider first whether you need a frame loop at all. If the value is a function
of elapsed time between two known endpoints, a CSS transition or
`element.animate()` does it with no JavaScript per frame and correct behaviour
in background tabs. Frame loops earn their place when the value depends on
something you cannot express as a keyframe: live data, physics, user input, a
canvas.

## Hint 2

An uncancelled `requestAnimationFrame` is a real leak, not just wasted work. The
callback closure holds a reference to everything it captured — your component's
props, its state, possibly a large data structure — and the browser keeps
scheduling it forever. In a single-page app where components mount and unmount
all day, a handful of these will show up as steadily climbing memory.

## Hint 3

On updating the DOM directly: this is one of the few places where bypassing
React is the right call, and it is worth knowing the boundary. Values that
change sixty times a second and are read only by the user's eyes — a counter, a
progress bar's width, a cursor position — do not need to be in React's state,
and putting them there means a full render per frame. Anything another component
needs to make a decision about does belong in state.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about why the obvious approach fails. You might try animating each item's
`top` from its old value to its new one — but the items are laid out by the
document flow, so they have no `top` to animate, and giving them one means
taking them out of flow and positioning everything manually. FLIP's insight is
that you do not fight the layout: you let it happen instantly and then lie about
it visually for 200ms.

## Hint 2

The all-reads-then-all-writes rule from ex3 applies here too and is easy to
violate. If your loop reads `getBoundingClientRect()` and immediately writes a
transform for each item, you force a layout per item. Collect all the rects
first, then apply all the transforms.

## Hint 3

Worth knowing where this is heading: the View Transition API does exactly this
in the browser. `document.startViewTransition(() => setItems(next))` snapshots
before and after and animates between them, correctly handling elements that
changed size, crossed containers, or were replaced. React 19 has been building a
`<ViewTransition>` component on top of it. Learning FLIP is still worth it —
the API is FLIP, and understanding it is how you debug the cases where the
built-in version does something you did not expect.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The problem is that unmounting is instantaneous — React removes the node and
there is nothing left to animate. So the component has to keep it mounted itself
for a while, which means the "is it in the DOM" question and the "does the
parent want it" question are two different pieces of state.

## Hint 2

Three states rather than two makes the logic tractable. `shown` is the steady
state. `exiting` is "the parent said no, I am animating out". Not mounted is the
end. The transition from `exiting` to unmounted is what the timer drives:

```tsx
const id = setTimeout(() => setMounted(false), durationMs);
return () => clearTimeout(id);
```

The cleanup returning `clearTimeout` is also what implements "cancel the exit if
`show` comes back", because the effect re-runs.

## Hint 3

On `transitionend`: treat it as an optimisation, not the mechanism. It does not
fire when the transition never started (the property did not change), when it
was interrupted, when the element was removed, or when the tab was backgrounded.
Building removal on it alone produces toasts that are still on the page five
minutes later.

If you do listen for it, check `event.target === event.currentTarget` — it
bubbles, so a transition on any child would otherwise trigger the removal.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a framing that makes this whole class of problem clearer: the DOM is a
cache of your state, and animation is the process of showing the cache lagging
behind deliberately. Enter animations are easy because the element exists before
you want it visible. Exit animations are hard because your state says "gone"
while the DOM still needs to show something.

## Hint 2

Note the ordering requirement hiding in the enter case, which the prompt does
not test but which you will hit immediately in real use. If you mount an element
with `opacity: 0` and set it to `1` in the same commit, the browser coalesces
and there is no transition — the same problem as FLIP's play step. The fix is
the same: one frame between mounting and changing the property.

## Hint 3

React has no built-in solution for this and it is a real gap. `react-transition-group`
is the long-standing answer and is essentially the state machine you are writing
here. Framer Motion's `AnimatePresence` is the modern one and is worth the
dependency if you have many exit animations. Knowing what they do — keep it
mounted, run a timer, then remove — means you can debug them when an element
mysteriously refuses to disappear.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `resize` listener answers a different question. It fires when the *window*
changes size and tells you nothing about your element — which can change size
because a sibling collapsed, a font loaded, a parent's flex basis changed, or
content arrived. All of those are silent to a window listener.

## Hint 2

The ref-callback requirement is about correctness, not style. A ref object plus
an effect looks equivalent but is not: the effect does not re-run when the ref's
`.current` changes, so a conditionally rendered node that remounts is never
observed. A ref callback fires with the new node and with `null` on detach,
which is exactly the lifecycle an observer needs.

```tsx
const ref = useCallback((node: T | null) => {
  observer.current?.disconnect();
  if (!node) return;
  observer.current = new ResizeObserver(...);
  observer.current.observe(node);
}, []);
```

## Hint 3

For "once per mode change, not once per entry": derive the mode from the
measured size during render and let React's own bail-out handle the rest, or
compare against the previous mode in a ref before calling `onLayout`. Calling a
callback from an observer on every entry is how a resize handler ends up firing
sixty times a second during a drag.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Worth asking whether you need JavaScript at all. **Container queries** —
`@container (min-width: 400px)` — do exactly this in CSS: style an element based
on its container's size rather than the viewport's. They are supported
everywhere now. Measuring in JavaScript is for when the *behaviour*, not just
the styling, depends on size: how many items to render, whether to virtualise,
what to put in a canvas.

## Hint 2

`ResizeObserver` has a specific failure you should know by name. If the callback
changes something that alters the observed element's size, the observer fires
again, and you get "ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered
notifications" in the console — the browser detecting an infinite loop and
bailing out. It surfaces as an unhandled error in some setups, which sends
people hunting in entirely the wrong place.

## Hint 3

There is a subtlety in what the entry reports. `entry.contentRect` is the
content box, excluding padding and border. `entry.borderBoxSize` is the border
box. They differ by however much padding you have, and mixing them up produces
an off-by-padding bug that only shows up on elements with padding — which is to
say, in production and not in your test fixture.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The bug this exercise is built around is reading the value once:

```tsx
const [reduced] = useState(() => matchMedia(QUERY).matches);   // wrong
```

That is a snapshot of a value that can change. Users toggle the setting; on some
platforms it follows a schedule. A snapshot in `useState` never updates.

## Hint 2

`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` is built for
exactly this shape — an external source with a subscription and a current value:

```tsx
useSyncExternalStore(
  (onChange) => {
    const mql = matchMedia(QUERY);
    mql.addEventListener("change", onChange);
    return () => mql.removeEventListener("change", onChange);
  },
  () => matchMedia(QUERY).matches,
  () => false
);
```

The third argument is the server snapshot, which is why this does not throw
during SSR.

## Hint 3

For the drawer, be precise about what reduced motion asks for. It does not ask
you to remove the drawer or to stop it opening. It asks you not to move large
things across the screen. So: `transform` transition duration goes to zero (or
the transform is not used at all), and a short opacity fade stays — a fade is
generally considered acceptable under reduced motion and preserves the sense
that something changed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about why this is a correctness requirement rather than a nicety. For
people with vestibular disorders, large-scale motion — parallax, zooms, big
slides — causes genuine physical symptoms: dizziness, nausea, migraine. The
operating system setting is the user telling you this. Ignoring it is not a
missed polish item.

## Hint 2

There is a strong argument for handling this in CSS rather than JavaScript,
and you should know it even though the exercise asks for the hook. A media
query in your stylesheet — `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { *
{ transition-duration: 0.01ms !important } }` — applies globally, needs no
React, and cannot be forgotten in one component. The JavaScript hook is for when
the *logic* changes, not just the styling: skipping an autoplay, choosing a
different component, not starting a frame loop at all.

## Hint 3

Two details about `useSyncExternalStore` worth carrying beyond this exercise.
The `getSnapshot` function must return a value that is stable by `Object.is`
when nothing changed — returning a fresh object every call causes an infinite
re-render loop, which is the most common way people get bitten by this hook.
Booleans and strings are safe; objects need caching. And `subscribe` must be
stable across renders, or React resubscribes on every render.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The core obstacle is that CSS cannot interpolate to or from `auto`, because
`auto` is not a length until layout resolves it. So every solution is a way of
supplying a number where `auto` would have been — or of avoiding height
entirely.

## Hint 2

The three approaches, so you can pick deliberately:

- **`max-height` with a guessed maximum.** No measurement. Fails when the guess
  is far above the real height: the transition spends most of its duration
  animating through space that does not exist, so the panel appears to open
  instantly and then wait.
- **Measured pixel height, then `auto` on completion.** Measure with
  `scrollHeight`, transition to that pixel value, and set `height: auto` on
  `transitionend` so later growth works. Correct, and the most code.
- **`grid-template-rows: 0fr → 1fr`.** A grid row *can* interpolate between
  fractions. No measurement at all, and it handles content growth natively. The
  child needs `min-height: 0` and `overflow: hidden`.

## Hint 3

The reversal requirement is what rules out the naive versions of the first two.
Reversing from the current height means the transition must start from the
element's *computed* height at that instant — which for the measured approach
means reading `getBoundingClientRect().height` before switching to the closed
value, and for the grid approach comes free because the browser interpolates
from wherever it is.

The grid approach also makes reduced motion trivial: set the transition duration
to zero and the row snaps.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before optimising the animation, settle the semantics, because they constrain
it. "Collapsed content must not be rendered" and "height animates from the
content's real height" are in tension: you cannot measure what does not exist.
The resolution is that the content mounts when opening begins, at zero height,
and unmounts when closing completes — the same delayed-unmount state machine as
ex6, applied to a different property.

## Hint 2

The scrollbar flash in the requirements is a real artefact and worth
understanding. A panel transitioning height with `overflow: visible` shows its
content overflowing the shrinking box; with `overflow: auto` it grows a
scrollbar for the frames where content exceeds height, which flickers.
`overflow: hidden` during the transition and restored afterwards is the standard
answer — and "afterwards" matters, because a permanently hidden overflow clips
focus rings and dropdowns inside the panel.

## Hint 3

If you take the grid route, the shape is smaller than you expect:

```css
.panel { display: grid; grid-template-rows: 0fr; transition: grid-template-rows 220ms; }
.panel[data-open="true"] { grid-template-rows: 1fr; }
.panel > div { overflow: hidden; min-height: 0; }
```

The `min-height: 0` is not optional — grid items default to `min-height: auto`,
which refuses to shrink below their content and silently defeats the whole
thing. That single line is the most commonly missed part of this technique.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — three causes of one stutter

Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. The stub exports a `Sparkline` that drops frames
while it animates. There are three independent causes:

1. the highlight marker is animated by writing `style.left` from a frame loop;
2. the label-positioning pass reads `getBoundingClientRect()` and writes a
   `style.transform` inside the same loop iteration, once per point;
3. the frame loop is started in an effect that has no cleanup, so it keeps
   running after unmount and after the animation should have stopped.

Fix all three, keeping the visible result identical:

- the marker still moves to the same pixel position;
- the labels still end up at the same offsets;
- the loop still runs while `animating` is true and not otherwise.

Also export `const CAUSES: string[]` — three strings, each naming one cause and
the pipeline stage or mechanism it abuses.

The gate counts forced layouts during a labelling pass, asserts the marker's
position comes from a `transform`, and asserts no frame callback runs after
unmount.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc04_animation_layout review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Take them in order of how much they cost, which is not the order they are
listed. The read-write interleave is the biggest: with fifty points it is fifty
forced layouts per pass, easily tens of milliseconds. The `left` animation is
next: layout plus paint every frame instead of a compositor move. The
uncancelled loop is the smallest per frame and the worst over time, because it
never stops.

## Hint 2

The three fixes are each mechanical once identified:

- `style.left = x + "px"` becomes `style.transform = "translateX(" + x + "px)"`;
- the loop splits into a read pass collecting rects and a write pass applying
  transforms;
- the effect returns `() => cancelAnimationFrame(id)` and stores the id in a
  ref so the cleanup sees the latest one.

## Hint 3

Verify each fix independently rather than all at once, because they mask each
other in a profile. With the interleave still present, the forced layouts
dominate and the `left` animation looks free. With the loop still uncancelled,
the numbers keep drifting after you think you have stopped measuring.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Practise the diagnosis rather than jumping to the fixes, because in real code
nobody hands you a numbered list. The workflow: record a Performance trace while
the stutter happens; look for long tasks over 50ms; inside them, look for purple
Layout blocks — many small ones in a row means an interleave, one large one
means a big invalidation; check whether the animation continues while the main
thread is blocked, which tells you whether it is on the compositor.

## Hint 2

The uncancelled loop is worth dwelling on because its symptom is not jank in the
component you are looking at. It is jank *elsewhere*, later, after this
component is gone — a page that gets progressively worse the longer the session
runs, with no single culprit in the profile because the cost is spread across
dozens of orphaned loops. Every animation, listener, observer and timer you
start needs a cleanup, and this is the reason.

## Hint 3

When you write `CAUSES`, force yourself to name the mechanism rather than the
symptom. "Animating left is slow" is not an explanation. "Animating `left`
invalidates layout, so every frame runs style, layout, paint and composite on
the main thread instead of a compositor-only move" is one, and it is the version
that transfers to the next property you are tempted to animate.

lessons.title: V3·RC5 — Routing patterns and the URL as state
lessons.summary: The URL is the only piece of your application's state that survives a reload, arrives intact in a colleague's chat message, and works with the back button. This sector is about treating it as state rather than as an address: what belongs in it, how to read and write it without mirroring, and how to build the routing primitives you have been importing.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC5 — Routing patterns and the URL as state

Someone filters a table to unpaid invoices from last quarter, sorted by amount,
page three. They find the problem, and they paste the link into chat. Whether
their colleague sees the same thing is a decision you made months earlier, when
you chose whether the filter lived in `useState` or in the query string.

The URL is the only state your application has that is durable across a reload,
transferable to another person, addressable by the back button, indexable by a
search engine, and restorable when the browser reopens the tab a week later.
Nothing you put in React state has any of those properties. So the question for
every piece of state in a screen is not "how do I store this" but "does this
belong in the URL", and the answer is yes far more often than most applications
behave as if it is.

You have all the mechanics already: state, effects, custom hooks,
`useSyncExternalStore` from the animation sector. What is new here is that the
browser owns a piece of your state, that it can change it without telling you —
the back button — and that reading it correctly means subscribing to it rather
than sampling it.

This sector builds the primitives rather than importing a router. Not because
you should ship a hand-rolled router, but because every routing bug you will
ever debug is a bug in one of these five pieces, and they are much easier to
reason about once you have written them.

## Concept — the URL, the history stack, and the drift bug

**Three places to put something, with different meanings.**

```
https://app.example.com/teams/42/invoices?status=unpaid&sort=amount#totals
                        └── path ──────┘ └──── query ───────────┘ └hash┘
```

The **path** identifies the resource: which page, which record. It is
hierarchical, it is what a server would route on, and it is what belongs in a
sitemap. The **query** modifies the view of that resource: filters, sort, page,
search. It is unordered and repeatable. The **hash** is a position within the
page and, uniquely, is never sent to the server.

**What does not belong in the URL:** half-typed text before it is committed,
transient UI like which tooltip is open, anything secret — URLs are logged by
proxies, stored in history, and pasted into tickets — and anything large enough
to hit a length limit.

**`URLSearchParams` has semantics worth knowing.** Keys can repeat:
`?tag=a&tag=b` is two values, `getAll("tag")` returns both, and `get("tag")`
returns only the first. `set` replaces every occurrence; `append` adds one.
`delete` removes all. Values are percent-encoded automatically when you use the
API and not when you build the string by hand, which is the source of an entire
category of bug involving `+`, `&` and non-ASCII characters. Order is preserved
as written, so two logically identical URLs can differ as strings — worth
normalising if you use the URL as a cache key.

**push versus replace decides what the back button does.** `pushState` adds an
entry, so Back returns to the previous state. `replaceState` overwrites the
current one, so Back skips it entirely. The rule that falls out: a *deliberate
navigation* pushes; a *continuous adjustment* replaces. Clicking a filter chip
pushes. Typing in a search box replaces, or you leave the user with forty
history entries and a back button that walks them backwards through their own
typing one character at a time.

**The History API has a hole in it.** `popstate` fires when the user navigates
with Back or Forward. It does **not** fire when *you* call `pushState` or
`replaceState`. So a component subscribed only to `popstate` sees the user's
navigations and misses its own application's, which is why every router in
existence either wraps those two methods or maintains its own event.

**Derive, do not mirror.** The single most common routing bug in React:

```tsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState(searchParams.get("q") ?? "");   // wrong
```

Now there are two sources of truth. The user presses Back, the URL changes, the
state does not, and the input shows something the URL disagrees with. The URL is
the state; read it during render and write it on change. This is the same
"derive, do not store" rule from the lists sector, applied to a source you do
not own.

**Route-level code splitting** is where `lazy` and `Suspense` earn their keep,
because a route boundary is a natural place for a chunk. The pairing to get
right is the guard: a redirect decided in an effect renders the protected
content for one frame first, which is a real security-adjacent bug, not a
cosmetic one.

**Navigation has accessibility consequences** you met in the accessibility
sector: nothing loaded, so focus stays where it was and no page title was
announced. Moving focus to the new view's heading is the standard fix, and
restoring scroll on Back is the other half of making an SPA behave like the web.

# Reading — react/v3rc05_routing_url_state

## Notes

**A client-side router is three things.** A subscription to the current
location, a matcher from a location to a component, and a way to change the
location without a document load. Everything else — nested layouts, data
loading, transitions — is built on those three.

**`pushState` fires no event, by design.** The specification's reasoning is that
the caller already knows it navigated. The consequence for library authors is
that every router monkey-patches `history.pushState` and `history.replaceState`
to dispatch a custom event, or keeps its own subscriber list and requires you to
navigate through its API. Knowing this explains why a `window.location.href`
assignment or a third-party script's navigation can leave your router's state
stale.

**`useSyncExternalStore` is the correct primitive** for reading the location.
It handles subscription lifecycle, guarantees the value React renders with is
the value at render time, and provides a server snapshot. Its one sharp edge:
`getSnapshot` must return something `Object.is`-stable when nothing changed.
Returning `new URL(location.href)` on every call is an infinite render loop.
Return the string and parse downstream, or cache.

**Encoding is not optional.** `new URLSearchParams({ q: "a&b" }).toString()` is
`q=a%26b`. Building `?q=${value}` by hand gives you `?q=a&b`, which is two
parameters. The same applies to path segments: `encodeURIComponent` for the
value, and `decodeURIComponent` when you read it back out of a match.

**Layout routes are a nesting of matches**, not a separate concept. A path
matches a chain of route definitions; each renders and places the next in an
outlet. The value this adds over a flat list is that the layout's state — a
sidebar's scroll position, an open panel — survives navigation between its
children, because the layout component never unmounts.

**A redirect in an effect is a frame too late.** Effects run after commit, so
the protected content rendered and painted before you redirected. The fix is to
decide during render and return the redirect instead of the content, doing the
actual `history.replaceState` in an effect afterwards.

**Scroll restoration is manual in an SPA.** Browsers restore scroll for real
document navigations; for a `pushState` navigation they do not, because they
have no idea when your content finished rendering. Save `scrollY` per history
entry — `history.state` is a good place — and restore it after the new view
commits.

## ex1 — reading without copying

The hook reads the parameter during render from a subscribed location. No
`useState`, no effect syncing one to the other. Once you have written it this
way the drift bug becomes structurally impossible, which is a better guarantee
than remembering to keep two things in sync.

## ex2 — the history stack as a user-facing artefact

The decision rule is about intent: a discrete choice the user would expect to
undo is a push; a continuous adjustment is a replace. The exercise makes this
measurable by counting `history.length`, which is the only honest test — a
version that "works" but leaves thirty entries is broken in a way no rendering
assertion catches.

## ex3 — the subscription

Three sources must be covered: `popstate` for Back and Forward, and the two
patched methods for your own navigations. The patch must be installed once and
removed on the last unsubscribe, which means reference counting if you write it
as a module-level store — and a module-level store is the right shape, because
every consumer wants the same location.

## ex4 — matching

A matcher is a small parser: split on `/`, compare segment by segment, collect
`:name` segments into an object. The details that separate a toy from a usable
one are trailing slashes, empty segments from a double slash, decoding, and a
catch-all. Returning `null` for no match rather than an empty object keeps the
caller honest.

## ex5 — repeated keys

`getAll`/`append` are the whole API, and the two traps are ordering and empty
sets. Rebuilding the params in a deterministic order keeps the URL stable as a
string, which matters for caching and for tests. Deleting the key when the set
is empty keeps `?tags=` out of the URL, which is a value that reads as "the
empty string" rather than "absent" when parsed.

## ex6 — the outlet

Rendering `children` from a layout is the same composition idea from the
component API sector, with the twist that the child comes from the route match
rather than from the call site. The reason the layout must not unmount between
sibling routes is state preservation, and the reason it does not is that React
sees the same element type at the same position — reconciliation, doing exactly
what the lists sector described.

## ex7 — lazy and guarded

Two independent things that interact badly if you get the order wrong. The lazy
import must be created once, at module scope or in a memo, or every render
starts a new import. The guard must be decided during render, or the protected
component mounts, runs its effects — including its data fetch — and paints
before the redirect.

## ex8 — focus and scroll

Focus goes to the new view's heading, which needs `tabIndex={-1}` to be
focusable, exactly as in the accessibility sector. Scroll restoration keys on
the history entry, not on the path, because the same path visited twice can have
two different scroll positions.

## challenge — composition of the pieces

The interesting bug is the double history entry: changing a filter must also
reset the page to 1, and doing those as two writes gives you two entries and a
back button that goes to a state the user never saw. One write, computed from
the whole next state.

## review1 — the drift

The fix is a deletion, mostly: remove the `useState`, remove the effect that
syncs it, read from the URL. The remaining work is that the input needs to stay
responsive while the URL updates are replaced rather than pushed.

## Further reading

- [MDN — History API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History_API) — `pushState`, `replaceState`, and the note that neither fires `popstate`.
- [MDN — `URLSearchParams`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/URLSearchParams) — `get` versus `getAll`, `set` versus `append`, encoding.
- [MDN — `popstate` event](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/popstate_event) — when it fires and what `event.state` contains.
- [react.dev — `useSyncExternalStore`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore) — the snapshot stability requirement.
- [React Router — Picking a router](https://reactrouter.com/start/library/routing) — how the production version organises the same three pieces.
- [MDN — `scrollRestoration`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/scrollRestoration) — turning off the browser's guess so yours can win.

# Long reading — how the address bar became application state

## The mechanics underneath

A client-side router does something the web platform did not originally support:
it changes the address bar without asking the server for a document. Two APIs
made it possible.

The first was the **fragment identifier**. Changing everything after `#` never
triggers a document load, and `hashchange` tells you it happened. That is why
every router built before 2012 used URLs like `example.com/#/users/42`. It
worked, it was ugly, and it had a real cost: the fragment is not sent to the
server, so the server could not render the right page, and search engines saw
one URL for the entire application.

The second was **`history.pushState`**, from the HTML5 History API. It changes
the URL, adds an entry to the session history, and does not navigate. This is
what made real paths possible in a single-page app, and it introduced the
requirement that defines SPA deployment: the server must respond to *every*
path with the application shell, because a user pressing refresh on
`/users/42` makes a genuine request for that path. Every "works locally, 404s in
production" routing bug is this rewrite rule missing.

`pushState` deliberately fires no event. The specification's view is that the
code calling it already knows. That single decision is why every routing library
either wraps `history.pushState` or insists you navigate through its own API,
and why an application with two routers, or a router plus a third-party widget
that navigates, gets into inconsistent states.

`popstate` fires for Back, Forward, and `history.go()`. It carries the `state`
object you passed to `pushState`, which is a serializable slot attached to that
history entry — a good and under-used place to keep per-entry data like scroll
position.

## The evolution of routing in React

**Hash routers** (2013-2014) came first, for the reasons above.

**`react-router` v1-v3** introduced the idea that routes are a tree, declared
statically, and matched against the location — with nesting that mapped
naturally onto component composition. Route configuration was a separate
artefact from the component tree.

**v4** (2017) made the famous reversal: routes became components. `<Route path>`
rendered where it appeared, matching was dynamic, and the router lost its
separate configuration. This was elegant and had a specific casualty: because
the route tree was only discoverable by rendering it, nothing could know in
advance what data a route needed. Every route fetched in an effect after it
mounted, which produced the waterfalls the performance sector talks about.

**Data routers** (v6.4, 2022) and Remix put static configuration back, with
loaders attached to routes. Because the router can match a URL to a route chain
*before rendering*, it can start every level's data fetch in parallel, and it
can even start them on link hover. This is the same insight that Next.js's App
Router encodes differently: knowing the route tree ahead of time is what lets
you prefetch.

**Server-driven routing** — Next.js App Router, React Server Components — moves
matching back to the server, where it started, with the client retaining enough
to make navigation feel instant. The interesting property is that route
segments can be server components that never ship to the client at all.

The through-line is that routing keeps oscillating between "configuration" and
"components", and the current position is configuration for the *tree* and
components for the *content* — because the tree is what tooling needs to reason
about, and the content is what humans need to compose.

## Performance notes

**Code splitting at route boundaries** is the highest-value split in most
applications, because a route is exactly the unit a user does not need until
they go there. `lazy(() => import("./Settings"))` at module scope, wrapped in a
`Suspense` above the outlet, is the whole pattern.

**Prefetching on hover** turns a 300ms chunk load into an invisible one, because
the median time between hovering a link and clicking it is longer than most
chunk fetches. The `lazy` component's import function can simply be called
early — imports are cached — which is a two-line implementation of what routers
expose as `<Link prefetch>`.

**Waterfalls** are the routing-specific performance failure. Layout fetches,
then renders, then the child fetches, then renders, then the grandchild. Three
sequential round trips where one parallel batch would do. The structural fix is
knowing the route chain before rendering; the tactical fix is hoisting fetches
to the highest component that knows what is needed.

**URL length** has practical limits — around 2,000 characters for
interoperability, though browsers allow more. Encoding a large filter set into
the URL is fine; encoding a document is not.

## When not to put state in the URL

The URL is public in every sense that matters. It appears in browser history, in
server logs, in proxy logs, in `Referer` headers sent to third parties, in
screenshots, and in the chat message where somebody pasted it. Anything you
would not want in a log file does not go in the URL, and this includes things
that feel innocuous: an email address in a query parameter is personal data
leaking into every analytics system you use.

The URL is also a commitment. Once a shape of URL exists, people bookmark it and
link to it, and changing it breaks those links. Query parameters are cheap to
add and expensive to remove — the same asymmetry as component props, for the
same reason.

And it is not a good store for high-frequency values. Every write is a history
operation and, if you push, a new entry. A value that changes on every keystroke
or every mouse move should live in state, with a debounced write to the URL if
it needs to be shareable at all. The pattern that works: the input is controlled
by local state for responsiveness, the URL is updated with `replaceState` after
the user pauses, and the URL remains the source of truth for anything derived
from it — a small, deliberate exception to "do not mirror", made for latency and
documented as such.

Finally, some state genuinely is not about what the user is looking at. A
half-composed message, an unsaved form, an optimistic update in flight, a
scroll-triggered animation's progress: putting any of those in the URL makes it
noisy without making it more useful, and the back button then does something
nobody asked for.

Status: {value}

`, or `

Status: any

` when the parameter is absent; - an empty value (`?status=`) is the empty string, not `null` — the badge must render `Status: ` with nothing after it, not `Status: any`. The gate sets `?status=unpaid`, mounts, asserts the text; calls `history.pushState` to `?status=paid`, asserts the text changed without a remount; then navigates to a URL with no `status` and asserts the fallback. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc05_routing_url_state ex1 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The value already exists, in `window.location.search`. The only reason a naive
version reaches for `useState` is to make React re-render when it changes — but
that is a subscription problem, not a storage problem, and copying the value to
solve it creates a second source of truth that can disagree with the first.

## Hint 2

`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot)` is exactly this: subscribe to the
thing that changes, and read the current value on demand.

```tsx
const search = useSyncExternalStore(
  subscribeToLocation,
  () => window.location.search
);
return new URLSearchParams(search).get(key);
```

Note what the snapshot returns: a string. Returning a `URLSearchParams` object
would be a fresh object on every call and React would loop forever.

## Hint 3

The empty-versus-absent distinction is a `URLSearchParams` fact worth
remembering. `get` returns `null` for a key that is not there and `""` for
`?status=`. So the fallback test must be `value === null`, not `!value` — the
latter would turn an explicit empty filter into "any", which is a different
query.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The bug this exercise exists to prevent looks harmless:

```tsx
const [status, setStatus] = useState(params.get("status") ?? "");
```

Everything works until the user presses Back. The URL changes, React state does
not, and the badge now says something the address bar contradicts. There is no
error, no warning, and the reproduction requires the back button, which is why
this survives code review and ships.

## Hint 2

Think about which direction the data flows. In the mirrored version there are
two writes for every change — one to state, one to the URL — and any path that
updates only one produces drift. In the derived version there is exactly one
write, to the URL, and the render is a pure function of it. Removing a source of
truth removes a class of bug rather than a specific instance of it.

## Hint 3

A note on why the subscription is not an effect. You could write
`useEffect(() => subscribe(forceUpdate), [])` and it would mostly work. What
`useSyncExternalStore` adds is a guarantee that concurrent rendering cannot
show you a value that was current at the start of a render but stale by the time
it committed — "tearing". For a location that changes rarely this is subtle;
the habit is worth forming anyway, because the alternative is knowing when it
matters.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The decision rule is about what the user would expect Back to undo. Picking a
value from a dropdown is a discrete choice — undoing it should restore the
previous choice, so it pushes. Typing is one continuous adjustment that happens
to consist of several keystrokes; undoing it one character at a time is not
what anybody means by Back.

## Hint 2

Build the next URL with the `URL` and `URLSearchParams` APIs rather than string
concatenation, and the encoding is handled for you:

```tsx
const url = new URL(window.location.href);
url.searchParams.set(key, value);
history.pushState(history.state, "", url);
```

Passing `history.state` through rather than `null` preserves whatever the
current entry was carrying — which matters once you start storing scroll
positions there in ex8.

## Hint 3

`delete` on empty is the detail the gate checks. `url.searchParams.set("q", "")`
produces `?q=`, which parses back as the empty string — an active filter
matching everything, rather than no filter. Treat `null` and `""` identically at
the write boundary and the ambiguity never enters your URLs.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try the wrong version deliberately and use the browser's back button. Push on
every keystroke and a five-character search leaves five entries; pressing Back
walks you backwards through your own typing, one character per press, and the
input flickers as it goes. Users interpret this as the back button being broken,
because from their point of view it is.

## Hint 2

There is a middle position worth knowing about that this exercise does not
require: push once per *episode* of typing. The first keystroke after a pause
pushes, subsequent ones replace, so Back returns to the state before the user
started typing rather than to the previous character. Routers rarely give you
this for free and it is the behaviour most people actually want.

## Hint 3

The "leave the rest of the URL untouched" requirement is not busywork. A common
bug is building the next URL from the pathname plus your own parameters, which
silently drops every other parameter — so setting the sort order clears the
filter. Starting from `new URL(window.location.href)` and mutating one key makes
that impossible by construction.

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. Build the location store the previous exercises
assumed.

```tsx

Requirements:

  how many subscribers exist, and the originals are restored when the last
  subscriber unsubscribes;
- the patch must call the original method with the original arguments and
  preserve its return value;
- `getLocationSnapshot` returns a string, so it is `Object.is`-stable;
- `useLocation` uses `useSyncExternalStore` and returns the three parts of the
  location, recomputed only when the snapshot changes;
- a server snapshot exists so the hook does not throw during SSR.

The gate mounts two components using `useLocation`, asserts
`window.history.pushState` was patched exactly once, navigates by each of the

```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`pushState` and `replaceState` fire no event. That is deliberate — the
specification's view is that the code calling them already knows — and it is why
every router in existence patches them. Subscribing only to `popstate` gives you
a store that notices the user's navigations and misses your own.

## Hint 2

The patch is a wrapper that calls through and then notifies:

```tsx
const original = history.pushState;
history.pushState = function (...args) {
  const result = original.apply(this, args);
  emit();
  return result;
};
```

`apply(this, args)` rather than `original(...args)` keeps `this` bound to the
history object, which matters because the native method requires it.

## Hint 3

"Patched once, restored on last unsubscribe" is a reference count. Keep a
`Set` of listeners at module scope; install the patch when the set goes from
empty to non-empty, and restore when it goes back to empty. Restoring means
holding the original functions somewhere — a module variable — and assigning
them back.

Watch the ordering: install before adding the listener, and remove the listener
before checking whether to restore, or a re-subscribe during teardown patches
a patched function.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider what a *module-level* store buys you over a per-component one. Every
consumer wants the same location, so there is exactly one thing to subscribe to
and no reason for each component to install its own listener. That also makes
the patch tractable: patching a global from inside a component effect, once per
mounted component, is how you end up with a wrapper wrapping a wrapper.

## Hint 2

The restore-on-last-unsubscribe requirement is more than tidiness. In a test
environment, modules persist across test cases while components mount and
unmount; a patch that is never removed accumulates, and by the twentieth test
each `pushState` call runs twenty wrappers. Symptoms are mysterious slowness and
duplicate notifications, and the cause is invisible in the component under test.

## Hint 3

There is a newer alternative worth knowing: the **Navigation API**
(`navigation.addEventListener("navigate", …)`) reports every navigation
including `pushState`, with no patching at all. It is not universally supported
yet, which is why the patch remains the portable answer, but it is what this
code will eventually be replaced by — and knowing it exists tells you the
patching was always a workaround, not a design.
