| `/` | `/` | `{}` |
| `/Users` | `/users` | `null` |

Rules that follow from those:

- a trailing slash on either side is insignificant;
- a parameter never matches an empty segment;
- parameter values are percent-decoded;
- a `*` segment is a catch-all matching one or more remaining segments, captured
  undecoded as a single joined string under the key `*`;
- matching is case-sensitive for literal segments;
- no match returns `null`, never `{}` — an empty object is the correct answer
  for a pattern with no parameters that *did* match.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc05_routing_url_state ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Resist reaching for a regular expression built by string substitution. It is the
first instinct and it goes wrong at exactly the cases in the table: escaping
literal segments that contain regex characters, the trailing slash, and the
distinction between "no match" and "matched with no parameters". Splitting on
`/` and walking segments is more code and far easier to get right.

## Hint 2

Normalise both sides the same way before comparing, or the trailing-slash cases
each need their own branch:

```tsx
const norm = (s: string) => s.replace(/\/+$/, "");
const patternSegments = norm(pattern).split("/");
const pathSegments = norm(pathname).split("/");
```

Note what this does to `/`: it becomes `""`, which splits to `[""]` — one empty
segment on each side, which compare equal. That is the `/` → `{}` row.

## Hint 3

Handle the catch-all before the length check, because it is the one case where
the lengths legitimately differ. When you reach a `*` in the pattern, everything
remaining in the path joins into the value and the match succeeds — provided
there is at least one segment left, which is what makes `/docs` not match
`/docs/*`.

For everything else: equal lengths, then segment by segment, `:name` captures
(rejecting an empty value) and literals compare exactly.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before writing the matcher, write the failing cases down as questions about
intent, because they are design decisions rather than technical ones. Should
`/users/` be the same route as `/users`? Almost always yes, and search engines
agree. Should `/Users` match `/users`? Almost always no — paths are
case-sensitive by specification, and treating them otherwise means the same page
has infinite URLs.

## Hint 2

The decoding rule is the one with a real trap behind it. A path segment
containing an encoded slash — `%2F` — decodes to a slash, so if you decode
*before* splitting, `/files/a%2Fb` becomes `/files/a/b` and matches a completely
different route. Split first, decode the captured values afterwards. This
ordering bug is the reason some frameworks reject `%2F` in paths outright.

## Hint 3

On `null` versus `{}`: it is tempting to return an empty object for no match and
let the caller check emptiness, and it is wrong, because a pattern with no
parameters that matched correctly also produces an empty object. Making "did it
match" and "what did it capture" two different questions with two different
answer types is what stops the caller from having to guess.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`URLSearchParams` supports repeated keys and has three methods for them that are
easy to confuse. `get` returns only the first value. `getAll` returns all of
them. `set` replaces every occurrence with one value — which is the method that
silently collapses a multi-select to a single item and is the bug this exercise
is built around. `append` adds without removing.

## Hint 2

The clean write is delete-then-append rather than trying to surgically edit:

```tsx
const url = new URL(window.location.href);
url.searchParams.delete(key);
for (const value of [...next].sort()) url.searchParams.append(key, value);
```

If `next` is empty the loop does nothing and the key stays deleted, which is the
"no `?tags=`" requirement satisfied without a special case.

## Hint 3

The sorting requirement is about determinism, not aesthetics. Without it, the
same logical set produces different URL strings depending on the order the user
clicked, which breaks anything using the URL as a cache key, makes two
equivalent links look different in a bug report, and produces churn in snapshot
tests. Note that reading is *not* sorted — `values` reports the URL as it is.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that the URL is doing something React state would need a `Set` for, and
doing it in the format the server will eventually receive. `?tags=a&tags=b` is
how HTML forms have submitted checkbox groups since 1995, and every server
framework parses it into a list without configuration. Encoding a JSON array
into a single parameter works but throws that away.

## Hint 2

The push-versus-replace choice here is worth a moment. A checkbox toggle is a
discrete decision, so it pushes — a user who ticks four filters and presses Back
expects the fourth to come off. Contrast with ex2's search input. The rule
holds: discrete choices push, continuous adjustments replace.

## Hint 3

There is an ordering subtlety in `toggle` that the examples pin down. Removing
"the one occurrence" matters if the URL somehow contains a duplicate —
`?tags=a&tags=a` — which can happen from a hand-edited link or a buggy earlier
version. Deciding whether your set semantics deduplicate on read or on write is
a real choice; deduplicating on write, as the sorted rebuild does, means the URL
self-heals the first time the user touches it.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Do the matching and the rendering as two separate passes and both get simpler.
First walk the route tree and produce an array of matched route definitions
plus the accumulated parameters. Then fold that array from the inside out,
building each element with the previous one as its outlet.

## Hint 2

The fold is the part worth writing carefully:

```tsx
let outlet: ReactNode = null;
for (let i = chain.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
  outlet = chain[i].element({ params, outlet });
}
return <>{outlet}</>;
```

Building from the end means each iteration already has its child in hand.

## Hint 3

The "does not unmount" requirement is not something you implement — it is
something you avoid breaking. React preserves a component instance when it sees
the same element type at the same position in the tree. So as long as the layout
element is produced by the same function on both renders and sits at the same
place, its state survives.

What breaks it: giving the layout a `key` derived from the pathname, or wrapping
it in a differently-shaped tree per route. Both are easy to do accidentally.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The value of nested routes is not tidiness, it is state and network preservation.
A layout that holds a sidebar's scroll position, an open filter panel, or a
loaded list of teams should keep all of that while the user moves between its
children. Flattening the routes means the layout unmounts and remounts on every
navigation, and the user watches the sidebar reset.

## Hint 2

Note what the outlet pattern is: a slot, exactly as in the component API sector.
The layout does not know which child it is rendering, does not import it, and
places it. The only difference from an ordinary `children` prop is where the
content comes from — the route match rather than the call site — which is why
routers name it something else.

## Hint 3

Parameter accumulation has a collision case worth deciding consciously. If a
parent captures `:id` and a child also captures `:id`, one shadows the other.
Most routers let the child win, on the grounds that it is nearer. Whatever you
choose, the real lesson is to avoid the situation by naming parameters
specifically — `teamId` and `memberId`, not `id` twice — which also makes call
sites readable.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1 The reason a redirect-in-an-effect is a real bug: effects run after commit. So the sequence is render the protected page, commit it, paint it, *then* run the effect that redirects. The user sees the page. Their browser has requested its data. Its effects have run. On a page showing somebody else's account, that is not cosmetic. ## Hint 2 Decide during render and return early: ```tsx if (!user) return

Redirecting…

; return <>{children}; ``` The `children` prop being an element is not the same as it being rendered — `` creates the `Settings` *element* (cheap, just an object) but React only calls the component if it appears in the returned tree. So an early return genuinely prevents the mount. ## Hint 3 The lazy component must be created at module scope, not inside a render. `lazy()` returns a component that caches its import promise; calling `lazy()` again produces a *different* component with a *different* cache, so a fresh import starts on every render and the Suspense fallback never goes away. For the Suspense placement: put it inside `RequireAuth`'s children, so an unauthorised user does not see "Loading settings…" for a page they will never get.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach the guard by asking what the protected component does on mount, not
what it looks like. It probably fetches. It may write an analytics event, open a
websocket, or start a subscription. All of those happen in effects, and all of
them run before your redirect effect does — so "it only flashed for a frame" is
about the visual half of a problem whose other half is network requests made on
behalf of a user who is not allowed to make them.

## Hint 2

There is a related pattern worth recognising as wrong. Rendering the children
inside a wrapper with `display: none` while redirecting hides the content
visually and mounts it fully — every effect runs, every request fires. Anything
that keeps the component in the tree fails this requirement, whatever CSS you
apply.

## Hint 3

On the `lazy()` placement: this mistake produces a specific and confusing
symptom. The route never finishes loading, the fallback flickers or persists,
and the network panel shows the same chunk requested repeatedly. It happens most
often when someone parameterises the import — `lazy(() => import(path))` inside
a component — and the fix is always to hoist the `lazy()` call to a module
constant or a `useMemo` with a genuinely stable dependency.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Browsers restore scroll for real document navigations because they know when the
document finished loading. For a `pushState` navigation they have no such
signal — your content might arrive in three seconds — so they guess, usually
badly. `history.scrollRestoration = "manual"` turns the guess off so your
restoration is not fighting theirs.

## Hint 2

The place to store the offset is `history.state` on the entry you are leaving:

```tsx
history.replaceState({ ...history.state, scrollY: window.scrollY }, "");
```

Keyed by entry rather than by pathname, because the same path visited twice can
legitimately have two different positions — think of a list you scrolled, opened
an item from, went back to, then opened a different item from.

## Hint 3

`element.focus()` scrolls the element into view by default, which would
immediately undo your restoration. `focus({ preventScroll: true })` is the
option you want, and it is the detail that makes these two features coexist
rather than fight.

The heading needs `tabIndex={-1}` to be focusable at all — the same
programmatically-focusable trick from the accessibility sector.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Both halves of this exercise fix a regression that single-page applications
introduced. A real navigation resets scroll, moves focus to the top of the new
document, and announces the new title. A `pushState` navigation does none of
those, so the user is left mid-page with focus on a link that no longer exists,
in a document whose title may not even have changed.

## Hint 2

The focus target is a judgement call. Moving focus to `<body>` resets the tab
order but announces nothing. Moving it to the `<h1>` announces the new page's
name, which is why it is the common recommendation. Some applications use a
visually hidden live region to announce "Navigated to Settings" instead, which
avoids moving focus at all — defensible, and harder to get right.

## Hint 3

On ordering: the restore must happen after the new view committed, or you are
scrolling a document that is still the old height and the browser clamps you to
its maximum. A `useLayoutEffect` in the new view runs after its commit and
before paint, which is the right slot — with the caveat that if content loads
asynchronously the height changes again afterwards, which is why real
implementations either wait for the data or re-apply the offset when the height
settles.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Make the whole state one value and write it in one place. If you have five
separate setters that each edit one parameter, the reset-page rule forces two
of them to run together and you get two history entries. A single
`update(partial)` that merges into the parsed state and serialises the result is
one write by construction.

## Hint 2

The reset rule then becomes a small piece of logic inside that one function:

```tsx
function update(patch: Partial<ListState>, mode: "push" | "replace") {
  const current = parseListState(window.location.search);
  const resets = "q" in patch || "tags" in patch || "sort" in patch;
  const next = { ...current, ...patch, ...(resets ? { page: 1 } : null) };
  write(serialiseListState(next), mode);
}
```

## Hint 3

For "omit defaults", write `serialiseListState` against a defaults object and
compare field by field. Two things to watch: `tags` is an array, so compare its
length rather than the value, and `page: 1` is the default so a URL for page one
carries no `page` at all — which means `parseListState("")` and
`parseListState("?page=1")` must produce the same object, or your round-trip is
not stable.

Totality is worth being deliberate about: `Number("banana")` is `NaN`, and
`NaN < 1` is false, so a naive clamp lets it through. Check
`Number.isInteger` explicitly.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by writing `parseListState` and `serialiseListState` and testing them
against each other, before any component exists. If `parse(serialise(state))`
does not deep-equal `state` for every state you can construct, everything built
on top will have a bug you cannot see. That round-trip property is the whole
foundation, and it is much easier to establish in isolation.

## Hint 2

The "one history entry" rule has a user-facing meaning worth holding onto.
History entries are states the user was in. If changing a filter writes twice —
once for the filter, once for the page reset — then Back takes the user to a
state that existed for a microsecond and that they never saw: the new filter
with the old page number. They press Back expecting the previous view and get a
third thing. Every "the back button does something weird" bug report has this
shape.

## Hint 3

The totality requirement is about a real threat model, not tidiness. URLs are
edited by hand, truncated by chat clients, mangled by email link-rewriters, and
generated by an older version of your own code. A parser that throws on
unexpected input turns any of those into a white page. A parser that clamps and
defaults turns them into a slightly wrong view, which the user can fix by
clicking something.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count the sources of truth. There is `selected` in React state, and there is
`team` in the URL, and the effect exists to copy one into the other. Any design
with a copying step has a direction of flow that only works one way — here,
state to URL — so the other direction, URL to state, is simply missing. Back
changes the URL, and nothing tells the state.

## Hint 2

The fix removes rather than adds. Read the parameter during render and use it as
the select's value; write it in the change handler. That is the whole component,
and it has no state to drift and no effect to fire on mount.

```tsx
const selected = new URLSearchParams(search).get("team") ?? "";
```

## Hint 3

Fault 2 disappears for free once the effect is gone, which is the tell that all
three share a root cause. Fault 3 needs one deliberate line: treat the empty
string as "delete the parameter" at the write boundary, exactly as in ex2.

For `ROOT_CAUSE`, name the mistake rather than the symptom — the phrase you are
reaching for involves copying state that the browser already owns.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A useful reframing: which component owns `team`? In the broken version, both the
URL and the component claim to. Ownership is not shareable — for every piece of
state there must be exactly one place that decides its value, and everybody else
reads. Here the browser owns it, because the browser can change it without
asking you, so the component must be a reader.

## Hint 2

Notice how an effect used for synchronisation is almost always a smell. The
React documentation has a whole page named "You Might Not Need an Effect", and
its largest section is about effects that copy one piece of state into another.
The general test: if an effect's only job is `setB(f(a))` or "write `a`
somewhere else", the value should probably have been derived during render or
never duplicated in the first place.

## Hint 3

There is a legitimate exception to "never mirror", and it is worth stating so
you do not over-apply the rule. A text input that writes to the URL on every
keystroke has a latency problem: the write, the subscription, the re-render.
Some applications keep local state for the input's responsiveness and debounce
the URL write. That is a deliberate, documented exception made for a measured
reason — and it still treats the URL as the source of truth for everything
derived from it, so the drift is bounded to the input itself.

lessons.title: V3·RC6 — Testing components the way users use them
lessons.summary: A test that asserts on state, class names or a snapshot passes when the component is broken and fails when it is merely refactored. This sector is about the alternative: driving components through the accessibility tree with real event sequences, so the test breaks exactly when the user experience does.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC6 — Testing components the way users use them

Here is a test that is worse than no test:

```tsx
const wrapper = shallow(<Counter />);
expect(wrapper.state("count")).toBe(0);
wrapper.instance().increment();
expect(wrapper.state("count")).toBe(1);
```

It passes if the button is not wired up. It passes if the number never renders.
It passes if the component is invisible, unreachable by keyboard, or throws in
an effect. And it fails the moment somebody renames `count` to `value`, which is
a change no user could detect.

The principle that replaced this is one sentence, from Kent C. Dodds: *the more
your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can
give you*. Everything in Testing Library follows from it. You find elements the
way a user finds them — by their role and their name. You interact the way a
user interacts — a real click has a pointerdown, a mousedown, a focus, a
mouseup and a click, in that order. You assert on what the user can perceive.

There is a second payoff that people underrate. Querying by role means your test
walks the same accessibility tree a screen reader walks. If `getByRole("button",
{ name: "Save" })` cannot find your control, neither can a screen reader user,
and neither can voice control. The accessibility sector's rules become
enforceable rather than aspirational, checked on every commit, for free.

## Concept — queries, interactions, async, and boundaries

**The query ladder** is a priority order, and it is a design instruction as much
as a testing one:

1. `getByRole` — with the `name` option. Covers almost everything, and matches
   the accessibility tree.
2. `getByLabelText` — form fields, where the label is the point.
3. `getByPlaceholderText`, `getByText`, `getByDisplayValue` — text a user reads.
4. `getByAltText`, `getByTitle` — images and the rare title.
5. `getByTestId` — the escape hatch, for things with no perceivable identity.

Reaching for `getByTestId` is a signal. Sometimes it is right — a chart canvas
has no accessible identity worth inventing. Usually it means the component is
missing a role or a name, and the fix belongs in the component.

**Three query prefixes, three failure modes:**

| prefix | not found | found | use for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `getBy` | throws immediately | returns | it should be there now |
| `queryBy` | returns `null` | returns | asserting absence |
| `findBy` | rejects after a timeout | resolves | it will be there soon |

`getBy` for an absent element throws with the whole rendered DOM in the message,
which is far more useful than `expect(queryBy…).toBeTruthy()` failing with
"expected null to be truthy". Use `queryBy` only for `not.toBeInTheDocument()`.

**`userEvent`, not `fireEvent`.** `fireEvent.click(el)` dispatches one synthetic
click. `await user.click(el)` dispatches the whole sequence a browser would, so
it catches a handler on `mousedown`, respects `pointer-events: none`, moves
focus, and refuses to click a disabled control. `fireEvent.change` sets a
value in one go; `await user.type(el, "abc")` fires three keydown/keypress/input
/keyup cycles, which is what a `maxLength` or a keystroke handler actually sees.

**`await` everything.** `userEvent` returns promises and `findBy*` returns
promises, and both wrap their work in `act` internally. Which means the modern
answer to the act warning is not "wrap it in `act`" — it is "you forgot an
`await`, or something updated state outside a user interaction". An act warning
you cannot explain is a real bug: usually a state update after unmount, or a
timer nobody cleaned up.

**Mock at the boundary, not in the middle.** Stubbing `global.fetch` per test
couples every test to the shape of your fetch calls. Mocking your own
`api/invoices.ts` module means the test no longer exercises the code that parses
the response. Intercepting at the network layer — MSW-style request handlers —
keeps everything from the component to the request serialisation under test, and
the handlers are reusable across component tests, integration tests, and the
browser during development.

**Do not test what the user cannot observe.** No state assertions, no instance
methods, no counting renders in a behaviour test, no full-DOM snapshots — a
snapshot fails on every change and communicates nothing about which changes are
wrong, so people update them without reading.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/v3rc06_testing_like_users

## Notes

**The query priority is a design tool.** When `getByRole` cannot find something,
you have learned a fact about the component, not about the test. That feedback
loop is the reason teams that adopt role queries end up with more accessible
applications without running an audit — the audit runs on every commit.

**`getByRole` computes the accessible name** using the same algorithm the
browser uses, which is why `{ name: /save/i }` matches a button labelled by
`aria-labelledby`, by `aria-label`, or by its own text. It is also why role
queries are the slowest ones: the name computation walks the tree. On a very
large DOM this shows up, and the answer is to scope the query with `within(…)`
rather than to abandon roles.

**`findBy` is `getBy` plus `waitFor`.** `waitFor` polls — every 50ms by default
— and also re-runs on DOM mutations via a `MutationObserver`, until the callback
stops throwing or the timeout expires. It does not know about your promises; it
just retries. Which is why `await findByText("Done")` is reliable and
`await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 100))` is a flaky test waiting to happen.

**`act` is React's "I am about to do something that updates state" bracket.** It
flushes effects and state updates so that by the time it returns, the DOM
reflects them. `render`, `userEvent` and `findBy*` all wrap their work in it.
The warning "An update to X was not wrapped in act(...)" means state changed
outside any of those — a timer, a promise resolution, a subscription — and in a
test that usually means the update escaped the interaction that caused it.

**Fake timers break `userEvent` by default**, because `userEvent` waits between
its synthetic events using real timers that are now frozen, and the test hangs.
`userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })` gives it a way to
move the clock itself.

**Testing a hook through a component is the default** because that is how hooks
are used. `renderHook` is right when the hook's surface is genuinely the return
value and building a host component would only obscure it — a `useDebounce`, a
`useLocalStorage`. It is wrong when the hook's job is to affect rendering, since
then you are testing the return value and not the outcome.

## ex1 — what disappears when you climb the ladder

Rewriting the suite is mechanical; the interesting part is that one or two of
the original assertions have no equivalent, because they were checking something
the user cannot perceive. Deleting them is correct, and noticing why is the
exercise.

## ex2 — the sequence matters

`fireEvent.click` on a control whose handler is on `mousedown` passes and
proves nothing. `user.click` fires the full sequence, so the test exercises the
same path a real click does — including focus moving, which is what makes a
subsequent `user.keyboard("{Enter}")` go to the right element.

## ex3 — no sleeps

`findBy` resolves as soon as the element appears rather than after a fixed
delay, so the suite is both faster and more reliable. The `queryBy` half is the
one people get wrong: `expect(getByText("Error")).not.toBeInTheDocument()` can
never pass, because `getBy` throws before the assertion runs.

## ex4 — the boundary

Handlers at the network layer keep your fetch code, your response parsing and
your error mapping inside the test. Stubbing your own module removes exactly the
code most likely to be wrong. The other benefit is reuse: the same handlers run
in the browser during development, so a mock that drifts from reality is
visible immediately rather than only in CI.

## ex5 — two clocks

The failure without `advanceTimers` is a hang, not an assertion error, which
sends people looking in the wrong place. Once wired, the pattern is: type, then
`vi.advanceTimersByTime(300)`, then `await findBy…`.

## ex6 — the host component

The host renders the hook's output as text and exposes buttons for its actions,
so the test drives it the way a component would. It is more code than
`renderHook` and it tests the thing that actually ships.

## ex7 — the repair belongs upstream

The test asserts `toHaveClass("is-open")`, which is an implementation detail —
rename the class and the test fails while the user notices nothing. The right
fix is `aria-expanded` on the trigger, which is simultaneously the accessible
behaviour and the assertable one.

## ex8 — the warning was right

A `setTimeout` that resolves after the component unmounted sets state on an
unmounted component. React 18 stopped warning about that specific case, but the
act warning in tests still surfaces it, and the underlying leak — a timer nobody
cleared — is real in production too.

## challenge — testing a widget whose focus is a lie

`document.activeElement` is the input, always, so every assertion about "which
option is focused" has to read `aria-activedescendant` instead. That is the
whole difficulty, and it is a good demonstration that the test should assert
what the user's assistive technology observes.

## review1 — losing nothing

The discipline is to enumerate what the old suite genuinely checked before
deleting it. Most snapshot lines check nothing; one or two encode a real
requirement that must survive the rewrite.

## Further reading

- [Testing Library — About queries](https://testing-library.com/docs/queries/about/#priority) — the priority ladder, in its canonical form.
- [Testing Library — `user-event`](https://testing-library.com/docs/user-event/intro) — the event sequences, and `setup({ advanceTimers })`.
- [Testing Library — Common mistakes](https://kentcdodds.com/blog/common-mistakes-with-react-testing-library) — the definitive list, still accurate.
- [MSW — Getting started](https://mswjs.io/docs/getting-started) — request handlers at the network boundary.
- [Vitest — Fake timers](https://vitest.dev/api/vi.html#vi-usefaketimers) — what is faked and what is not.
- [react.dev — Testing overview](https://react.dev/learn) — including why `act` exists.

# V3·RC6 — Testing components the way users use them

## Why this sector exists

Test suites fail in two directions. A **false negative** — a test that fails when
nothing is broken — costs time and, worse, teaches the team to ignore red
builds. A **false positive** — a test that passes when the feature is broken —
costs an incident. Implementation-detail testing produces both at once, because
it is coupled tightly to things that change freely and loosely to the things
that matter.

The user-centric approach is not a style preference. It is a strategy for making
the coupling match reality: tests break when behaviour changes and survive when
structure changes.

## Concepts

### The query ladder in practice

```tsx
// Bad: coupled to markup that is free to change.
getByTestId("submit-btn");
container.querySelector(".btn-primary");

// Good: coupled to what the user perceives.
getByRole("button", { name: /save changes/i });
getByLabelText("Email address");
getByRole("alert");                    // error messages
getByRole("status");                   // polite announcements
getByRole("tab", { selected: true });  // state, not class
```

The `name` option is where most of the value is, and it is why the ladder starts
at roles: `getByRole("button")` alone matches every button on the page, and
`{ name }` is what makes the query specific *and* meaningful.

Role queries also accept state options that map onto ARIA:
`{ expanded: true }`, `{ checked: false }`, `{ selected: true }`,
`{ pressed: true }`, `{ current: "page" }`. Every one of those is an assertion
you would otherwise have written against a class name.

### `userEvent` versus `fireEvent`

```tsx
const user = userEvent.setup();

await user.click(button);        // pointer + mouse + focus + click
await user.type(input, "hello"); // per-character keydown/input/keyup
await user.keyboard("{Enter}");
await user.tab();                // real tab-order traversal
await user.selectOptions(select, "b");
await user.upload(fileInput, file);
```

`user.tab()` is the one to remember: it traverses in the browser's actual tab
order, so it will discover a positive `tabIndex` or an unreachable control
without you asserting anything about the DOM.

### Async, correctly

```tsx
// Arrival: findBy resolves when it appears.
expect(await screen.findByRole("row", { name: /invoice 42/i })).toBeVisible();

// Absence, after something settled.
await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByRole("status"));
expect(screen.queryByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument();

// Never:
await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 500));
```

`waitFor` takes a callback that must throw until the condition holds. Putting a
side effect inside it means the side effect runs on every poll, which is a
common and confusing mistake.

### Mocking at the boundary

```tsx
const server = setupServer(
  http.get("/api/invoices", () => HttpResponse.json([{ id: "1", total: 10 }]))
);

beforeAll(() => server.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: "error" }));
afterEach(() => server.resetHandlers());
afterAll(() => server.close());

it("shows the failure state", async () => {
  server.use(http.get("/api/invoices", () => new HttpResponse(null, { status: 500 })));
  render(<Invoices />);
  expect(await screen.findByRole("alert")).toHaveTextContent(/could not load/i);
});
```

`onUnhandledRequest: "error"` is the setting that makes this trustworthy: a
request you forgot to handle fails loudly instead of hanging.

### Testing a hook through a host

```tsx
function Host({ delay }: { delay: number }) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState("");
  const debounced = useDebounced(value, delay);
  return (
    <>
      <input aria-label="value" value={value} onChange={(e) => setValue(e.target.value)} />
      <output>{debounced}</output>
    </>
  );
}
```

The host is disposable and exists only in the test file. It is more honest than
`renderHook` because it exercises the hook inside a render cycle with real
re-renders.

## Common mistakes

- **`expect(getByText(x)).not.toBeInTheDocument()`.** `getBy` throws first;
  this assertion can never pass. Use `queryBy`.
- **`await waitFor(() => {})` with a side effect inside.** Runs on every poll.
- **Wrapping things in `act` to silence a warning.** The warning was pointing at
  a real update happening outside your interaction.
- **`fireEvent` for user actions.** Misses focus, ordering, and disabled state.
- **Not awaiting `userEvent`.** Its methods return promises; unawaited, the
  assertions race the events.
- **Fake timers without `advanceTimers`.** The test hangs rather than fails.
- **Mocking your own modules.** Removes the code most likely to be broken.
- **Full-DOM snapshots.** Fail on every change, communicate nothing, get
  updated unread.
- **Testing a `useEffect` by asserting it ran.** Assert its observable effect.
- **`screen.debug()` left in.** Slow and noisy in CI.
- **Shared state between tests.** `cleanup` runs automatically in modern
  setups, but module-level caches, MSW handlers and fake timers do not reset
  themselves.

## The interview angle

The question is often "how do you decide what to test?" and the answer that
lands has two parts. First, a level heuristic: pure logic gets unit tests,
anything involving rendering and interaction gets a component test driven
through the accessibility tree, and the two or three flows whose failure would
be an incident get an end-to-end test in a real browser. Second, a coupling
argument: tests should be coupled to the contract with the user and decoupled
from structure, which is exactly what role queries and `userEvent` buy you.

If you want to sound like you have done this in anger, mention that role queries
double as an accessibility check, and that an act warning is usually a real bug
rather than a testing nuisance.

## Check yourself

1. State the guiding principle of Testing Library in one sentence.
2. Give the query priority order and say what reaching for `getByTestId`
   signals.
3. What does `getBy` do that `queryBy` does not, and when is each right?
4. Why can `expect(getByText(…)).not.toBeInTheDocument()` never pass?
5. Name three things `user.click` does that `fireEvent.click` does not.
6. What does `waitFor` actually do while it waits?
7. What is `act` for, and what does an act warning usually indicate?
8. Why do fake timers make `userEvent` hang, and what is the fix?
9. Why is mocking your own API module worse than intercepting the request?
10. What does `onUnhandledRequest: "error"` protect you from?
11. When is `renderHook` the right tool, and when is a host component better?
12. Why does asserting `toHaveClass("is-open")` produce a fragile test, and what
    would you assert instead?
13. Give two assertions that a full-DOM snapshot makes and one it does not.
14. How would you test that a component does *not* fetch when it is not visible?
15. What does `user.tab()` verify that no explicit assertion would?

# Long reading — what the test runner is actually doing

## jsdom is not a browser, and it matters where

Component tests in a Node runner execute against **jsdom**, a JavaScript
implementation of the DOM and a subset of the browser's APIs. It has an element
tree, event dispatch, `getComputedStyle`, `MutationObserver`, and enough of the
HTML specification to run most application code.

What it does not have is layout. Every element is zero by zero.
`getBoundingClientRect()` returns zeros, `offsetHeight` is `0`,
`scrollIntoView` is a no-op, and `IntersectionObserver` and `ResizeObserver` are
absent unless you polyfill them. Anything from the animation and layout sector
is therefore untestable in jsdom without stubbing, and that is the correct
boundary: measurement and jank belong in a real browser, driven by Playwright.

jsdom also does not paint, so visibility assertions are approximate.
`toBeVisible()` checks `display`, `visibility`, `opacity`, `hidden` and the
`hidden` attribute — not whether something is behind an overlay or scrolled out
of view. Knowing the edge of the tool prevents both false confidence and a fruitless
afternoon.

## How queries and `waitFor` work

`getByRole` is implemented on top of `dom-accessibility-api`, a JavaScript
reimplementation of the accname and role-mapping specifications. It walks the
element, resolves its implicit or explicit role, and computes its accessible
name using the same priority order a browser does. This is genuinely a
reimplementation, so it can diverge from a specific browser in edge cases — but
for the mainstream cases it is faithful, and it is the reason a role query is a
meaningful accessibility signal rather than a syntactic one.

It is also why role queries are the expensive ones. Every candidate element
needs a name computation, which walks its subtree. On a page with thousands of
nodes this is measurable, and the fix is `within(section).getByRole(...)` to
narrow the search rather than switching to `querySelector`.

`waitFor` combines two strategies: a `MutationObserver` on the container, so it
retries immediately when the DOM changes, and an interval, so it also retries
when the condition depends on something other than a mutation. It has no
knowledge of your promises, your timers, or React's scheduler — it simply retries
a callback until it stops throwing. That naivety is a feature: it works with any
async mechanism, including ones that did not exist when it was written.

## Where the industry came from

**Enzyme**, from Airbnb, dominated React testing from 2015 to about 2020. Its
signature feature was **shallow rendering**: render one component without
rendering its children, then assert on the resulting element tree. The appeal
was isolation and speed, and the API let you reach into state, call instance
methods, and find components by class.

The problems accumulated. Shallow rendering means the thing you assert on never
existed as DOM, so it cannot tell you whether the component works. Every
assertion was coupled to internal structure, so refactors broke suites wholesale.
And when hooks arrived in 2019, shallow rendering had no coherent story — there
were no instances to inspect, and effects did not run.

**react-testing-library** (2018) inverted every one of those choices: render the
whole tree into a real DOM, expose no way to reach internals, and query the way
a user would. The trade was slower tests for tests that mean something, and the
industry took it. Enzyme's React 18 adapter never fully materialised, which
settled the matter.

The residue of the enzyme era is still visible in codebases: `data-testid` on
everything, snapshot files nobody reads, and tests named "renders correctly".
Recognising them as artefacts of an older strategy makes them easier to replace
than to defend.

## `act`, concurrency, and the warning

React needs to know when a batch of work is finished so it can flush state
updates and effects before you assert. `act` is that bracket. In practice you
almost never write it, because `render`, every `userEvent` method and every
`findBy*` wrap their own work in it.

The warning appears when a state update happens outside all of those. The three
common causes, in order of frequency: an unawaited promise that resolves after
the test's synchronous section; a timer that fires later; and a subscription
that emits. All three are the same underlying situation — something updated the
component and the test was not watching — and all three are worth investigating
rather than silencing, because in production the same code paths produce updates
after unmount, memory retention, and requests nobody is waiting for.

Concurrent rendering does not change this, but it does change how much you
should assume about intermediate states. React may render a component more than
once for a single update, and may discard renders. Any test that counts renders
is testing an implementation detail of the scheduler, which is exactly the kind
of coupling this sector argues against.

## Speed, flakiness, and what to test where

A component test in jsdom typically costs single-digit milliseconds to render
plus whatever your queries and waits take. Role queries and `waitFor` dominate a
slow suite far more often than rendering does. Scoping queries with `within` and
using `findBy` instead of long `waitFor` chains is usually worth more than any
configuration change.

Flakiness in a component suite has a small number of causes: real timers in
async code, shared module state between tests, unhandled requests that hang, and
assertions that race an interaction because an `await` was omitted. All four are
fixable, and a flaky suite that gets `retry: 2` added instead is a suite that
will stop being trusted.

The level heuristic that holds up: **unit tests** for pure functions — parsers,
reducers, formatters, the path matcher from the routing sector — where they are
fast and precise. **Component tests** for anything involving rendering,
interaction and state, which is most of a front end. **End-to-end tests**, in a
real browser, for the two or three flows whose failure is an incident — sign in,
checkout, the thing that takes money — plus anything that genuinely needs
layout, real navigation, or a service worker.

## When not to write a component test

Do not write one to test a pure function that happens to live in a component
file. Extract it and unit-test it; you get a faster, more precise test and a
more reusable function.

Do not write one for visual appearance. jsdom has no layout, so an assertion
about spacing, overflow, or z-order is either meaningless or a lie. Visual
regression tooling in a real browser is the tool for that, and no amount of
`toHaveStyle` substitutes.

Do not write one to pin down every branch of a component with many props. Eight
prop combinations produce eight slow tests that mostly assert the same thing.
Test the behaviour that differs and let the type system handle the combinations
— which is another argument for the discriminated unions from the component API
sector: a case that cannot be constructed does not need a test.

And do not write one where the honest answer is an end-to-end test. If the
thing you are worried about is "does this work when the real API responds
slowly, in Safari, after a redirect", no amount of jsdom will tell you. Knowing
which question you are asking is most of testing.

## Exercise 1 — climb the query ladder

Edit `ex1/solution.tsx`. **This mission asks you to write the test file.** The
stub provides a `LoginForm` component; your file exports its test suite.

The existing suite (in the stub's comments) queries everything by test id:

```tsx

getByTestId("login-password");
getByTestId("login-submit");
getByTestId("login-error");
```

Write a `describe("LoginForm")` block using `vitest` and
`@testing-library/react` with four tests, using **no `getByTestId` at all**:

1. the email and password fields are found by their labels, and both start
   empty;
2. the submit control is found by `getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i })`;
3. submitting with an empty email shows an error found by
   `getByRole("alert")`, whose text mentions `email`;
4. with valid input, no `alert` is in the document — asserted with `queryByRole`.

Your file must export the suite as a module (a plain `.tsx` file containing
`describe`/`it` at the top level) and must not import `screen.getByTestId` or
use `container.querySelector`.

The gate runs your suite against the correct component and asserts all four
tests pass; then runs it against a mutated component whose submit button has
lost its accessible name, and asserts your suite **fails** — a suite that still
passes was not really querying by name.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start from the question "how would a person find this element?" They would look
for the field labelled Email, and for the button that says Sign in. Those are
`getByLabelText("Email")` and `getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i })`. Test
ids answer a different question — "which element did the developer tag" — and
that is why they survive breaking the user experience.

## Hint 2

The `name` option is where the value is. `getByRole("button")` on a page with
three buttons is ambiguous and throws a helpful error listing all of them.
`getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i })` is specific *and* asserts that the
control has an accessible name at all — which is what the gate's mutated variant
is checking.

Use a regular expression rather than an exact string for anything with
punctuation or casing you do not want to pin down.

## Hint 3

For the fourth test, remember which prefix asserts absence. `getByRole` throws
when nothing matches, so `expect(getByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument()`
can never reach the assertion. `queryByRole` returns `null`, which is what
`not.toBeInTheDocument()` needs.

And prefer `role="alert"` over finding the error by its text: the role is the
contract (it is announced assertively), the text is a wording decision that a
copywriter may change tomorrow.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice what happens to the suite's *meaning* as you rewrite it. The test-id
version passes if the button is a `div`, if it has no accessible name, and if
the error message is announced to nobody. The role version fails in all three
cases. You have not just changed the syntax of the queries — you have added
three accessibility assertions you did not write.

## Hint 2

That is the argument for the ladder that persuades people who do not care about
tests. Adopting role queries means every commit runs a partial accessibility
audit, catching precisely the class of defect from the v3rc03 sector — a control
with no name, a div pretending to be a button, an error nobody is told about —
without anybody scheduling an audit.

## Hint 3

There is a legitimate use for `getByTestId` and it is worth being able to state,
so that avoiding it does not become superstition: an element with no
perceivable identity of its own. A chart canvas, a layout wrapper you need to
scope a `within` query to, a third-party embed. The signal to watch for is
reaching for a test id on something a *user* would name — a button, a field, a
message — because then the missing name is the bug.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — a real interaction

Edit `ex2/solution.tsx`. **Write the test file.** The stub provides an
`AddressForm` with a text input, a `<select>`, a checkbox and a submit button,
plus an `onSubmit` prop receiving the payload.

Write `describe("AddressForm")` with three tests:

1. filling every field and submitting calls `onSubmit` **once** with exactly
   `{ street: "12 Elm St", country: "no", billing: true }`;
2. the form can be completed entirely from the keyboard: `user.tab()` from the
   street field reaches the country select, then the checkbox, then the submit
   button, in that order;
3. clicking submit while the street field is empty does not call `onSubmit`, and
   focus ends up on the street field.

Constraints:

- use `userEvent`, never `fireEvent`;
- `await` every `userEvent` call;
- assert on the payload, not on any intermediate rendered value;
- do not query the DOM for the option elements to pick a country — use
  `user.selectOptions`.

The gate runs your suite against the correct component, then against a variant
whose submit handler is bound to `onMouseDown` instead of `onClick`, and asserts
your suite still passes — proving you used a real click sequence rather than a
synthetic one.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The difference the gate is probing: `fireEvent.click(el)` dispatches exactly one
`click` event. `await user.click(el)` dispatches the sequence a browser produces
— `pointerdown`, `mousedown`, `focus`, `pointerup`, `mouseup`, `click` — so a
handler attached anywhere in that sequence runs.

## Hint 2

`user.tab()` traverses the browser's real tab order, which is what makes test 2
meaningful. It is not "the next element in the DOM"; it respects `tabIndex`,
skips `disabled` and hidden controls, and would catch a positive `tabIndex`
anywhere on the page without you asserting anything about attributes.

```tsx
await user.tab();
expect(screen.getByLabelText(/country/i)).toHaveFocus();
```

## Hint 3

For the payload assertion, `toHaveBeenCalledExactlyOnceWith` (or
`toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` plus `toHaveBeenCalledWith`) is stronger than
checking the arguments alone — a double-submit bug passes a `toHaveBeenCalledWith`
check happily.

And note the ordering trap in test 3: assert `onSubmit` was not called *and*
that focus moved. A form that blocks submission but leaves the user with no idea
where the problem is has only done half the job, which is the accessibility
sector's point arriving in a test.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at this from what a synthetic event cannot tell you. `fireEvent.change(input,
{ target: { value: "abc" } })` sets the value in one assignment. It never fires a
keydown, so a `maxLength`, an input mask, a key handler that blocks digits, or a
component counting keystrokes all go untested — and all of them are exactly the
code most likely to be wrong.

## Hint 2

There is a cost worth acknowledging: `userEvent` is slower than `fireEvent`,
sometimes by an order of magnitude on a long `type`. That is a real trade, and
the answer is not to switch to `fireEvent` but to type less — seed the form with
`defaultValue`s and type only the field under test. A test that types forty
characters into six fields is testing the typing.

## Hint 3

`userEvent.setup()` returns a session and should be called once per test, before
`render`. Calling the bare `userEvent.click` (the pre-v14 API) still works but
skips the setup that installs the clipboard and pointer state, and it is the
source of confusing behaviour around focus and selection. One `const user =
userEvent.setup()` at the top of each test is the idiom.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — async without sleeping

Edit `ex3/solution.tsx`. **Write the test file.** The stub provides a
`UserCard({ userId })` that fetches a profile and renders, in turn: a
`role="status"` reading `Loading`, then the user's name in an `<h2>`, or a
`role="alert"` on failure. The stub also exports `mockProfile(id, response)`
which installs a promise the component will consume.

Write `describe("UserCard")` with four tests:

1. the loading status is present immediately after render;
2. once the profile resolves, the name appears — asserted with `findBy`;
3. once the profile resolves, the loading status is **gone** — asserted with
   `waitForElementToBeRemoved`, and the `alert` is absent, asserted with
   `queryBy`;
4. when the promise rejects, an `alert` appears and the name never does.

Constraints:

- no `setTimeout`, no `await new Promise(...)`, no fixed `waitFor` timeouts
  anywhere in your file;
- no `act` calls;
- every assertion about something that has not happened yet must use `findBy` or
  `waitFor…`, and every assertion about absence must use `queryBy`.

The gate scans your source for `setTimeout` and for a bare `act(` and fails on
either; then runs the suite against a component whose fetch resolves after an
artificial delay, and asserts your tests still pass — a suite built on fixed
sleeps would break.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A sleep encodes a guess about how long something takes. On a fast machine the
guess is wasteful; on a loaded CI runner it is wrong, and the test fails for
reasons unrelated to the code. `findBy` has no guess in it — it resolves as soon
as the element appears and only fails if it never does.

## Hint 2

The three tools and their jobs:

```tsx
await screen.findByRole("heading", { name: /ada/i });          // it will appear
await waitForElementToBeRemoved(() => screen.queryByRole("status")); // it will go
expect(screen.queryByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument();   // it is not there
```

`waitForElementToBeRemoved` takes a *callback* returning the element, not the
element itself, so it can re-query on each poll.

## Hint 3

Test 4 has an ordering subtlety. Asserting "the name never appears" is not
something you can wait for — you can only assert it at a moment. The honest
version is to wait for the `alert` to arrive, and *then* assert with `queryBy`
that the heading is absent: by the time the error state has rendered, the
success state definitively did not.

Also make sure the rejected promise is handled by the component, or Node will
report an unhandled rejection and fail the run for a reason that looks unrelated.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what makes a suite flaky, because this exercise is a vaccination
against the most common cause. A flaky test is one whose result depends on
timing you did not control. Fixed sleeps introduce exactly that dependency;
`findBy` removes it by making the *condition* the thing you wait for rather than
the clock.

## Hint 2

The rule "`getBy` for now, `findBy` for soon, `queryBy` for absent" is worth
committing to memory as three sentences rather than a table, because the failure
messages differ so much. `getBy` failing prints the entire rendered DOM, which
is the single most useful debugging output the library produces. `queryBy`
failing prints "expected null not to be null", which tells you nothing — so
never use `queryBy` where `getBy` would do.

## Hint 3

There is a related trap with `waitFor` worth avoiding while you are here. Its
callback runs on every poll, so putting a side effect inside — a click, a
`fetch`, a `console.log` — runs that side effect up to twenty times. `waitFor`
should contain assertions and nothing else, and if you find yourself wanting to
act inside one, the interaction belongs before it.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — three states, mocked at the boundary

Edit `ex4/solution.tsx`. **Write the test file.** The stub provides an
`InvoiceTable` that calls `fetch("/api/invoices")`, parses the JSON, maps it
through a `toInvoice` function that normalises the amount, and renders a table —
with a loading status and an error alert.

Write `describe("InvoiceTable")` with four tests, intercepting at the **network
boundary** using the `msw` setup the stub provides (`server`, `http`,
`HttpResponse`):

1. a successful response renders one `role="row"` per invoice plus the header
   row, and the first data row's accessible name contains the formatted amount
   `£12.50` for a raw value of `1250`;
2. a 500 response renders an `alert` mentioning `could not load`;
3. a 200 response with malformed JSON renders the same `alert` — the parse
   failure must be handled, not thrown;
4. the request carries an `Accept: application/json` header.

Constraints:

- do not stub `global.fetch`;
- do not mock `./to-invoice` or any other module of the component's own;
- configure the server with `onUnhandledRequest: "error"`;
- reset handlers between tests.

The gate runs your suite, then breaks `toInvoice`'s amount formatting and
asserts your suite fails — a suite that mocked the module would not notice.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex4
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a second reason to intercept at this layer that has nothing to do with
test quality. The same handlers run in a browser via a service worker, so the
whole team can develop against them before the backend exists, and a handler
that has drifted from the real API is discovered by a human clicking around
rather than by a test that has been green for months.

## Hint 2

Test 3 — malformed JSON — is the one people omit and the one that catches real
bugs. `response.json()` rejects on invalid JSON, and a component whose
`.catch()` only handles HTTP status codes will throw an unhandled rejection.
Whether that reaches an error boundary is exactly the v3rc02 question, and
including a malformed-response case in every data-fetching suite is a cheap
habit.

## Hint 3

A word on what *not* to assert. Do not assert the number of times `fetch` was
called, or the exact request body serialisation, unless the contract genuinely
requires it. Those are implementation details of your data layer, and pinning
them means a refactor to a different HTTP client breaks a suite that should not
care. Assert the URL, the method, and anything the server actually depends on.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — fake timers and a debounce

Edit `ex5/solution.tsx`. **Write the test file.** The stub provides a
`SearchBox({ onSearch, delayMs })` that debounces: it calls `onSearch` only
after the user has stopped typing for `delayMs`.

Write `describe("SearchBox")` with three tests, using vitest's fake timers:

1. typing `react` and advancing the clock by less than `delayMs` calls
   `onSearch` **zero** times;
2. advancing past `delayMs` calls it exactly once, with `"react"`;
3. typing, waiting past the delay, then typing again calls it twice, with
   `"react"` then `"reactive"` — proving the debounce resets rather than
   accumulating.

Constraints:

- `vi.useFakeTimers()` in `beforeEach` and `vi.useRealTimers()` in `afterEach`;
- `userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime })` — without this
  the test hangs rather than fails, and the gate checks for it;
- no real waiting anywhere;
- wrap the clock advance so that React processes the resulting update before you
  assert.

The gate runs your suite, then reruns it with a component whose debounce is
implemented with an accumulating timeout (a common bug: it never resets), and
asserts test 3 fails.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The hang, not the failure, is the thing to understand first. `userEvent` waits a
tick between its synthetic events using real timers. `vi.useFakeTimers()` freezes
those timers. So `user.type` schedules a wait that will never elapse, the promise
never resolves, and the test sits there until the runner's global timeout kills
it with a message about the test, not about the clock.

## Hint 2

`advanceTimers` is the fix and it is a single option:

```tsx
const user = userEvent.setup({ advanceTimers: vi.advanceTimersByTime });
```

It hands `userEvent` a function it can call to move the fake clock forward
itself, so its internal waits complete.

## Hint 3

After `vi.advanceTimersByTime(delayMs)`, the debounce's callback has run and
called `setState` — but React may not have processed it before your assertion.
Wrap the advance in `act`, or follow it with an `await` on a Testing Library
query that waits. This is one of the very few places where writing `act`
yourself is correct, because the update genuinely originates outside any user
interaction.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Consider first whether fake timers are the right tool here at all, because they
are a large hammer. They replace every timer in the process, which means
anything else relying on real time — a library's internal retry, an animation, a
polling health check — is also frozen and may behave strangely. A test that
merely needs to observe an eventual result is usually better served by `findBy`
with real timers and a short delay.

Where fake timers genuinely earn their place is asserting that something did
**not** happen yet, which is test 1 here. You cannot wait for an absence in real
time without guessing.

## Hint 2

The third test exists because of a specific, very common debounce bug. The
correct implementation clears the previous timeout before setting a new one; the
buggy one does not, so every keystroke schedules its own callback and the
handler fires once per character after the delay. Both implementations pass
tests 1 and 2. Only a test that types twice with a settle in between
distinguishes them.

## Hint 3

A note on hygiene that saves hours. `vi.useFakeTimers()` without a matching
`vi.useRealTimers()` leaks into every subsequent test file in the same worker,
where it manifests as unrelated tests hanging. Pair them in `beforeEach` and
`afterEach`, never in the body of a single test, and treat a suite that hangs
only when run together with others as a timer-leak symptom.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — testing a hook

Edit `ex6/solution.tsx`. **Write the test file**, and both approaches.

The stub provides two hooks:

- `useSelection<T>(items: T[])` — returns `{ selected, toggle, clear, allSelected }`
  and is used to drive a list's checkboxes;
- `useLocalStorage(key, initial)` — returns `[value, setValue]` and persists to
  `localStorage`.

Write `describe` blocks for both:

**`useSelection`** must be tested through a **host component** defined in your
test file: a list with a checkbox per item and a "Clear" button, driven with
`userEvent`. Assert that toggling two items selects both, toggling one again
deselects only it, and Clear empties the selection — all by reading checkbox
states, never the hook's return value directly.

**`useLocalStorage`** must be tested with `renderHook` from
`@testing-library/react`. Assert that it reads an existing value on mount,
writes through on update, and that `rerender` with a different key reads the new
key's value.

Also export `const WHY: string` — one sentence on why each hook got the
treatment it did.

The gate runs both blocks and additionally checks that your `useSelection` tests
contain no reference to a `result.current`.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex6
```
exercises.importantHints: ## Hint 1 There is a strong default worth stating plainly: test hooks through components unless you have a reason not to. A hook is not a unit a user interacts with; it is a fragment of a component. Testing it in isolation is testing a thing that never ships in that configuration, and the classic symptom is a hook with a perfect test suite that misbehaves in the component that uses it, because the component re-renders in ways `renderHook` never triggered. ## Hint 2 `renderHook` earns its place for hooks whose entire observable surface is their return value and whose behaviour does not depend on how a component renders. `useLocalStorage`, `useDebounce`, `useMediaQuery`, `usePrevious`. The tell is that a host component for one of these would consist of nothing but `{JSON.stringify(value)}`, which is `result.current` with extra steps. ## Hint 3 The `rerender` assertion is the interesting one and worth generalising. A large class of hook bug is "captured on first render and never updated" — a key, a callback, a config object read once into a ref or a `useState` initialiser. The only way to catch it is to render with one set of arguments and then re-render with another, which is exactly what `rerender` is for and exactly what a single-render test cannot do.

## Exercise 7 — fix the component, not the test

Edit `ex7/solution.tsx`. **This mission asks you to fix the component**, and the
test is given to you.

The stub provides an `Accordion` whose only signal of open state is a class:


and a legacy test that reads it:


```tsx

expect(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /details/i })).toHaveAttribute("aria-expanded", "true");
expect(screen.getByRole("region", { name: /details/i })).toBeVisible();
await user.keyboard("{Enter}");

```

```tsx

```

- the trigger is a real `<button type="button">` carrying `aria-expanded` and
  `aria-controls`;
- the panel is a `role="region"` labelled by the trigger, rendered only while

- the `is-open` class may stay for styling, but nothing may depend on it;

  bullet right.

The gate runs the replacement test, then renames every CSS class in the
component and asserts the test still passes.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Notice which artefact is at fault. The test was reaching for a class name
because the class name was the only evidence of state that existed. The
component published its state to a stylesheet and to nobody else — not to a
screen reader, not to voice control, not to a test. That is the defect.

## Hint 2

The repair is the v3rc03 disclosure pattern verbatim: `aria-expanded` on the
trigger, `aria-controls` pointing at the panel, `role="region"` with
`aria-labelledby` back at the trigger, and `useId` to generate the two
identifiers.

## Hint 3

Getting the Enter key working requires nothing at all, provided the trigger is a
`<button>`. That is the whole argument for the platform element: keyboard
activation, the focus ring, the role and the tab stop arrive together. If you
find yourself adding an `onKeyDown` to handle Enter, the element underneath is
wrong.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The general principle: when a test is hard to write without reaching into
implementation, that is information about the component. The instinct to add a
test id, a class hook, or a `data-state` purely so the test can see something is
worth resisting for one minute while you ask whether a *user* can see it. Very
often they cannot, and the missing signal is the actual bug.

## Hint 2

The class-name test is fragile in a specific, expensive way. It passes when the
component is broken for keyboard users, and it fails when somebody runs a
CSS-modules migration that hashes the class names. So it is wrong in both
directions at once: no confidence, and high maintenance. Attribute assertions
against ARIA state are the opposite — they change only when the behaviour does.

## Hint 3

Worth noting where the line is, since `data-*` attributes appear in the design
systems sector as a legitimate styling hook. `data-state="open"` for styling is
fine. Asserting on `data-state` in a test is only acceptable when there is no
ARIA equivalent — and for open/closed there always is. Prefer the attribute that
also does a job for the user.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the warning as a report rather than a nuisance. It says: something updated
this component outside any interaction the test knew about. In a test that is
noise; in production the same code updates a component that no longer exists,
holds its entire closure alive, and issues requests for a screen the user has
left.

## Hint 2

Defect 1 is a missing cleanup. Every `setInterval` needs a matching
`clearInterval` returned from the effect, and the effect's dependency array is
what makes a changed `endpoint` tear the old interval down and start a new one:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(poll, intervalMs);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, [endpoint, intervalMs]);
```

## Hint 3

Defect 2 needs an alive flag, because a promise cannot be cancelled:

```tsx
let alive = true;
fetchStatus(endpoint).then((s) => { if (alive) setStatus(s); });
return () => { alive = false; };
```

A local variable inside the effect is better than a ref here — it is scoped to
this run of the effect, so a re-run gets its own flag and cannot be confused by
StrictMode's double invocation.

Defect 3 is solved by the same dependency array as defect 1: an effect that
depends on `endpoint` re-creates its closure when `endpoint` changes.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The three defects share a root cause worth naming: the effect started work whose
lifetime is longer than the effect's own. An interval outlives its effect unless
cleared. A promise outlives its effect unless guarded. A closure outlives its
render unless the effect re-runs. Every asynchronous thing an effect starts
needs an answer to "and what stops it".

## Hint 2

There is a subtlety about the alive flag worth knowing, since it looks like
cargo cult. React 18 removed the "cannot perform a React state update on an
unmounted component" warning, on the grounds that a stray `setState` on an
unmounted component is harmless in itself. That was true and widely
misunderstood: the *update* is harmless, the *leak that caused it* is not. The
guard is not there to silence a warning, it is there because the work should not
have been running.

## Hint 3

For an interval that must not drift and must survive prop changes, there is a
well-known refinement worth mentioning: keep the callback in a ref updated each
render, and give the effect only `[intervalMs]` as its dependency. The interval
then never restarts on a changed callback while still calling the latest one.
This exercise deliberately does not want that — a changed `endpoint` *should*
restart — but recognising which behaviour you want is the real skill.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a suite for the combobox

Edit `challenge/solution.tsx`. **Write the test file** for the
`aria-activedescendant` combobox from the accessibility sector. The stub
provides the component and a `mockOptions` helper that resolves options
asynchronously.

Write `describe("Combobox")` covering:

1. the input is found by `getByRole("combobox", { name: /city/i })` and starts
   with `aria-expanded="false"` and no listbox in the document;
2. typing opens the listbox and filters it — typing `os` leaves exactly the
   options whose labels contain `os`, asserted via `getAllByRole("option")`;
3. ArrowDown moves the active option: after two presses,
   `document.activeElement` is still the **input**, and the input's
   `aria-activedescendant` equals the second option's `id`;
4. the active option is the only one with `aria-selected="true"`;
5. Enter selects the active option, calls `onSelect` once with its id, sets the
   input's value to its label, and removes the listbox;
6. Escape closes without selecting;
7. typing again after selecting resets the active option to the first;
8. options that arrive asynchronously are awaited with `findAllByRole` and never
   with a sleep.

Constraints: `userEvent` throughout, `await` every call, no `fireEvent`, no
`container.querySelector`, no `setTimeout`.

Honest difficulty note: nothing here is a new API. The difficulty is that this
widget's notion of "focused option" is an attribute rather than
`document.activeElement`, so the obvious assertions are wrong — and asserting
the obvious thing would pass against a broken implementation that moved real
focus, which is the bug the pattern exists to prevent.

```
uv run dojo test react v3rc06_testing_like_users challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Test 3 is the one that decides whether this suite is worth anything. The naive
assertion is `expect(options[1]).toHaveFocus()` — and it is wrong, because in a
correct combobox DOM focus never leaves the input. Worse, it would *pass*
against an implementation that moved real focus into the list, which is the
broken behaviour: typing would stop working.

## Hint 2

So the assertion pair is:

```tsx
expect(screen.getByRole("combobox")).toHaveFocus();
expect(screen.getByRole("combobox"))
  .toHaveAttribute("aria-activedescendant", options[1].id);
```

Both halves matter. The first says focus did not move; the second says the
widget published which option is active.

## Hint 3

For the async options, `findAllByRole("option")` is the tool, and it should
appear once at the point where you first need the list. After that the list is
present and `getAllByRole` is correct — using `findAll` everywhere adds latency
and hides which assertion is the asynchronous one.

Keyboard input is `await user.keyboard("{ArrowDown}")`, `"{Enter}"`,
`"{Escape}"`. Note it goes to whatever currently has focus, which is why test 3
proving focus stayed on the input is load-bearing for tests 5 and 6.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach this by writing down, before any code, what a screen reader user
perceives at each step: an editable combobox, collapsed; then expanded with N
options; then "option 2 of 4, selected"; then the input containing the chosen
label. Every one of those is an assertion, and none of them mentions a class, a
`data-` attribute, or `document.activeElement` on an option. Your suite should
read like that list.

## Hint 2

Test 7 — the active option resetting when the filter changes — is the subtle
correctness requirement, and it is worth understanding why it is a *bug* and not
a preference. If the user has arrowed to option 4 and then types another
character, the filtered list is different; index 3 may not exist, or may be a
completely unrelated entry. A user pressing Enter would then select something
they never looked at. Resetting is the only safe behaviour.

## Hint 3

Consider what you are *not* asserting, and why that is deliberate. Do not assert
the number of renders, the internal `activeIndex` state, or the exact DOM
structure of the list. All three change freely without any user-visible
difference. The one structural thing worth pinning is that the option ids the
input points at are ids of elements that exist — because a dangling
`aria-activedescendant` is silently ignored by assistive technology, which is
precisely the failure that looks fine in a screenshot.
