exercises.hints: ## Hint 1 Do the audit before writing anything. Read each legacy test and ask: if this fails, what did the user lose? For the snapshot the answer is "unknown" — a snapshot fails on any change, so its failure carries no information. For the class assertions the answer is "nothing a user perceives". For the test id assertion, likewise. ## Hint 2 The three replacements are all "assert what the user perceives": ```tsx render(); expect(screen.getByText("£12.50")).toBeVisible(); expect(screen.getByText(/previous price/i)).toBeInTheDocument(); ``` For the strikethrough, the requirement is not the line through the text — that is decoration — it is that a non-sighted user learns this price is superseded. `` plus visually hidden text, or an `aria-label`, is the component's job; your test asserts the text exists. ## Hint 3 The zero case deserves a moment. `{amount && {format(amount)}}` renders a bare `0` for a free item — the classic trap — and a snapshot taken with a non-zero fixture never sees it. Write the test with `amount={0}` and assert the formatted string is present, which catches both the missing render and the stray zero.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is a discipline in this exercise beyond the code, and it is the one that
makes migrations like this survivable: never delete a test without stating what
it checked. Teams that delete a snapshot suite wholesale usually lose one or two
genuine requirements that nobody remembers until an incident. Enumerating first
turns "we deleted 400 assertions" into "we replaced three real checks and
discarded 397 that asserted nothing".

## Hint 2

Snapshots are not universally wrong, and the honest version of the argument is
about scope. A snapshot of a *small, stable, serialised value* — a reducer's
output, a formatted string, a generated query — is a reasonable regression
guard. A snapshot of a whole DOM subtree is not, because it fails on every
change including the intended ones, and the ritual response is to press `u`.
An assertion nobody reads is an assertion that does not exist.

## Hint 3

Notice how many of the missed requirements are accessibility requirements, and
that this is not a coincidence. Class-based tests describe appearance;
behaviour-based tests describe what is communicated. A strikethrough that is
only a strikethrough is invisible to a screen reader, and no test written
against `.price__old` could ever have discovered that — because the class was
present and the information was not.

lessons.title: V3·RC7 — Profiling and fixing real performance problems
lessons.summary: Everything you know about `memo` and `useMemo` is useless until you know which of six different problems you have. This sector is about measurement first: reading a Profiler trace, attributing a render to the prop that caused it, telling a slow render from a slow commit from an effect waterfall, and choosing the intervention the evidence supports.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC7 — Profiling and fixing real performance problems

You already know the tools. `memo` skips a render when props are shallow-equal.
`useMemo` caches a computation. `useCallback` stabilises a function's identity.
Moving state down and passing content as `children` are structural fixes that
cannot go stale. None of that is repeated here; assume it.

What this sector is about is the step before all of it, which is the step people
skip: finding out what is actually slow.

The reason it gets skipped is that guessing feels productive. Somebody says the
dashboard is sluggish, you open the file, you see a list rendering without
`memo`, and you add `memo`. It is a plausible fix, it takes four minutes, and
roughly a third of the time it changes nothing at all — because the problem was
three sequential fetches, or one component sorting fifty thousand rows during
render, or a third-party script blocking the main thread for 400ms, or a
committed DOM with 30,000 nodes.

Worse, memoisation is not free. A wrong dependency array produces a stale value,
which is a correctness bug that reproduces intermittently. Trading a speculative
performance gain for a real correctness risk is a bad trade, and it is the trade
you make every time you optimise without measuring.

## Concept — decide what slow means, then find where it goes

**"Slow" is at least six different problems.** Before touching code, decide
which one:

| symptom | metric | usual cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| typing lags | INP, input latency | too many renders per keystroke |
| a click takes a second | INP | one expensive render or commit |
| the page takes ages to appear | LCP, TTFB | waterfalls, bundle size |
| scrolling stutters | dropped frames | layout thrash, huge DOM (see v3rc04) |
| the tab gets slower over hours | memory | leaked subscriptions and timers |
| the fan spins | CPU | an uncancelled loop, a runaway effect |

They have different diagnostics and different fixes, and the most common mistake
in a performance investigation is applying the fix for one to the symptoms of
another.

**The React Profiler is two things.** The DevTools Profiler records a session
and shows you, per commit, which components rendered and how long each took —
the flamegraph for structure, the ranked chart for cost order. Turn on "Record
why each component rendered" in its settings; it turns "this rendered" into
"this rendered because prop `onSelect` changed", which is the whole
investigation for a large class of problem.

The `<Profiler>` component is the programmatic version, and it works in tests
and in production builds:

```tsx
<Profiler id="sidebar" onRender={(id, phase, actual, base, start, commit) => …}>
```

- `phase` is `"mount"`, `"update"` or `"nested-update"`;
- `actualDuration` is the time spent rendering this subtree **for this commit**,
  including memoised children that were skipped (as zero);
- `baseDuration` is the estimated time to render the whole subtree with no
  memoisation at all — so `actual` well below `base` means your memoisation is
  working;
- `startTime` and `commitTime` bracket the work.

What it excludes matters as much: it does not include browser layout, paint, or
the time your effects take. A commit that is fast in the Profiler and slow to
the user is a commit whose *DOM* was expensive, and that belongs in the
Performance panel.

**Development numbers are not real numbers.** A development build does extra
work per render, StrictMode invokes your components twice, and the Profiler
itself adds overhead. Relative comparisons — this is ten times that — survive.
Absolute numbers do not. Profile a production build when the number matters.

**`useTransition` and `useDeferredValue` are not debounces.** A debounce drops
work: it decides not to do anything until the user pauses, so the result is
late and intermediate states never render. A transition does all the work but
marks it interruptible, so React renders the urgent update — the keystroke —
immediately and works on the expensive one in the background, abandoning it if
another keystroke arrives. The user sees a responsive input *and* results as
soon as they are ready.

**The React Compiler changes the economics, not the skills.** It inserts
memoisation automatically where it can prove safety, which removes most manual
`useMemo` and `useCallback`. It does not find your waterfall, your 30,000-node
DOM, or your leaked interval. Measurement is the part that does not automate.

lessons.explanation:
# Reading — react/v3rc07_profiling_perf

## Notes

**Measure the user's complaint, not a proxy for it.** "Too many renders" is a
proxy. A component rendering two hundred times per second is fine if each render
costs 0.01ms; a component rendering once is a disaster if that render takes
900ms. Render *count* is a diagnostic; render *time* and interaction latency are
the outcomes.

**`actualDuration` versus `baseDuration` is the memoisation report.** If
`actual` is close to `base`, nothing is being skipped and your memoisation is
either absent or defeated. If `actual` is a small fraction of `base`, it is
working. Watching the ratio across a session tells you more than any single
number.

**Concurrent rendering complicates the numbers.** React may start rendering,
abandon it because something more urgent arrived, and start again.
`actualDuration` accumulates across those attempts within a commit, so a
transition that was interrupted twice reports the total work including the
discarded passes. That is honest — the CPU really was used — but it means a
number larger than the visible latency is not necessarily a bug.

**The Performance panel answers what the React Profiler cannot.** Long tasks
over 50ms, forced layout, paint cost, script evaluation, and — crucially — time
spent in code that is not React at all. A commit React reports as 2ms that is
followed by 300ms of style recalculation is a DOM problem, not a render problem,
and only one of the two tools can see it.

**`performance.mark` and `performance.measure`** put your own names into that
panel. They also feed `PerformanceObserver`, so the same instrumentation can
report from real users' sessions rather than only from your laptop.

**Effect waterfalls are latency, not CPU.** Three sequential 200ms requests take
600ms while using almost no processor time, so they are invisible in a
flamegraph and obvious in the network panel. The fix is structural: start
independent requests together.

**Windowing bounds the commit, not the render.** Rendering 10,000 elements is
expensive; committing 10,000 DOM nodes is worse, and keeping them is worse
still — every subsequent layout, style recalculation and accessibility-tree
update walks all of them. Windowing addresses all three by never creating them.

## ex1 — the numbers, and what they exclude

Wiring `<Profiler>` is four lines; the exercise is reading what comes out. The
`phase` distinction matters because a slow mount and a slow update have
different causes — a slow mount is usually the work of building, a slow update
usually means too much is re-rendering.

## ex2 — attribution

A render count tells you something is happening. The prop that changed tells you
what to fix. The hook compares the current props object against the previous one
key by key and reports the differences — which is exactly what DevTools' "why
did this render" does, and building it yourself makes the output unmysterious.

## ex3 — naming your own work

`performance.mark("x:start")`, then `performance.mark("x:end")`, then
`performance.measure("x", "x:start", "x:end")`. The measure appears in the
Performance panel's timings track and is readable via
`performance.getEntriesByName`. The discipline worth forming is marking the
*interaction*, from the event to the paint that answers it, rather than marking
a function.

## ex4 — two causes wearing one costume

A context whose value is a fresh object every render re-renders every consumer —
`useMemo` fixes that. A context that *legitimately* changes often re-renders
every consumer too, and no memo helps, because the value really did change. The
fix for the second is to split: put the rarely-changing half and the
frequently-changing half in separate contexts so a consumer subscribes only to
what it uses.

## ex5 — the waterfall

The tell is a network panel with three requests forming a staircase. The cause
is almost always that each fetch lives in a component that only mounts after its
parent's data arrived. Hoisting the requests to a component that knows all three
ids, and starting them with `Promise.all`, turns 600ms into 200ms without making
anything faster.

## ex6 — deferring

`useDeferredValue(value)` returns the previous value while React renders the new
one at low priority. So the input renders with every keystroke and the list lags
behind by however long it takes — visibly stale, never blocking. The gate proves
it by counting renders of each half separately.

## ex7 — transitioning

`startTransition` marks an update as interruptible, and `isPending` gives you
the pending state to show. The contrast with a debounce is the point: a debounce
would not have started rendering at all, so a user who pauses for exactly the
debounce interval waits the full render time on top. A transition has been
working the whole time.

## ex8 — windowing

Fixed row height makes the mathematics trivial: `startIndex =
floor(scrollTop / rowHeight)`, `visibleCount = ceil(viewportHeight / rowHeight)`,
plus overscan on both sides so a fast scroll does not show blank space. The
container's total height is `rowCount * rowHeight` so the scrollbar is honest.

## challenge — ordering matters

Two of the three problems look like "too many renders" in a naive trace. Fixing
the wrong one first makes the second harder to see, which is the realistic
experience of a performance investigation and the reason to measure between
every change rather than at the end.

## review1 — including "do nothing"

The trace where the right answer is to leave it alone is the most important one.
A component rendering forty times in a session at 0.2ms each is not a problem,
and memoising it adds a dependency array that can go stale in exchange for
nothing measurable.

## Further reading

- [react.dev — `<Profiler>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Profiler) — every argument to `onRender` and what it means.
- [react.dev — `useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue) — including the comparison with debouncing.
- [react.dev — `useTransition`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition) — interruptible updates and `isPending`.
- [web.dev — Interaction to Next Paint](https://web.dev/articles/inp) — what INP measures and why it replaced FID.
- [Chrome DevTools — Performance features reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/performance/reference) — long tasks, forced reflow, the timings track.
- [MDN — Performance API: `mark` and `measure`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Performance/measure) — User Timing, and reading it back.

# V3·RC7 — Profiling and fixing real performance problems

## Why this sector exists

Performance work has a failure mode that looks like success. Somebody reports
slowness, an engineer spends a day adding `memo` and `useCallback` across a
feature, the diff is large, the PR is approved, and the application is exactly
as slow as before — but now has forty dependency arrays that can go stale.

The discipline that avoids this is unglamorous: reproduce, measure, form a
hypothesis, change one thing, measure again. This sector is that loop, applied
to the six categories of React performance problem.

## Concepts

### Instrumenting with `<Profiler>`

```tsx
type Sample = {
  id: string;
  phase: "mount" | "update" | "nested-update";
  actual: number;
  base: number;
};

const samples: Sample[] = [];

<Profiler
  id="invoice-table"
  onRender={(id, phase, actualDuration, baseDuration) => {
    samples.push({ id, phase, actual: actualDuration, base: baseDuration });
  }}
>
  <InvoiceTable />
</Profiler>
```

`actual / base` is the memoisation report card. Near 1.0 means nothing is being
skipped. `onRender` fires for every commit that includes this subtree, which is
also how you count commits without instrumenting components individually.

### Attributing a render

```tsx
export function useWhyDidYouRender(name: string, props: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const previous = useRef<Record<string, unknown>>();
  useEffect(() => {
    if (previous.current) {
      const changed = Object.keys({ ...previous.current, ...props }).filter(
        (key) => !Object.is(previous.current![key], props[key])
      );
      if (changed.length) console.log(`[${name}] re-rendered because:`, changed);
    }
    previous.current = props;
  });
}
```

The output that matters is a key whose *value looks identical* but whose
identity changed — `onSelect`, `style`, `items`. That is a memoisation defeat,
and it is invisible without this.

### User Timing

```tsx
function onFilterChange(next: string) {
  performance.mark("filter:start");
  setFilter(next);
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    requestAnimationFrame(() => {
      performance.mark("filter:end");
      performance.measure("filter", "filter:start", "filter:end");
    });
  });
}
```

The double `requestAnimationFrame` is the idiom for "after the browser painted":
the first callback runs before paint, the second after. Measuring to paint
rather than to the end of your handler is what makes the number match what the
user experiences.

### Splitting a context

```tsx
// Before: one context, everything re-renders on every keystroke.
const AppContext = createContext<{ user: User; query: string; setQuery: Fn }>(…);

// After: two contexts, and consumers subscribe to what they use.
const UserContext = createContext<User>(…);       // changes on sign-in
const QueryContext = createContext<QueryApi>(…);  // changes on every keystroke
```

A consumer reading only `UserContext` no longer renders when the query changes.
No `memo` achieves this, because `memo` does not stop a context-driven render.

### Deferring versus transitioning versus debouncing

| | work starts | intermediate states | result latency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| debounce | after the pause | never rendered | pause + render |
| `useDeferredValue` | immediately, low priority | stale value shown | render |
| `useTransition` | immediately, interruptible | pending flag shown | render |

Use a debounce when the work has a *cost outside the browser* — a network
request, a database query. Use a transition or deferred value when the work is
rendering, because rendering can be interrupted and a request cannot.

### Windowing

```tsx
const start = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight) - overscan);
const end = Math.min(rowCount, Math.ceil((scrollTop + viewport) / rowHeight) + overscan);
```

with an outer container of height `rowCount * rowHeight` and the visible rows
absolutely positioned at `top: index * rowHeight`. Bounded DOM, honest
scrollbar.

## Common mistakes

- **Optimising without reproducing.** The fix cannot be validated.
- **Profiling a development build and quoting the numbers.** Inflated by
  StrictMode's double render and dev-only work.
- **Treating render count as the metric.** It is a diagnostic; latency is the
  metric.
- **Adding `memo` to a component whose props are objects built inline.** Never
  skips anything.
- **Memoising everything.** Dependency arrays are a maintenance and correctness
  cost paid for nothing measurable.
- **Debouncing a render.** Adds the pause to the latency instead of hiding it.
- **Fixing the context value's identity when the value genuinely changes.**
  `useMemo` cannot help; split the context.
- **Virtualising a 40-row list.** Adds scroll bugs, keyboard bugs and
  accessibility work for no gain.
- **Ignoring the commit.** A 30,000-node DOM is slow forever, not once.
- **Not measuring after the change.** Half of performance fixes do nothing, and
  you only find out by looking.

## The interview angle

"The app feels slow — how do you approach it?" is the question, and it is
testing process, not API knowledge. The answer that lands: reproduce it and get
specific about which interaction and which metric; profile with the React
Profiler for render cost and attribution, and the Performance panel for
everything React cannot see; classify the problem — too many renders, one
expensive render, an expensive commit, a waterfall, third-party script, a leak;
apply the smallest intervention that addresses the class you found; measure
again; and leave a regression guard behind.

Mentioning that memoisation trades a correctness risk for a speed gain, and that
you would therefore reach for structural fixes first, marks the answer as coming
from experience rather than a blog post.

## Check yourself

1. Name six distinct problems that all present as "the app is slow".
2. What do `actualDuration` and `baseDuration` mean, and what does their ratio
   tell you?
3. What does `<Profiler>` not measure?
4. Why are development-build timings unusable as absolute numbers?
5. What does "record why each component rendered" reveal that a render count
   does not?
6. Give two causes of a context re-rendering every consumer, and say which one
   `useMemo` fixes.
7. How do you recognise an effect waterfall, and why is it invisible in a
   flamegraph?
8. Contrast debouncing, `useDeferredValue` and `useTransition` on when work
   starts and what the user sees.
9. When is a debounce the right tool despite all that?
10. Write the two lines of arithmetic at the heart of a fixed-height windowed
    list.
11. Why is overscan necessary?
12. What does INP measure, and why did it replace FID?
13. What does the double `requestAnimationFrame` idiom achieve?
14. Give a case where the correct performance intervention is to do nothing.
15. What does the React Compiler remove from this workflow, and what does it
    leave?

# Long reading — measurement, scheduling, and the honest number

## How the React Profiler collects its data

React maintains a tree of fibers, one per component instance. In a **profiling
build** — the development build, and the production build when explicitly
enabled — each fiber carries timing fields, and React records a timestamp before
and after it calls your component function.

At commit time it walks the tree and produces, for each fiber, an
`actualDuration`: the summed time of work performed for this commit in that
subtree. A component skipped by `memo` or by a bail-out contributes zero, which
is exactly what makes the number useful — the difference between `actualDuration`
and `baseDuration` *is* the memoisation's value.

`baseDuration` is not measured for the current commit; it is an estimate from
the last time each component actually rendered, summed across the subtree. So it
answers "how long would this have taken with no optimisation at all", using the
most recent evidence available.

Enabling profiling in production costs a small amount of CPU and bundle size,
and is worth it for any application where performance is a feature. The bundler
alias is `react-dom/profiling`, and the numbers it produces are the only ones
that describe what users experience.

## What concurrent rendering does to the numbers

Before React 18, a render was a single synchronous pass: start it, finish it,
commit it. The timings were unambiguous.

Concurrent rendering can **interrupt** a low-priority render to handle a
high-priority one, and then start the low-priority work again from the
beginning. So a single visible update may involve three partial renders and one
complete one, and `actualDuration` accumulates all of them. A transition that
was interrupted twice reports substantially more time than the user waited.

This is honest — that CPU time really was spent — but it changes how you read a
trace. A large `actualDuration` on a transition is evidence of interruption,
which is evidence the scheduler was doing its job. The number to compare against
is not the elapsed wall-clock time of the interaction.

It also means **render counts are a weaker signal than they used to be**. React
may render a component twice for one update and discard one of them; StrictMode
deliberately double-invokes in development. Any test or diagnostic that asserts
an exact render count is asserting an implementation detail of the scheduler.

## Why INP replaced FID

**First Input Delay** measured only the gap between a user's first interaction
and the moment the browser could begin processing it. It ignored how long the
handler took, how long the resulting render took, and every interaction after
the first. A page could score well on FID and be unusable, because the
expensive part happened after the delay FID stopped counting.

**Interaction to Next Paint**, which became a Core Web Vital in March 2024,
measures the full duration from the user's input to the next frame that reflects
it, and reports approximately the worst interaction of the session. That is a
much harder target and a much more honest one: it is exactly the number a user
would report if they could.

For React applications, INP maps almost directly onto the work in this sector.
Input delay is the main thread being busy — long tasks, third-party scripts.
Processing time is your handler plus React's render. Presentation delay is
commit, style, layout and paint. A slow INP tells you which of the three to look
at, and the two profilers tell you where inside it.

The practical threshold is 200ms for a good score, and the practical technique
for getting there is that anything expensive triggered by an interaction should
either be interruptible — a transition — or not happen on the interaction at
all.

## The React Compiler, and what does not automate

The React Compiler analyses components and inserts memoisation where it can
prove the memoisation is safe: caching values, stabilising callbacks, and
skipping re-renders of children whose inputs did not change. On codebases that
follow the rules of React — no mutation of props or state, hooks called
unconditionally — it removes most of the manual `useMemo` and `useCallback` that
this ecosystem has accumulated.

That is a large change to one category of problem: too many renders, and renders
that redo work unnecessarily. It is no change at all to the other five. The
compiler cannot parallelise your three sequential fetches, cannot shrink a
30,000-node DOM, cannot clear a leaked interval, cannot make a third-party tag
manager stop blocking the main thread, and cannot decide that a feature should
paginate rather than render everything.

What it does raise is the value of understanding the model rather than the API.
When the compiler declines to optimise something, the reason is that your code
does something it cannot prove safe — and reading that diagnosis requires
knowing why the memoisation would have been unsound.

## Regression guards

A performance fix that nobody protects regresses within two quarters, because
the next feature adds one prop and defeats the memoisation, and nothing fails.

The cheap guard is a test that asserts a bound rather than a number: this
interaction commits fewer than *N* times; this list commits fewer than *N* DOM
nodes; this component's `actualDuration` stays under some multiple of its
`baseDuration`. Bounds are stable across machines in a way that millisecond
budgets are not, and they fail for the right reason — somebody reintroduced the
structural problem.

For latency itself, a real-user monitoring integration reporting INP by route is
worth more than any synthetic test, because it measures the devices your users
actually have rather than the laptop CI runs on.

## When not to optimise

The strongest argument against premature optimisation in React is not that it
wastes time. It is that the main tool has a correctness cost. A `useMemo` with a
missing dependency serves a stale value. A `useCallback` with a stale closure
calls yesterday's handler. Both produce bugs that reproduce intermittently and
resist reduction, and both were introduced to fix something nobody measured.

So the bar for optimising should be evidence: a user complaint, a metric, a
trace. In its absence, prefer the structural fixes, which cannot go stale —
render less, fetch in parallel, put less in the DOM, do work on the server.

And accept that some code is fast enough. A component that renders forty times
in a session at 0.2ms is eight milliseconds of your user's life. Spending an
afternoon and a dependency array on it is not a trade worth making, and being
able to say so with a number in hand is the skill this sector is really about.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`<Profiler>` is a real component from `react` and it renders nothing of its own
— it is a marker React notices when it walks the tree. Its `onRender` receives
six positional arguments: `id`, `phase`, `actualDuration`, `baseDuration`,
`startTime`, `commitTime`. Only the first four are needed here.

## Hint 2

The ratio is the exercise's actual content. `baseDuration` estimates the cost of
rendering the subtree with no memoisation at all; `actualDuration` is what it
really cost this commit, counting skipped components as zero. So:

```tsx
const savedRatio = baseDuration > 0 ? 1 - actualDuration / baseDuration : 0;
```

A number near zero means nothing was skipped, which usually means the
memoisation is absent or defeated.

## Hint 3

Guard `summarise` against an empty array before reaching for `Math.max` or a
reduce with no initial value — both fail in different, annoying ways. And note
`"nested-update"`: React reports it when a commit was caused by a state update
inside a layout effect from an earlier commit in the same tick, and for counting
purposes it belongs with updates.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Before writing it, be precise about what these numbers do *not* include, because
that boundary is where most misreadings happen. `<Profiler>` measures the time
React spent calling your components. It does not include the browser's style
recalculation, layout, or paint, and it does not include the time your effects
take. A commit that reports 2ms and feels like 300ms to the user is a DOM
problem, and this tool is blind to it.

## Hint 2

The mount-versus-update distinction is worth more than it looks. A slow mount is
usually the cost of *building* — creating elements, running initialisers, laying
out for the first time — and the fix is usually to build less: lazy loading,
windowing, deferring. A slow update usually means too much is re-rendering, and
the fix is scoping. Applying a mount fix to an update problem is a common wasted
afternoon.

## Hint 3

On the "not during render" requirement: it looks pedantic and it is protecting
you from a specific confusion. In development, StrictMode calls your component
function twice per render. Anything you push into an array from a render body
therefore appears twice, and you spend twenty minutes convinced a component
renders twice as often as it does. The profiler callback fires once per commit
regardless, which is why it is the right place.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The previous props have to survive between renders without causing one, which
is the definition of a ref. Store the props object in a ref, compare against it,
then overwrite it — and do all three in an effect, so the comparison happens
once per commit rather than once per render attempt.

## Hint 2

Comparing "key by key including added and removed" means iterating the union of
both key sets:

```tsx
const keys = new Set([...Object.keys(previous), ...Object.keys(next)]);
const changed = [...keys]
  .filter((key) => !Object.is(previous[key], next[key]))
  .map((key) => ({ key, from: previous[key], to: next[key] }));
```

`Object.is` rather than `===` so `NaN` compares equal to itself and does not
report as a change on every render.

## Hint 3

The `"other"` case is the one that carries real information. If the props are
identical and the component rendered anyway, the cause is state, a context it
consumes, or a parent render that `memo` would have blocked. Distinguishing that
from a prop change is what stops you adding `memo` to a component whose problem
is a context subscription — which `memo` cannot help with at all.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The output to look for is not a key whose value changed meaningfully — that is
just the component doing its job. It is a key whose value looks *identical* and
whose identity changed: `onSelect`, `style={{}}`, `items={[]}`, `config={{}}`.
Every one of those is a new object literal created during the parent's render,
and every one of them defeats `memo` completely and silently.

## Hint 2

This is a diagnostic, not production code, and the distinction matters for how
you write it. Real implementations of this idea — the `why-did-you-render`
package, DevTools' own "record why each component rendered" — are gated to
development and compiled out. Leaving a per-render object comparison in a
production hot path would be its own performance problem, which would be a
funny way to end a performance investigation.

## Hint 3

There is a limit worth knowing: this hook can tell you *that* `onSelect` changed
identity, not *where* it came from. The next step is always to look at the
parent, and the fix is one of three: wrap it in `useCallback`, hoist it out of
the component entirely if it closes over nothing, or restructure so the child
does not need it. The third is usually best and is the one people consider last.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The habit worth forming is measuring the *interaction*, not the function. It is
tempting to wrap your handler in marks and call the result the cost of
filtering. That number excludes React's render, the commit, style
recalculation, layout and paint — which is to say, it excludes most of what the
user waits for. Measuring from the event to the paint that answers it is the
only span that corresponds to a complaint.

## Hint 2

The reason to do this at all, when DevTools already profiles, is that these
measures survive outside your laptop. A `PerformanceObserver` for `"measure"`
entries can report them from real users' sessions, on real devices, over real
networks. Synthetic profiling tells you about your machine; user timing plus
real-user monitoring tells you about the ninety-fifth percentile of your
audience, which is the number that matters.

## Hint 3

There is a related platform feature worth knowing about: `performance.getEntries`
also exposes `"event"` and `"first-input"` entries, and the `PerformanceEventTiming`
entries are what INP is computed from. So for interaction latency specifically,
the browser is already measuring — your own marks are for the spans it cannot
name, like "the part of this interaction that is our filtering logic".

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There are genuinely two problems in the stub and only one of them is the famous
one. The famous one is a context value that is a new object every render, which
`useMemo` fixes. The other is that the value *legitimately changes* on every
keystroke, and no memo helps with that — the value really is different, so every
consumer really does need to be notified.

## Hint 2

The fix for the second is to stop having one value. Split the context by *rate
of change*:

- `user` and `theme` change on sign-in and on a theme toggle — rarely;
- `query` changes on every keystroke.

Three contexts, and a consumer subscribes only to what it reads.

## Hint 3

The setter deserves its own context, and this is the detail that makes the third
requirement pass. `setQuery` from `useState` is already stable, so a context
holding only the setter never changes value — meaning a component that dispatches
but does not read never re-renders. This split, value in one context and updater
in another, is worth recognising as a general pattern; it is what makes a
reducer-plus-context architecture scale.

Note also that `memo` cannot save you here, which is why the gate forbids it:
`memo` compares props, and a context-driven render is not caused by props.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach this by asking what a context subscription actually is. Every consumer
of a context is registered with that context's provider, and when the provider's
`value` changes by `Object.is`, React re-renders every one of them — regardless
of props, regardless of `memo`, regardless of whether they read the part that
changed. Context has no selector. That single fact explains every context
performance problem you will meet.

## Hint 2

The `useMemo`-on-the-value advice is correct and insufficient, and it is worth
knowing why it is so widely repeated. It fixes the case where a provider
re-renders for an unrelated reason and hands consumers a fresh but equivalent
object. It does nothing for the case where the value is genuinely new, which is
the case in any context holding frequently-changing state — and that is the case
people actually have.

## Hint 3

For the general shape of this problem, know the escape hatches beyond splitting.
A context holding a *store* rather than a value — a stable object with a
`subscribe` method, read through `useSyncExternalStore` — lets each consumer
select the slice it wants and re-render only when that slice changes. That is
what Zustand, Redux and Jotai all do underneath, and it is why they exist at all
given that context is built in.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write out the dependency graph before writing code. `fetchUser` depends on
nothing. `fetchPopular` depends on nothing. `fetchOrders` depends on
`fetchUser`. Two of those three can start at time zero, and the fact that they
did not is purely an artefact of where the code happened to live.

## Hint 2

The mechanical fix is to start the independent promises before awaiting either:

```tsx
const userPromise = api.fetchUser(accountId);
const popularPromise = api.fetchPopular();   // started, not awaited

const user = await userPromise;
const orders = await api.fetchOrders(user.id);
const popular = await popularPromise;        // long since resolved
```

Calling the function starts the work; `await` only decides when you look at the
result.

## Hint 3

For the degradation rule, `Promise.allSettled` or a `.catch(() => [])` on the
popular promise keeps one optional failure from rejecting the whole load. Attach
the catch at the point you create the promise, not at the `await` — an unhandled
rejection between those two moments is reported by Node and by the browser even
though you were going to handle it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason this pattern is so common is architectural rather than careless. Each
component fetches what it needs, which is good encapsulation, and each component
only mounts once its parent has data, which produces the staircase. Nobody wrote
a waterfall; the waterfall is emergent from a reasonable component structure.
That is why the fix is also structural: hoist the requests to a place that knows
about all of them.

## Hint 2

This is precisely the problem that route loaders and server components solve
generally. If the framework knows the route tree before rendering, it knows
every request the route will make and can start them together. Recognising the
shape here is what makes those features legible as a solution rather than as
architecture for its own sake.

## Hint 3

A waterfall is invisible in a React flamegraph, and knowing that saves an
afternoon. The CPU time is near zero — everything is waiting on the network — so
the Profiler shows a few fast commits with long gaps and nothing looks wrong.
The diagnostic tool is the network panel, where the staircase is unmistakable:
each request starting exactly when the previous one finished.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The problem is that one piece of state is driving two things with very different
costs. The input needs the newest value immediately or typing feels broken. The
list can be a few frames behind and nobody minds. `useDeferredValue` is the hook
that lets one state serve both.

## Hint 2

```tsx
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
const deferred = useDeferredValue(query);
const stale = query !== deferred;
```

`deferred` holds the previous value while React renders the new one at low
priority. Comparing the two is how you know you are showing stale results — that
comparison is the documented way to build a "pending" indication for this hook.

## Hint 3

`memo` on the list component is load-bearing and easy to leave out. Without it,
the list re-renders whenever `SearchScreen` re-renders, which is on every
keystroke — and the deferral achieves nothing, because the expensive component
runs anyway with the same deferred value. Check the props you pass it too: an
inline arrow or a fresh array defeats the memo entirely, which is the ex2
lesson arriving.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The comparison worth having clear is with a debounce, because they look like the
same feature. A debounce *does not start* the work until the user pauses, so
after a 300ms pause the user then waits the full render time — the two delays
add. `useDeferredValue` starts immediately at low priority, so by the time the
user pauses, the work is often already done and there is nothing left to wait
for.

## Hint 2

The other difference is what happens under sustained typing. A debounce shows
nothing new until the pause. A deferred value shows *something* — the previous
results — the whole time, which is far more comfortable to use because the
screen is never blank and the user can see their earlier query's results while
refining.

## Hint 3

Know when this is the wrong tool. `useDeferredValue` defers *rendering*, and
rendering is interruptible. It does nothing about work that is not rendering: a
network request, a database query, a write to storage. Those should be
debounced, because the cost is paid on a server or a disk and cannot be
abandoned halfway. Filtering ten thousand rows in memory is a render cost;
asking an API to filter them is not.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two updates happen on a click and they have completely different urgency. "Which
tab is selected" must be instant, because it is direct feedback on a click.
"What is in the panel" can lag, because the user is waiting for content anyway.
`useTransition` is the hook that lets you say which is which.

## Hint 2

```tsx
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
const [selected, setSelected] = useState(tabs[0].id);
const [panelId, setPanelId] = useState(tabs[0].id);

function pick(id: string) {
  setSelected(id);                                   // urgent
  startTransition(() => setPanelId(id));             // interruptible
}
```

Two pieces of state, because the urgent one and the deferred one genuinely
differ during the transition — that difference is the whole feature.

## Hint 3

The "outgoing panel remains visible" requirement falls out of this structure for
free: the panel renders from `panelId`, which has not changed yet, so the old
content is still on screen. That is deliberately better than a spinner —
replacing content with a loading state is a step backwards in information for
the user, and React's transitions are designed around not doing it.

Interruption is what caps `onPanelRender` at two: React abandons the in-progress
low-priority render when a new one arrives.

## Hint 1

For `WHY_NOT_DEBOUNCE`, reason it through concretely. With a 300ms debounce on
the tab click, a user who clicks once and waits gets: 300ms of nothing, then the
render. The tab does not even look selected during that time unless you split
the state anyway. And the render still takes exactly as long as it would have —
the debounce added latency and removed feedback, in exchange for saving work the
user was going to need regardless.

## Hint 2

The distinction that decides between the two tools: is the work abandonable? A
render is — React can throw away a partial render and nobody knows. A network
request is not: it has left the machine, the server is doing the work, and the
cost is paid whether you use the answer or not. So debounce things that leave
the process, and transition things that do not.

## Hint 3

`isPending` deserves care in how you use it. Showing a spinner during a
transition defeats the purpose — the point is that the old content stays
readable. The right treatments are subtle: `aria-busy`, a slight opacity change,
a progress bar at the top of the page. If the transition is long enough that
subtlety is not enough, that is a signal the panel should be split so part of it
can arrive sooner.

## Hint 1 Fixed row height makes the arithmetic trivial, which is why it is the version to build first: ```tsx const first = Math.floor(scrollTop / rowHeight); const visible = Math.ceil(height / rowHeight); ``` Everything else is clamping those into range and adding overscan. ## Hint 2 The spacer is what makes the scrollbar honest. Without an element of the full `items.length * rowHeight`, the container has only the height of the rendered rows and the scrollbar claims the list is twenty items long. Absolute positioning inside it puts each row where it belongs: ```tsx
{window.map((item, i) => (
))}
``` ## Hint 3 Read `scrollTop` from the event's `currentTarget` rather than from a ref, and store it in state. Reading it from a ref inside the handler is a layout read on every scroll event — the forced-synchronous-layout problem from v3rc04 — whereas the event already carries the element and the browser computed the value anyway. Overscan exists because scrolling and rendering are not synchronised: a fast flick can move the viewport past what has been rendered, producing visible blank space. Three rows either side is usually enough.

## Hint 1

Be clear about which cost windowing addresses, because it addresses three and
people usually name only one. Rendering 10,000 elements is expensive — that is
the one everybody says. Committing 10,000 DOM nodes is worse. And *keeping*
them is worst: every subsequent style recalculation, layout, and accessibility
tree update walks all of them, forever, whether or not anything changed. That
last one is why a huge DOM makes a page permanently sluggish rather than just
slow to load.

## Hint 2

`aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` are not decoration and are the single most
commonly omitted part of a virtualised list. Without them, assistive technology
reports the DOM it can see — "item 3 of 20" — and a user has no idea the list has
ten thousand entries or where they are in it. Windowing without them trades a
performance problem for an accessibility one.

## Hint 3

Know the limits of this implementation so you can recognise when to reach for a
library. Fixed row height is a large simplification; variable heights require
measuring rendered rows and maintaining an offset index, which is where
`@tanstack/virtual` and its peers earn their keep. Also: browser find-in-page
cannot find unrendered rows, Ctrl+End does not go to the true end, and printing
shows only the window. Each has a workaround and none is free.

## Hint 1

Take them one at a time and re-measure after each, which is the actual lesson.
Start with the context split from ex4: it is the cheapest change, it is
structural rather than memoisation, and it removes two of the three components
from the keystroke path entirely — which makes what remains much easier to
attribute.

## Hint 2

Then the table. Two separate things are needed and it is worth being explicit
about which does what. Windowing (ex8) bounds the *committed DOM*, which is what
makes scrolling and every subsequent layout cheap. `useDeferredValue` (ex6)
keeps the *input* responsive while the filtering renders. Neither substitutes
for the other: a windowed list still blocks the input if it re-renders
synchronously on every keystroke, and a deferred non-windowed list still commits
4,000 nodes.

## Hint 3

The waterfall (ex5) is last because it is independent of the other two and
invisible in the same traces. Its diagnostic is the network panel, not the
Profiler. Hoist the three fetches to one function, start the independent ones
together, and put a single `Suspense` boundary over the summary so it has one

## Hint 1

The ordering warning in the prompt is the real content of this exercise, so take
it seriously rather than treating it as flavour. If you window the table first,
typing gets noticeably faster — because the table was the biggest cost — and the
context problem becomes a small residual that looks like noise. You would ship
it, and the sidebar would keep re-rendering on every keystroke, and six months
later somebody puts something expensive in the sidebar.

## Hint 2

Notice which of the three fixes are structural and which are not. Splitting the
context and parallelising the fetches change the shape of the program and cannot
go stale. Windowing changes what is committed and cannot go stale. Only the
deferral involves React's scheduler, and even that has no dependency array.
There is not a single `useMemo` in the required solution, which is worth
noticing given what most people would have reached for first.

## Hint 3

Write down the measurement you would take for each problem before you fix it,
even though the gate does it for you. Problem 1: render counts per component
during a keystroke burst. Problem 2: committed DOM node count, and input latency
under sustained typing. Problem 3: the timestamps at which each request started.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read each trace as a story before writing any rules.

- A: forty commits sounds alarming and each costs 0.2ms. Eight milliseconds
  total. Nobody can perceive this.
- B: one commit, 780ms. One render is doing all of it — a transition lets the
  click respond while it happens.
- C: barely any CPU, and three requests forming a perfect staircase.
- D: 31,000 committed nodes and sixty scroll commits at 22ms each.

## Hint 2

The discriminating numbers, roughly:

- a very high `committedNodes` points at windowing regardless of commit counts;
- requests whose start times each follow the previous end point at
  parallelisation;
- a single commit dominating the total points at a transition;
- everything small points at doing nothing.

Order the checks so the most specific runs first — D has both many commits and
many nodes, and the node count is the real story.

## Hint 3

For trace A, the temptation is to memoise because forty renders "looks wrong".
Resist it and encode why in the `because` string: `baseVsActual` near 1 means
nothing is being skipped, and it does not matter, because 8.4ms across the whole
interaction is below anything a person can perceive. Adding `memo` here buys
nothing and costs a dependency array that can go stale.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The verdict of "do nothing" is the hardest one to give and the most valuable.
Performance work has a bias towards action — a PR with no diff is a hard sell,
and "I measured and it is fine" feels like a wasted afternoon. It is not: you
now have a number, the ticket can be closed, and nobody spends a week on it
later. Writing that down is the deliverable.

## Hint 2

Notice that the four traces need four different *instruments*, not just four
different fixes. A and B come from the React Profiler. C's story is entirely in
the network panel and is invisible in a flamegraph, because waiting uses no CPU.
D's node count comes from the DOM, and its per-commit cost is browser layout
that React does not measure at all. "Profile it" is not one action.

## Hint 3

A caution about the rules you are writing. Real traces are messier than these
four: two problems overlap, the numbers are noisy, and a component can be slow
because a library it uses is slow. Treat this heuristic as a triage step that
tells you which instrument to pick up next, not as a diagnosis. The step after
every verdict is always to confirm it by measuring the specific thing it
predicts.

lessons.title: V3·RC8 — Design systems, theming and styling strategies compared
lessons.summary: A design system is not a component library, it is a set of tokens and the discipline of never writing a value outside them. This sector covers token tiers, why CSS custom properties beat a theme object in context, the honest trade-offs between five styling strategies, and the flash of wrong theme that everyone ships once.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·RC8 — Design systems, theming and styling strategies compared

Two years into a product, somebody counts the colours. There are ninety-one.
Fourteen of them are within one hex digit of each other. Three are the brand
blue, typed slightly wrong on three different afternoons. Nobody can rebrand
this, nobody can add a dark mode to it, and the button component — which is
beautiful, documented and well-tested — is irrelevant to the problem, because
the colours are not in the button. They are in four hundred other files.

That is the observation this sector is built on: the components are the visible
part of a design system and the tokens are the load-bearing part. A team with
good tokens and mediocre components can fix the components. A team with good
components and no tokens has nothing.

The second thing this sector is about is the choice you make once and live with:
how styles get onto the page. There are five serious answers, the arguments
between them are heated, and most of the heat comes from people comparing them
on one axis. The honest comparison has six axes and produces different winners
depending on what you are building.

## Concept — tokens, custom properties, and the strategy grid

**Tokens come in three tiers**, and the tiers are the entire idea:

```
primitive   →   semantic          →   component
blue-600        color-accent          button-bg-primary
space-4         space-inline-md       card-padding
```

**Primitives** are the raw palette: every colour, every step of the spacing
scale, every font size. They are named after what they *are*.

**Semantics** are named after what they are *for*: `color-danger`,
`color-surface`, `color-text-muted`, `space-section-gap`. This tier is what
survives a rebrand — swap the primitive that `color-accent` points at and the
whole product changes. It is also the tier that makes dark mode possible, since
`color-surface` means "the background of a raised thing" in both themes and
resolves to different primitives.

**Component tokens** are optional and worth it once a component has several
callers who need to override one thing: `button-bg-primary` gives them a hook
that does not require knowing which semantic token you used.

Skipping the semantic tier is the common failure. `<Button color="blue-600">`
is a primitive at the call site, and it means the rebrand has to visit every
call site.

**CSS custom properties are the runtime theming mechanism**, and they beat a
JavaScript theme object in context on every axis that matters:

```css
:root { --color-surface: #fff; --color-text: #111; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --color-surface: #16181d; --color-text: #f2f3f5; }
```

They inherit, so scoping a theme to a subtree is one attribute on one element.
They resolve in the browser, so **changing a theme re-renders nothing** — a
context-based theme re-renders every consumer. They work in `::before`, in media
queries, in third-party CSS, and in stylesheets your JavaScript never sees. And
they survive server rendering and streaming with no hydration concerns, because
they are just CSS.

**The five strategies, honestly compared:**

| | runtime cost | SSR/streaming | dynamic theming | dead code | RSC |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CSS / CSS Modules | none | trivial | via custom properties | per-file | fine |
| Utility-first (Tailwind) | none | trivial | via custom properties | excellent | fine |
| Runtime CSS-in-JS | per-render | awkward | native | good | poor |
| Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS | none | trivial | via custom properties | good | fine |
| Inline styles | per-render | trivial | none | n/a | fine |

The row that changed the debate is the last column. Runtime CSS-in-JS needs to
run during render to produce class names, which server components cannot do, and
which conflicts with streaming because the styles for a chunk are only known
once that chunk renders. That is why the ecosystem moved toward compile-time
approaches, not because anyone decided the ergonomics were bad.

**Variants are the other half of a component's styling API.** Three mechanisms:
conditional class strings (unstructured, ends in bugs), `data-*` attributes
(`data-state="open"`, styled from CSS, also useful to tests and to assistive
technology when the attribute is an ARIA one), and a variant function — the
`cva` shape — that maps typed props to class strings with compound variants and
defaults.

**Dark mode has one famous bug.** If the theme is stored in `localStorage` and
applied by React, the server renders light, the browser paints light, and then
your JavaScript switches to dark. The user sees a white flash. The fix is a tiny
blocking script in `<head>` that sets the attribute before first paint, plus
`color-scheme` so the browser's own form controls and scrollbars match.

# Reading — react/v3rc08_design_systems_theming

## Notes

**A token is a decision with a name.** The value matters less than the fact that
it is referenced rather than retyped. Once `--space-4` exists and is used, the
decision to change it costs one line; once `16px` is typed in two hundred
places, it costs a week and a regression.

**Custom properties are inherited, which is the whole trick.** Setting
`--color-surface` on any element applies to everything inside it, so a themed
subtree is one attribute. They also cascade normally, which means a
component-level override is just a more specific rule, and they are *live*: the
browser recomputes anything referencing them when they change, with no
JavaScript involved.

**`var()` takes a fallback**: `var(--button-bg, var(--color-accent))` reads "the
component token if defined, otherwise the semantic one". That two-level lookup is
how you offer a component-level override hook without requiring every consumer
to set it.

**A context-based theme re-renders every consumer.** That is not a small
detail — it is the reason large applications with `styled-components` themes see
a full-tree re-render on a theme toggle. Custom properties re-render nothing at
all, because React is not involved.

**Utility-first and tokens are not opposed.** Tailwind's configuration *is* a
token file; its classes are a shorthand for referencing them. The reason it
dead-code-eliminates so well is that the class names are statically visible in
the source, which is also why dynamically constructed class names silently do
not work.

**Specificity is where design systems go to die.** A base rule at 0-1-0 and a
consumer override at 0-1-0 means the later one in the stylesheet wins, and the
order of stylesheets is a bundler detail. **Cascade layers** solve this
properly: `@layer base, components, overrides;` fixes the precedence regardless
of source order, and a rule in a later layer beats one in an earlier layer no
matter how specific either is.

**`color-scheme` is the property everyone forgets.** It tells the browser which
theme its own UI should use — form controls, scrollbars, the default canvas
colour. A dark page without it gets white scrollbars and light-mode date
pickers.

## ex1 — types as the enforcement mechanism

A union of literal scale keys makes an off-scale value a compile error, which is
enforcement the linter cannot provide and the code review will eventually miss.
The design question is whether to accept an escape hatch — and the answer is
usually yes, but named clearly enough that it shows up in a search.

## ex2 — the tier that survives

The test is the rebrand: change one primitive and see the product change. If you
have to edit more than the primitive file, the semantic tier has a hole in it,
and the hole is usually a component that reached past the semantics to a
primitive.

## ex3 — theming for free

The provider sets custom properties in a `style` object on a wrapping element.
Nesting works because CSS inheritance works. The measurable claim is that a
theme change re-renders nothing below the element whose attribute changed, which
is what the gate counts.

## ex4 — earning the comparison

Building the context version is the point. It works, it is ergonomic, it types
well — and every consumer re-renders on a theme change, and the values are
invisible to any CSS you did not write in JavaScript. Both facts are worth
having measured rather than believed.

## ex5 — variants as a function

`cva`'s shape is: a base class, a map of variant names to value-to-class maps,
a list of compound variants, and defaults. Deriving the props type from the
config is what makes an undefined variant a compile error, and it is the reason
to build it rather than hand-roll conditionals.

## ex6 — state where CSS can see it

`data-state="open"` is one attribute that CSS selects on, tests read, and — when
the state has an ARIA equivalent — assistive technology already knows about. The
`className` merge is the other half: a component that replaces the caller's
class is broken, and one that lets the caller's class replace its own is also
broken.

## ex7 — the flash

Three parts. A blocking script in `<head>` that reads storage and sets the
attribute before first paint. `useSyncExternalStore` over `matchMedia` for the
system preference — the same hook as the reduced-motion one. And `color-scheme`
so the browser's own chrome follows.

## ex8 — container queries

`@container` styles an element by its *container's* size rather than the
viewport's, which is what makes a card genuinely reusable in a sidebar and in a
main column. The layout primitives are the other half: `Stack` and `Cluster` own
spacing so that no component ever writes a margin.

## challenge — the override

The interesting requirement is that a caller's `className` can change the
padding without losing the base styles. That is a specificity problem, and the
clean answers are cascade layers or a merge utility that removes conflicting
utility classes.

## review1 — the migration

Geometry unchanged is what makes it a migration rather than a redesign, and it
means finding the nearest scale step for every hardcoded value and being honest
when there is not one.

## Further reading

- [MDN — Using CSS custom properties](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Using_CSS_custom_properties) — inheritance, `var()` fallbacks, scoping.
- [MDN — `color-scheme`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/color-scheme) — why your scrollbars are the wrong colour.
- [MDN — CSS container queries](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries) — `container-type`, `@container`, and the containment it requires.
- [MDN — `@layer`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@layer) — cascade layers, and ending specificity wars.
- [`cva` — Class Variance Authority](https://cva.style/docs) — the variant-function shape this sector builds.
- [web.dev — `prefers-color-scheme`](https://web.dev/articles/prefers-color-scheme) — including the flash and the blocking-script fix.
