# Long reading — how styles actually get onto the page

## What a custom property costs

A CSS custom property is a declaration like any other: it participates in the
cascade, it inherits, and its value is a token stream that is not parsed until
it is substituted. That last detail explains two behaviours people find strange.
`--size: 10px` and `--size: banana` are both valid declarations, because the
value is not interpreted until something does `var(--size)` — at which point an
invalid substitution makes the *whole declaration* invalid at computed-value
time, and the property falls back to its inherited or initial value rather than
to the previous rule.

Performance is generally excellent, with one caveat worth knowing. Changing a
custom property on an element invalidates style for that element and everything
inheriting it, and the browser recomputes anything referencing it. Setting a
property on `:root` therefore invalidates the entire document's style. For a
theme toggle, once, that is exactly right and imperceptible. For a value that
changes per animation frame — a mouse position, a scroll offset — a root-level
custom property means a whole-document style recalculation sixty times a second,
which is a real cost and one of the few places the technique bites. Register
such properties with `@property` and scope them as tightly as possible, or use a
transform instead.

Compared with a JavaScript theme object, the asymmetry is stark. A custom
property change is style invalidation with no JavaScript, no React render, and
no reconciliation. A context value change is a re-render of every consumer,
which for a themed design system is most of the tree.

## A short history, and what changed the argument

**Global CSS with a naming convention** — BEM, roughly 2012 — was the first
serious answer to the fact that CSS has one global namespace. It worked, it
required discipline, and it fell apart at scale because nothing enforced it.

**CSS Modules** (2015) made the enforcement mechanical: write ordinary CSS, get
hashed class names, import them as an object. Scoping solved, no runtime, and
the composition story was weak.

**CSS-in-JS** — styled-components and emotion, 2016 onward — put styles in the
component. Colocation, real scoping, props-driven styles, and theming through
context. It was a genuine advance in ergonomics, and it had costs people
discovered later: a runtime that serialises styles and injects them during
render, a bundle of several kilobytes, and server rendering that needed a
collection step to extract the styles for the HTML.

**Utility-first** — Tailwind, 2019 onward — went the other way: a fixed set of
classes generated from a configuration, composed at the markup level. The
configuration is a token file, the class names are statically analysable so
unused ones are removed, and there is no runtime at all. The complaint is the
markup, which is a real ergonomic cost and a matter of taste.

**Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS** — vanilla-extract, Linaria, Panda — kept the authoring
experience and moved the work to build time. You write TypeScript, the build
extracts CSS files and class names, and nothing ships. Dynamic values are
handled with custom properties, which is the thing that made this possible at
all.

**React Server Components** settled the argument for server-rendered
applications. A runtime CSS-in-JS library must execute during render to produce
class names and inject styles; server components render on the server without a
client runtime, and streaming means a chunk's styles are not known until it
renders. Both are structural incompatibilities, not bugs. Frameworks that adopted
RSC effectively required a compile-time approach, and the ecosystem moved.

## Runtime injection, hydration, and critical CSS

The reason runtime injection is awkward in server rendering deserves detail,
because it is the concrete version of the abstract argument.

When a runtime CSS-in-JS library renders on the server, it accumulates the
styles that were used and you serialise them into the HTML's `<head>`. That
requires rendering to a string, collecting, and then emitting — which is
incompatible with streaming, where you emit the head before you have rendered
the body. Workarounds exist, involving injecting `<style>` tags inline as chunks
arrive, and they produce styles that arrive after the markup they apply to,
which is a flash.

Hydration adds a second problem. The client runtime must arrive at the same
class names as the server did, from the same style objects, or the markup does
not match. Any non-determinism — an incrementing counter, a `Math.random`, a
different insertion order — is a hydration mismatch, and hydration mismatches
are among the most confusing errors in the framework.

None of this applies to a build-time approach, where the stylesheet is a static
file that can be linked in the head before any rendering happens, cached
independently, and preloaded.

## Cascade layers and the end of the specificity war

Every shared component library eventually meets the same problem: a consumer
wants to change one property, writes a class, and it does not win. They raise
the specificity. The library raises its own to protect its defaults. Somebody
writes `!important`. Somebody else writes `!important` on top of it.

The underlying issue is that specificity conflates two questions — how
specifically does this rule select, and how much authority does it have — and
`@layer` separates them:

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities, overrides;
```

A declaration in a later layer beats one in an earlier layer, regardless of
specificity. So a library ships its styles in a `components` layer, consumers
override in an `overrides` layer with a single class, and nobody needs to
understand specificity at all. Unlayered styles beat all layered styles, which
is a sensible default for application code that has not opted in.

This is the correct architecture for a design system, it is supported
everywhere, and it is still under-used because most codebases predate it.

## When not to build a design system

A design system is infrastructure, and infrastructure has a fixed cost that must
be amortised. The cost is not building the components; it is documenting them,
versioning them, reviewing contributions, running the deprecations, and being
available to answer questions. For one product with three engineers, that cost
is not repaid — the right thing is a tokens file, a handful of shared components
in the same repository, and no separate package.

The threshold where it starts to pay is genuinely multiple products or multiple
teams, where the alternative is the same button implemented four times with
four subtly different focus behaviours.

Even then, do the tokens first and the components second, and resist the urge to
build a component before its second call site exists. A design system's failure
mode is not too few components; it is a hundred components, sixty of which have
one consumer, all of which must be maintained forever, and none of which quite
does what the next team needs — at which point they stop using it, and you have
a maintenance burden with no users.

The other genuine argument for restraint: a design system encodes decisions, and
decisions age. A system that makes the wrong thing hard is valuable; one that
makes the *new* thing hard is a tax on every future product. Building the escape
hatches deliberately — a merged `className`, component-level tokens, a documented
way to opt out — is what keeps a system in use for a decade rather than being
forked in year three.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The enforcement mechanism is the type, not a runtime check. A union of literal
numbers — `0 | 1 | 2 | …` — makes `13` unassignable, and the editor says so
before the commit. A runtime `if (!SPACE[step]) console.warn(...)` catches it in
a browser somebody has to open, which in practice means never.

## Hint 2

Emit `var(--space-N)` rather than the literal value. The component then does not
know what `--space-4` is, which means a theme can change the whole spacing scale
without touching a single component — and the value resolves in CSS, so it works
inside media queries and pseudo-elements too.

## Hint 3

For "omit the property entirely", build the style object conditionally rather
than assigning `undefined`:

```tsx
const style: CSSProperties = {
  ...(padding !== undefined ? { padding: `var(--space-${padding})` } : null),
  ...(gap !== undefined ? { gap: `var(--space-${gap})`, display: "flex" } : null),
  ...unsafeStyle,
};
```

Spreading `null` contributes nothing, which is tidier than a chain of `if`s. And
note the position of `...unsafeStyle` — last, so it wins.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the escape hatch is for and why it is named the way it is. A
design system with no way out gets forked; a design system whose way out is
called `style` gets used for everything. `unsafeStyle` is a compromise: it works,
it is honest about what it is, and `grep -r unsafeStyle` on a Friday tells you
exactly where the system is failing people. Making a thing possible but visible
is often better than making it impossible.

## Hint 2

Notice which failure mode the type actually prevents. It is not the developer
who deliberately wants 13 pixels — they will use the escape hatch, and that is
fine and rare. It is the developer who wrote `padding={16}` meaning sixteen
pixels, and got scale step 16 or a runtime `undefined`. Conflating "index into a
scale" with "a pixel value" is the actual bug, and the union of small integers
makes it impossible to express.

## Hint 3

There is a design question here that different systems answer differently and
you should be able to argue: should the prop be the index (`padding={4}`) or the
name (`padding="md"`)? Indices sort and interpolate naturally and read poorly.
Names read well and make "one step tighter" impossible to express. Most mature
systems end up with names for semantic spacing and indices for the primitive
scale, which is the same two-tier idea as colours.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The tiers are named for different things and that is the entire idea.
`blue600` is named for what it *is*. `--color-accent` is named for what it is
*for*. A component that says `blue600` has hardcoded a decision; a component
that says `--color-accent` has referenced one.

## Hint 2

The dark theme redefines the same names with different primitives:

```ts
const lightTheme = { "--color-surface": primitives.slate50, "--color-text": primitives.slate900 };
const darkTheme  = { "--color-surface": primitives.slate900, "--color-text": primitives.slate50 };
```

`--color-surface` means "the background of a raised thing" in both. Nothing
downstream of it changes, which is why the semantic tier is what makes dark mode
possible at all.

## Hint 3

Typing both as `Record<SemanticToken, string>` is what stops the themes
drifting. Adding a token to the union without adding it to both objects is a
compile error, which is the failure this catches — a dark theme missing one key
does not break loudly, it just renders one element in the light theme's colour
and nobody notices for a month.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The test of a semantic tier is the rebrand, and it is worth actually performing
it mentally. Change `primitives.blue600`. Does the product change? If any part
of it does not, that part reached past the semantics — a component with
`color="blue-600"` at the call site, or a stylesheet with a hex literal. Those
are the holes, and they are invisible until the day you need them not to be.

## Hint 2

Deciding how many semantic tokens to have is a real design problem with a bad
failure mode on each side. Too few and every component needs an override, which
puts the decisions back in the components. Too many — a token per component per
state — and the tier stops meaning anything, because nobody can pick between
`--color-surface-raised-hover-subtle` and its four neighbours. The useful test is
whether you can explain a token's meaning in one short sentence.

## Hint 3

Note that this exercise puts the tokens in TypeScript objects rather than in a
`.css` file, and that is a deliberate choice with a trade. The object is typed,
greppable and importable by tests, which is genuinely useful. The cost is that
CSS files cannot import it, so a build step must emit the `:root` block — which
is exactly what vanilla-extract and Panda do, and why they exist.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Custom properties inherit. That single fact is the whole implementation: set
them on an element, and every descendant resolves `var(--color-surface)` to that
value — until some nearer ancestor sets it again, which is nesting, for free,
with no code.

## Hint 2

A React `style` object accepts custom properties directly, and the theme objects
from ex2 already have the right shape:

```tsx
<div data-theme={theme} style={{ ...(theme === "dark" ? darkTheme : lightTheme), colorScheme: theme }}>
```

TypeScript's `CSSProperties` does not officially include arbitrary `--*` keys, so
a cast is usually needed; write it once with a comment rather than fighting it
at every call site.

## Hint 3

The zero-re-render requirement is the claim being tested, and understanding why
it holds matters more than the code. `Panel` does not consume a context and does
not receive a theme prop, so React has no reason to render it. The colour change
happens entirely in CSS: the browser sees `--color-surface` change on an
ancestor and recomputes the styles of everything inheriting it. React is not
involved at all.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Contrast this with the mechanism you would reach for by default. A theme in
context means every themed component is a consumer, so a toggle re-renders the
whole tree. On a large application that is tens of milliseconds of pure waste
for a change the browser could have done in style recalculation alone — and it
is why theme toggles in some CSS-in-JS applications feel sluggish.

## Hint 2

There is a second, less obvious advantage worth internalising: CSS you did not
write can see these values. A stylesheet from a third-party component, a
`::before` pseudo-element, a `@media print` block, a `::selection` rule, a
scrollbar style — all of them can say `var(--color-accent)`. A JavaScript theme
object is invisible to every one of those, so anything you did not style in
JavaScript is unthemed.

## Hint 3

`colorScheme` is the small thing that separates a theme that looks finished from
one that does not. Without it, a dark page gets a white scrollbar, light-mode
date pickers, a white `<select>` dropdown and a white flash on overscroll. It is
one property, it belongs on the same element as the tokens, and it is the most
commonly missed line in this whole sector.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Build it properly rather than sabotaging it, or the comparison proves nothing.
Memoise the context value, wrap the panel in `memo`, do everything the
performance sector would tell you to. The point is that a correctly built
context theme still re-renders every consumer, because that is what a context
value change means.

## Hint 2

`memo` does not help here and understanding why is the exercise's core.
`memo` compares props. A context-driven render is not caused by props — the
consumer is subscribed to the provider, and when the value changes by
`Object.is`, React re-renders it regardless of what `memo` says. There is no
prop-level fix for a context change.

## Hint 3

For `TRADEOFFS`, the non-re-render costs are the more interesting ones and are
worth thinking through rather than looking up. Where can a JavaScript theme
object *not* reach? A `::before` pseudo-element. A `@media print` block. A
third-party stylesheet. `::selection`. A scrollbar. The browser's own form
controls. Anything you did not style from JavaScript is simply unthemed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

There is an intellectual honesty point in this exercise that is worth more than
the code. It is easy to assert that approach A beats approach B; it is much more
persuasive — to yourself as well as to a team — to build B properly and measure.
Doing this once means you can state the trade-off from evidence rather than from
a blog post, including the parts where B is genuinely better.

## Hint 2

And B *is* better at some things, which the exercise does not ask for but you
should be able to name. A JavaScript theme object is typed, so an unknown token
is a compile error rather than a `var()` that silently resolves to nothing. It
can hold non-CSS values — durations used by a spring animation, a breakpoint used
in a `matchMedia` call, a boolean the component branches on. Custom properties
can do none of that.

## Hint 3

The mature answer combines them, and knowing that stops this from being a
religious question. Author your tokens in TypeScript so they are typed and
importable, and *emit* them as custom properties so the runtime cost is zero and
CSS can see them. That is exactly what vanilla-extract and Panda do, and it is
the reason those tools exist rather than being an ergonomic preference.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start with the runtime and the types will follow. Resolve each variant to
`props?.[key] ?? defaults?.[key]`, look the class up in the map, collect. Then
walk the compound variants and include each whose every named key matches the
*resolved* values — not the passed ones, which is the distinction the third
example tests.

## Hint 2

The types are three mapped types over one generic:

```tsx
{ [K in keyof V]: keyof V[K] }
```

reads "for each variant name, the allowed values are the keys of its map".
Wrapping it in `Partial` makes each optional, and that one expression is reused
for the props, the defaults and the compound-variant matchers.

## Hint 3

The ordering requirement is load-bearing for a reason worth knowing: with plain
CSS classes at equal specificity, the *stylesheet* order decides the winner, not
the class-attribute order — so the order here is about predictability and
diffing rather than about cascade. It becomes genuinely load-bearing under a
utility-first setup with a merge utility, which resolves conflicts by position.

Watch `Object.keys` order for the variants: insertion order for string keys,
which is what makes "config key order" a stable contract.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compound variants are the feature that justifies this abstraction, so make sure
you see why they cannot be decomposed. "Ghost buttons at large size need a
thinner border" is a fact about the *combination*; there is no class you can put
on `ghost` or on `lg` alone that expresses it. Without compound variants you
write nested conditionals, and variant logic becomes unreadable at about the
third one.

## Hint 2

Note what this function does *not* do: it does not merge conflicting classes.
`button({ className: "p-8" })` on a base that already sets padding produces both
classes, and which wins is a cascade question. Utility-first setups therefore
pair a variant function with a merge utility that removes earlier conflicting
utilities. Knowing the two are separate concerns saves confusion about why one
of them "does not work".

## Hint 3

The type-level requirement is where most of the value is, and it is worth
appreciating what it buys. `button({ intent: "danger" })` when you never defined
a `danger` intent is caught in the editor. The hand-rolled alternative —
`` `btn--${intent}` `` — accepts anything, produces a class that matches no rule,
and renders an unstyled button that nobody notices until it is in production.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The requirement that the class attribute never changes is the whole exercise.
State lives in attributes; classes describe what the thing *is*, not what it is
currently doing. CSS selects on the attribute:

```css
.chip[data-selected="true"] { background: var(--color-accent); }
.chip[data-disabled] { opacity: 0.5; }
```

## Hint 2

`data-selected` present in both states and `data-disabled` present only when
true is a deliberate asymmetry, and it maps onto how you select them. A
two-state value wants `[data-selected="true"]` and `[data-selected="false"]`; a
flag wants a bare `[data-disabled]` presence check. In React, `undefined`
removes an attribute and `false` for a `data-*` attribute renders the string
`"false"` — so use `disabled || undefined` for the flag.

## Hint 3

For the merge: `cx("chip", className)` puts the base first and the caller's
classes after. Replacing the base with the caller's class breaks every chip that
passes one; letting the base come last means the caller can never win a
same-specificity conflict. Base first, caller last, is the convention — and the
reason a class-merge utility exists in utility-first setups is to also *remove*
the base classes the caller's are conflicting with.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice that this exercise quietly satisfies three constituencies with one
attribute. CSS gets a selector that does not depend on JavaScript building a
string. Tests get something stable to assert on. And where the state has an ARIA
equivalent — which `selected` and `disabled` both do — assistive technology gets
it too, which is why `aria-pressed` and `aria-disabled` are also required rather
than being replaced by the data attributes.

## Hint 2

The rule about which to prefer is worth stating precisely, because the testing
sector took a harder line. If an ARIA attribute expresses the state, use it and
style from it: `[aria-expanded="true"]` is a perfectly good CSS selector and it
does a job for the user as well. Reserve `data-*` for states with no accessible
meaning — hover intent, an animation phase, a layout mode.

## Hint 3

On `aria-disabled` versus `disabled`: this chip uses `aria-disabled`, which
keeps it focusable and announced as unavailable, and therefore requires the
handler to return early. That is the v3rc03 trade-off appearing again, and the
choice here is deliberate — a filter chip that a keyboard user cannot reach is a
filter they do not know exists.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The flash exists because of an ordering problem no React code can solve. The
server renders light. The browser parses the HTML and paints. *Then* the
JavaScript bundle loads, React hydrates, an effect reads `localStorage` and
switches to dark. The user has already seen a white page. Nothing you write in a
component runs early enough.

## Hint 2

So the fix is a script that runs before the first paint, which means an inline
`<script>` in `<head>` — deliberately blocking, and small enough that the cost is
nothing against the flash it prevents:

```js
try {
  var stored = localStorage.getItem("theme");
  var dark = stored === "dark" || (stored !== "light" &&
    matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches);
  document.documentElement.dataset.theme = dark ? "dark" : "light";
  document.documentElement.style.colorScheme = dark ? "dark" : "light";
} catch (e) {}
```

The try/catch is not defensive padding: `localStorage` *throws* on access in
some privacy configurations, and an exception here leaves the page unthemed.

## Hint 3

`useSystemTheme` is the reduced-motion hook from v3rc04 with a different query
string — subscribe to the `MediaQueryList`'s `change` event, snapshot
`.matches`, and return a fixed value for the server. The snapshot must be a
string or boolean, not an object, or `useSyncExternalStore` loops.

Resolving is one line: `choice === "system" ? system : choice`, which is why
storing the *choice* rather than the resolved value is important — storing
`"dark"` when the user chose `"system"` on a dark machine means their preference
stops following the system tomorrow morning.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Be clear about why there are three options rather than two. A binary toggle
forces the user to pick a theme and then ignores their operating system forever,
which is wrong for the many people who have their machine switch at sunset.
"System" is not a third theme, it is a statement about where the decision comes
from — and that is exactly why it must be what you persist.

## Hint 2

The blocking script is a rare, deliberate exception to everything you know about
render-blocking resources, and it is worth being able to defend. It is inline,
so there is no request. It is a few hundred bytes, so parse time is negligible.
And the thing it buys — never showing the user a page in the wrong theme — is
visible on every single load. Weigh it against a `<link>` to an external script,
which would be a network round trip and is not acceptable.

## Hint 3

There is a related detail this exercise does not require but that production
needs: the boot script sets the attribute, and then React hydrates markup that
was server-rendered *without* knowing the theme. If any server-rendered content
depends on the theme — an icon, a logo variant — you have a hydration mismatch.
The way out is to make the theme purely a CSS concern, so the markup is
identical in both themes and only the custom properties differ. Which is another
argument for ex3's approach over ex4's.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A media query asks about the viewport, which is the wrong question for a
component. The same card in a 300px sidebar and a 900px main column has the same
viewport and needs different layouts. `@container` asks about the nearest
containing element that declared itself a container, which is the question you
actually meant.

## Hint 2

Two parts, and forgetting the first is the classic failure:

```css
.card-host { container-type: inline-size; }
.card { display: grid; }
@container (min-width: 400px) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 120px 1fr; }
}
```

Without `container-type` on an ancestor, `@container` silently matches nothing —
no error, no warning, just a card that never switches layout.

## Hint 3

The reason for the extra `.card-host` wrapper is a real constraint:
`container-type: inline-size` applies containment, and an element cannot query
*itself*. The queried container must be an ancestor of the elements whose styles
depend on it, so a card that wants to restyle its own layout needs a host
element outside it.

For the primitives: `gap` rather than margins is the whole point. Margins
collapse, they leak outside the component, and the last child always needs a
special case. `gap` does none of those things.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The layout primitives are a bigger idea than they look. If every component sets
its own margins, spacing decisions are distributed across the entire codebase
and no two lists have the same rhythm. If `Stack` and `Cluster` own all spacing,
there are two places where spacing is decided and everything else composes them.
This is "one job per component" applied to whitespace.

## Hint 2

The specific rule worth adopting: **a component never sets its own outer
spacing**. Margin is a statement about the relationship between siblings, which
is the parent's business, not the child's. A component that sets `margin-bottom`
is making a decision on behalf of a layout it cannot see, and the symptom is the
`:last-child` rule that every stylesheet accumulates.

## Hint 3

Container queries change what a design system can promise. Before them, a
"responsive component" was a fiction — the component responded to the viewport
and therefore to an assumption about where it had been placed. With them, a card
is genuinely reusable, which means the design system can ship it without
documenting which columns it works in. That is a real change in what these
libraries can offer, and it is recent enough that most existing systems have not
taken advantage of it yet.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Deal with the override requirement first, because it constrains the CSS. The
naive setup has the component's rule and the caller's rule at the same
specificity, so whichever the bundler happens to emit last wins — a non-
deterministic outcome that appears to work locally and breaks in production.

## Hint 2

Cascade layers fix this properly:

```css
@layer components, overrides;

@layer components {
  .btn { padding: var(--button-padding, var(--space-2)); }
}
```

A rule in `overrides` beats one in `components` regardless of specificity or
source order. Document the layer names, because a consumer who does not know
them cannot use them.

## Hint 3

The two-level `var()` lookup is the second override path and is worth offering
alongside the first:

```css
background: var(--button-bg, var(--color-accent));
```

A consumer can now set `--button-bg` on any ancestor — inline, in a wrapper
class, in a themed scope — and change the button without writing a rule that
must win a cascade fight at all. That is usually the nicer of the two paths, and
between them they cover almost every real override.

For the stable width while loading, render the spinner in the same slot the
start content occupied rather than adding an element beside it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Notice how many separate mechanisms have to agree on this one component, and
that keeping them separate is the actual skill. Tokens decide values. The
variant function decides classes. Data attributes decide state. Cascade layers
decide precedence. Slots decide content. If any two of those start doing each
other's job — a variant that sets an inline colour, a state that changes a class
— the component becomes hard to override in exactly the way this challenge is
testing.

## Hint 2

The `loading` requirement has a real accessibility subtlety worth getting right
rather than approximating. `aria-busy` says "this region is updating".
`aria-disabled` says "you cannot activate this now". A loading button is both,
and it must be `aria-disabled` rather than `disabled` — because a `disabled`
button loses focus the instant it becomes disabled, which throws a keyboard user
back to the top of the document mid-submit. That is a genuinely bad experience
and a common bug.

## Hint 3

On stable width: a button that shrinks when its label is replaced by a spinner
causes a layout shift, which moves everything after it — and if the user is
mid-click on the next control, they click the wrong thing. Keeping the geometry
identical while loading is not polish; it is the difference between a form that
is safe to use quickly and one that is not.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the migration Edit `review1/solution.tsx`. Move a component onto the token system without changing what it looks like. The stub exports a `PriceCard` written before the design system existed: ```tsx

{name}

{blurb}

{price}
``` Migrate it. Requirements: - every colour becomes a semantic token reference — and the card must therefore work in dark mode, which it currently cannot; - every spacing value becomes a scale step; the rendered geometry must be **unchanged**, so find the nearest step and say so when there is not an exact one; - the `marginBottom: 24` must disappear entirely: outer spacing is the parent's job, so the component sets none and callers use `Stack`; - the internal margins become a `Stack` gap — note the original has three different internal gaps (8, 12, and the implicit 0), so decide and document what changes; - font sizes become type-scale tokens; - also export `const MIGRATION_NOTES: string[]` — one entry per value that could **not** be migrated exactly, saying what you chose and why. The gate renders old and new side by side in the light theme and compares computed `padding`, `border-radius` and font sizes within one pixel; then renders the new one in a dark scope and asserts its background and text colours changed while the old one's did not. ``` uv run dojo test react v3rc08_design_systems_theming review1 ```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Work value by value and classify each one before changing it. `#ffffff` is a
surface. `#0f172a` is body text. `#64748b` is muted text. `#2563eb` is the
accent. `#e2e8f0` is a border. Those five classifications are the migration —
once each value has a *meaning*, the token to use is obvious and dark mode
follows for free.

## Hint 2

For spacing, map to the nearest scale step and be honest in the notes when it is
not exact. With the scale `[0,4,8,12,16,24,32,48,64]`, `16` is step 4 exactly,
`8` is step 2, `12` is step 3, `24` is step 5. All four are exact here, which is
common — scales are usually designed around the values people were already
typing.

## Hint 3

The interesting decision is the internal gaps. The original has 8px after the
heading and 12px after the blurb, which a single `Stack gap` cannot reproduce.
Three honest options: two nested `Stack`s, one `Stack` at the more common value
with a documented change, or keep the two values and accept that this component
is not purely composed. Pick one, and write down what a reader will see differ —
that note is the deliverable, not an apology.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The reason "geometry unchanged" is a requirement rather than a nicety: it makes
this a migration that can be reviewed. A diff that changes both the
implementation and the appearance is impossible to check — the reviewer cannot
tell an intended change from a mistake. Holding the output fixed means the diff
is purely mechanical and any visual difference in review is a bug.

## Hint 2

Notice that the hardcoded colours were not merely untidy: they made dark mode
*impossible* for this component, and no amount of theming elsewhere would have
helped. That is the concrete cost of skipping tokens, and it is why the argument
is not about consistency for its own sake. A hex literal is a decision that
cannot be revisited without editing this file.

## Hint 3

`MIGRATION_NOTES` is worth taking seriously as a practice rather than as an
exercise artefact. Real migrations of this kind involve hundreds of components
